Contributors 
Victoria Beatrix Fendel  (D.Phil. Oxford, 2018) is a researcher in historical 
linguistics at the University of Oxford, editor of the Classics section of the Literary 
Encyclopaedia and the Registered Reports in Linguistics, and language leader for 
Ancient Greek in the PARSEME (UniDive COST) initiative (www.ancientgreekmwe.
com). Her research focusses on language contact and multi-word expressions in 
literary, epigraphic, and papyrological sources. She is the editor of Support-verb 
Constructions in the Corpora of Greek: Between Lexicon and Grammar? (Language 
Science Press, 2024) and the author of Giving Gifts and Doing Favours: Literary 
Classical Attic Greek Support-verb Constructions (Brill, 2025).
Roberto A. Díaz Hernández  (Ph.D. Tübingen, 2013) is a junior lecturer in 
Ancient History at the University of Jaén. He is initiator and developer of the 
Egyptian-UJaen Treebank in Universal Dependencies, the first morphosyntactic 
treebank of Egyptian, and language leader for Egyptian in the PARSEME 
(UniDive COST) initiative. His current research focusses on language change 
in Egyptian and computational linguistics applied to Egyptian. He has recently 
published Evidence of Diglossia and Bilingualism in Old Egyptian Mortuary 
Literature of the Middle Kingdom  (Harvard Egyptological Studies 27, 2025) and 
Old Egyptian Multiword Expressions Consisting of a Head Word and ib “Heart”  
(Lingua Aegyptia 32, 2024).
Roland Hoffmann (Ph.D. Mainz, 1994) is a researcher in Latin linguistics, editor 
of the series Studien zur lateinischen Linguistik  (Buske), and member of the 
Mainzer Linguisten-Zirkel. His research focusses on Latin morphosyntax with a 
specific focus on Latin support-verb constructions, the history of grammar , and 
language typology. He is the author of Lateinische Verbalperiphrasen vom Typ 
«amans sum» und »amatus fui»: Valenz und Grammatikalisierung  (Peter Lang, 
1997) and Lateinische Linguistik: Morphosyntax und Syntax in einzelsprachlicher 
und typologischer Perspektive (Helmut Buske, 2018). 
Matthew T. Ireland (MA Cambridge, 2014) is a computer scientist. He is 
managing director of the company AAI Robotics Ltd and a fellow of Sidney 
Sussex College, Cambridge. In industry, Matthew works on RF instrumentation

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languagesx 
and high-performance compute, specialising in the hardware/software 
interface and digital signal processing. Matthew also has interests in the digital 
humanities, having worked on the automated analysis of musical works and 
automated tagging of linguistic corpora. 
María Isabel Jiménez  (Ph.D. Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2016) is 
Assistant Professor at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. Her research 
explores the semantic, syntactic, and lexical properties of transitive verbs, with 
a particular focus on verb-noun collocations in Latin and in the early stages 
of the Romance languages, approached from the functional and typological 
perspectives. She is the co-editor of Las colocaciones en la lingüística teórica y 
aplicada: de las lenguas clásicas a las lenguas romances (SEEC-Escolar , 2022). Her 
recent publications include “A Constructional Approach to Causative Support 
Verbs in Spanish” (co-authored with Chantal Melis), published in Constructions 
in Spanish (John Benjamins, 2023). 
Lucía Madrigal Acero (MA Valladolid, 2022) is a predoctoral researcher at the 
Universidad Complutense de Madrid. Her dissertation focusses on support-verb 
constructions with ποιέω poieō in post-classical Greek. She has collaborated 
on the Dictionary of Latin Collocations  ( https://dicolat.iatext.ulpgc.es/) and 
the Dictionary of Ancient Greek Collocations  ( https://dicogra.iatext.ulpgc.es/), 
coordinated by Baños and Jiménez López. She is a research associate for the 
project Interacción del léxico y la sintaxis en griego antiguo y latín 2: Diccionario 
de Colocaciones Latinas (DiCoLat) y Diccionario de Colocaciones del Griego 
Antiguo (DiCoGrA) (PID2021-125076NB-C42) funded by the Spanish Ministry of 
Science, Innovation and Universities (PRE2022/102525). 
Michael F. McOsker  (Ph.D. Michigan, 2015) is a researcher in papyrology at 
University College London in the ‘Hexameters Beyond the Canon’ project. He 
was previously an Alexander-von-Humboldt postdoctoral research fellow at 
the University of Cologne. His scholarship has focussed on the Herculaneum 
papyri, Epicureanism, and Greek prose stylistics. He is the author of On the Good 
Poem According to Philodemus (Oxford University Press, 2021) and, with David 
Armstrong (UT-Austin), editor and first English translator of Philodemus’ On 
Anger (SBL Press, 2020). He is also a member of the papyrological team for the 
Vesuvius Challenge. 
Cressida Ryan (Ph.D. Nottingham, 2010) has been a Classics teacher and outreach 
officer , and New Testament Greek lecturer , at the universities of Cambridge, 
Nottingham, and Oxford. She works on Greek tragedy, the New Testament, and 
the relationship between these, particularly in the reception of both in the early 
modern period. Her monograph Translating the New Testament in Reformation 
Germany: Reception, Methods, Luther’s Latin and Greek Tragedy  will come out

with Amsterdam University Press in 2026. She has further research interests in 
Neo-Latin, Classics pedagogy, and disability, which also relate to her 2025 roles 
as disability advisor at the University of Oxford, and fellow at Wolfson College, 
Oxford. 
Nina Speransky (Ph.D. Free University of Berlin, 2023) is a researcher in Coptic 
and Vietnamese linguistics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Her research 
focusses on the interplay between morphology, syntax, and semantics. She is the 
author of Transitivity and Aspect in Sahidic Coptic: Studies in the Morphosyntax 
of Native and Greek-origin Verbs (Widmaier , 2022). 
Elena Squeri  (Ph.D. Università di Genova/Sorbonne Université, 2023) is a 
researcher in linguistics at Sapienza University of Rome and a member of the 
working group for the annotation of Ancient Greek in the PARSEME (UniDive 
COST) initiative. Her research focusses on the morphosyntax-semantics interface 
in the Ancient Greek verbal system, on the birth and development of sectorial 
languages, and on the establishment of grammatical and linguistic concepts in 
antiquity. She is the author of La specializzazione semantica nel sistema verbale 
del greco antico e nella lingua della ginecologia ippocratica (Schwabe, 2026).

1. Prologue: Challenges and 
opportunities with multi-word 
expressions in corpus languages
 Victoria Beatrix Fendel
Multi-word expressions are multi-lexemic units that function as a single unit 
from the part-of-speech perspective: for example, English instead of functions 
as a preposition, event structure as a noun, first and foremost as an adverb, and 
to go up  as a verb. This volume is specifically interested in  verbal multi-word 
expressions, such as to go up . These take on the role of predicate phrases in 
the syntax of a sentence, more specifically complex predicate phrases (Bowern 
2008: 165). 
Structurally speaking,  verbal multi-word expressions consist of a verbal 
component and another component. This other component can be (i) a 
 particle, e.g. in  phrasal verbs like to go up , (ii) a lexical noun, e.g. in  support-
verb constructions like to make a suggestion, (iii) an adjective, e.g. in  causative 
structures like to make obvious , (iv) an adverbial phrase, e.g. in  support-verb 
constructions like to hold in high esteem , and (v) a verb, e.g. in serial-verb 
constructions like to come see (see Fendel 2025a: 25). The contributions to this 
volume (see especially Chapter 3 and Chapter 9) explore what sub-categories 
of  verbal multi-word expressions exist in the languages under investigation 
as well as how sub-categories that seem to be near-universally available are 
realised in language-specific ways (Savary et al. 2018: 96; Hoffmann 2023: 29–31; 
Haspelmath 2010).
Opinions are divided as to whether the components can appear as multiple 
orthographic words, i.e. separated by whitespaces (for example, Nagy et al. 
2013: 329 from a computational perspective), or whether the components 
can appear as one orthographic word (following  univerbation), as in French 
maintenir “to maintain” from Latin manu tenere (Lehmann 2020: 217), German 
zustandebringen “to achieve” from *zu Stande bringen (Peust 1975: 123), or Latin

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages2 
animadvertere from animum advertere  “to pay attention” (Rosén 2020: 266–
267). The former perspective is synchronically focussed and raises the issue of 
structural discontinuity, for example, to make the question obvious  (Savary et 
al. 2018: 123; Fendel 2024a), whereas the latter perspective adopts a  diachronic 
view. The contributions to this volume take various perspectives on this issue 
(see especially Chapter 5 and Chapter 7). 
Semantically speaking,  verbal multi-word expressions can be  compositional 
or non-  compositional, for example, to take heart  as compared to to make a 
suggestion, and transparent or non-transparent, for example, to spill the beans  
as compared to to kick the bucket  (Sheinfux et al. 2019: 42 and 50; Mel’čuk 
2023: 29–32 and 53; Nunberg et al. 1994). Opinions are divided over whether 
 compositionality is a binary choice (Mel’čuk 2023: 29–32) or operates on a 
continuum (for example, Langer 2004; 2005). Opinions are also divided over 
whether transparency is a “psychological property” (Mel’čuk 2023: 53) or part 
of the semantics (Sheinfux et al. 2019: 42).  Verbal multi-word expressions 
are ambiguous, i.e. between a multi-word-expression and a structurally and 
semantically  compositional reading (Fendel 2025b), and variable, i.e. lexically, 
morphologically, morphosyntactically, syntactically, semantically, pragmatically, 
and the list goes on (for example, Savary et al 2018: 123; Sag et al. 2002: 3). The 
contributions of to this volume explore both the exploitation of such ambiguity 
for context-specific purposes (see especially Chapter 4 ) and the  diachronic 
potential such variability proffers (see especially Chapter 6 and Chapter 10).  
The language varieties which this volume focusses on are only attested in 
written form at this point in time. They are not “dead”—for example,  Coptic 
is still used as the language of the  Coptic orthodox church (see Ayad 2024)—
or “ancient”—for example, Greek and Spanish boast continuous traditions 
of  diachronic development (for example, Horrocks 2014) –, they are simply 
different. Their native speakers are their corpora of texts (Fleischman 2000: 
34). This is why the term “corpus language” has been chosen here. In order to 
carry out tests for , for example, grammaticality or idiomaticity, we need to ask 
them—in the way that we can. We cannot invite them to attend an interview 
session at a laboratory, but we can observe them, interact with them, and learn 
from them (see for example, Vereeck et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2023). We have to 
adapt to the sampling population we can access, even if it is unbalanced and 
non-experimental (yet see Tagliamonte 2025: 153). We have to adapt the way 
in which we operationalise concepts (cf. Whyatt et al. 2025: 30; Ahrens and 
Janikowski 2025: 189), ask questions (Halliday 1992: 64; Viti 2024: 20–27) and 
analyse the data (see also Tagliamonte 2025: 110). This is what this volume is 
about. 
It has three main aims, which all the contributions subscribe to and work 
towards achieving:

1. Prologue  3
1. enhancing the  visibility of datasets, both physical and virtual ones, by 
showcasing the methodologies for doing so (see especially Part I); 
2. promoting the interoperability of methodological approaches, through 
transparent definitions and guidelines (see especially Part II); and 
3. furthering the replicability of analyses, through empirically founded 
approaches with interoperable datasets (see especially Part III). 
While the chapters, especially in Part III of the volume, offer interpretative 
approaches building on the analysis proffered, the volume itself does not focus 
on the interpretation stage (i.e. the laws of logic, critical thought, hot cognitive 
skills, etc.) but on the data-focussed pre-interpretation stages. For this reason, 
each chapter comes with an open-access dataset (and in some cases a codebase) 
so as to enable the reader not only to replicate the results presented but also to 
further build on the datasets developed to advance the field.   
We cover approaches ranging from computational ones (for example, virtual 
unrolling of  papyri, treebanking of textual corpora, and building  Sketch Engine 
corpora), through linguistic-typological ones (for example, the definition of verb-
 particle constructions in classical Greek and  light-verb constructions in  Coptic), 
sociolinguistic ones (for example,  politeness and in-group markers in (post-)
classical Greek), philological ones (for example, terminological choices amongst 
the  Epicureans of  Herculaneum and translation-language phenomena in the 
 Septuagint and  Vulgate), to  narratological ones (for example, the eschatological 
consequences of the framing of scenes in the  New Testament). Typologically 
speaking, Indo-European, i.e. (post-)classical Greek, (post-)  classical Latin, and 
 medieval Spanish, and Afro-Asiatic languages, i.e. Egyptian (  Old Egyptian and 
 Coptic) and biblical  Hebrew, are dealt with. The contributions cover a time 
period of four millennia starting with the texts by  Unas and  Teti from Old-
Kingdom Egypt (third millennium BCE) and finishing with texts from medieval 
Spain (fifteenth century CE). Geographically, our texts come from the area 
around the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent areas. 
We look at very different kinds of corpora. The biblical texts (Old and New 
Testaments,  Septuagint and  Vulgate) and the Homeric epics (Iliad and Odyssey) 
are corpora that exist in a multitude of manuscripts across time (see Ehrman 
2006; West 1973, 2015) and have been well digitised and made accessible and 
searchable in virtual settings (for example, the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae , 
the Perseus Digital Library , the Latin Library, the Thesaurus Linguae Latinae ). 
Conversely, the medical corpora associated with Hippocrates and Galen were 
long confined to the in-group of medical practitioners (Doody et al. 2012) and the 
 Herculaneum  papyri slept a Rapunzel sleep under the ashes of Mount Vesuvius 
and are still relatively confined to an in-group of researchers. These scenarios 
have brought with them less  visibility and accessibility of relevant texts in virtual

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages4 
settings too. Other corpora are prominent in specialised disciplines, for example, 
the  Pyramid Texts are one of the canonical texts which every Egyptology student 
will read, and the Byzantine vitae will be familiar to historians of Byzantium or 
theologians. In an effort to open up corpora that have not enjoyed wide-spread 
interest,  visibility, and accessibility, throughout the volume references to textual 
sources have been given in unabbreviated form, i.e. the discipline-internal 
abbreviations have been resolved. 
The chapters in Part I all revolve around underexplored datasets. Chapter 2 
(by McOsker) introduces the corpus of the so-called  Herculaneum  papyri, named 
after the place where they were discovered (accessible via the Thesaurus Linguae 
Graecae and  papyri.info). The  papyri were buried under the ashes of Mount 
Vesuvius in the first century CE, which carbonised them such that they survived, 
yet in rolled up form. Technological advancements make it possible nowadays 
to virtually unroll them without destroying the material. The texts relate to a 
school of  Epicurean philosophers active between the fourth and first centuries 
BCE. The chapter illustrates the use of multi-word expressions by the in-group 
in key terminological items. Chapter 3 (by Fendel and Ireland) introduces the 
corpora of medical writings associated with the physicians Hippocrates and 
Galen, dating from the fifth century BCE to the second century CE, along with 
the historiographical corpora by Thucydides and Xenophon (fifth and fourth 
centuries BCE) and Polybius (second to first centuries BCE) (datasets: https://doi.
org/10.5281/zenodo.18440945; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18441284; https://
doi.org/10.5287/ora-jbavbzvz0; codebase: https://github.com/MatthewIreland/
xml_lemmatiser_tagger#). While the medical corpora have long been confined 
to the in-group of medical practitioners, the historiographical corpora became 
canonical already in antiquity. This has impacted on their  visibility, including 
in digital settings. The chapter introduces the  Sketch Engine corpora built for 
both sets of corpora and illustrates their usefulness in the study of subject- 
and group-specific multi-word expressions. Chapter 4  (by Díaz Hernández) 
introduces the treebank built for the so-called  Pyramid Texts related to kings 
 Unas and  Teti (third millennium BCE) (UniDive release 2.17, November 2025 
https://universaldependencies.org/). The  Pyramid Texts are utterances that were 
found on the walls of the burial chambers in the kings’ tombs, the pyramids. 
The chapter illustrates how the Universal Annotation Guidelines for Multi-
Word Expressions developed in the  PARSEME initiative, originally for spoken 
languages yet adapted for pre-modern Greek too, can be applied to the  Old 
Egyptian  Pyramid Texts. Furthermore, this focus on multi-word expressions in 
a treebank addresses the frequently observed issue of multi-word expressions 
being a “  pain in the neck for N[atural]L[anguage]P[rocessing]” (Sag et al. 
2002; Fendel 2024b). Together , the chapters illustrate three approaches to 
underexplored datasets in order to make them accessible and visible in virtual

1. Prologue  5
settings as well as searchable and interoperable. 
The chapters in Part II all revolve around methodological novelties. Chapter 
5 (by Squeri) homes in on the issue of whether multi-lexemic units need 
to consist of multiple orthographic words, like  phrasal verbs, or can form 
one orthographic word, like  preverb-verb combinations in classical Greek 
(dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18340160). The history of  preverb-verb 
combinations in Greek is complicated, not least due to the question of tmesis, 
i.e. the appearance of  preverb and verb as two separate units in archaic Greek 
(eighth to sixth centuries BCE) in particular (for example, Bertrand 2014), and 
the absence of such tmesis in the Mycenaean tablets dating to the pre-archaic 
period (ca. fifteenth to twelfth centuries BCE) (for example, McConnell 2025: 130 
on the Horrocks vs. Morpurgo-Davies debate). Squeri links this age-old question 
to the category of verb-  particle constructions as defined in the Universal 
Annotation Guidelines for Multi-Word Expressions developed in the  PARSEME 
initiative, thus querying the language-specific realisation of a comparative 
concept. Chapter 6 (by Madrigal Acero) provides a detailed study of the semantic 
and pragmatic polyfunctionality of one specific  verbal multi-word expression, 
ἀγάπην ποιέω agapēn poieō  “love, favour” and “to do”, in fourth- to sixth-
century hagiographical texts (dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17491996). 
Not only does she illustrate the semantic and pragmatic range of this multi-
word expression at any one point in time but also the semantic and pragmatic 
evolution of this multi-lexemic unit over time, without it  univerbating. Chapter 
7 (by Speransky) also takes up the issue of whether multi-lexemic units form 
orthographic words or not, but in a language where the research tradition on 
how to define  wordhood is fundamentally complicated, that is  Coptic (see for 
example, Miyagawa 2024). Her focus is on  light-verb constructions, that is, 
combinations of a verb and a noun, in  Coptic literary (including biblical) texts. 
The verb in such phrases usually appears in the so-called construct state, that is 
a phonetically reduced form (dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20330827). 
The noun can be prototypically  eventive or reconceptualised as such and 
 cranberry items appear , for example, ⲁϩⲟⲙ ahom in ϥⲓ-ⲁϩⲟⲙ fi-ahom ( Bohairic 
dialect) “to utter a sigh”. Moreover , morphological innovations (in so-called 
stative forms) seem to indicate that  light-verb constructions form a phonological 
word in  Coptic, for example, ⲕⲁ-ⲣⲱ= ka-rô= “to keep silence” with the stative 
ⲕⲁⲣⲁⲉⲓⲧ karaeit  formed in analogy to pairs such as ϩⲕⲟ hko “to be hungry” 
and ϩⲕⲁⲉⲓⲧ hkaeit. Together , the chapters illustrate the complexity of defining 
 verbal multi-word expressions, the language- and variety-specific realisation 
of comparative concepts, and the synchronic ambiguity and  diachronic 
developmental potential inherent in  verbal multi-word expressions of different 
types and across typologically unrelated languages. 
The chapters in Part III all revolve around critical analysis. Chapter 8  (by

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages6 
Ryan) takes an eschatological perspective on the use of combinations of a 
 participle with the verb “to be” in the  imperfect tense in scene-setting in the 
Greek  New Testament (first and second centuries CE) (dataset: https://doi.
org/10.5281/zenodo.18510208). Structures like this have often been dealt with 
under the label “ periphrastic” (for example, Bentein 2016) and the being verb has 
variously been questioned as a support verb, given its morphosyntax (Jiménez 
López 2021; Fendel 2026). Ryan touches upon her experimenting with an  AI tool 
(Gemini) in order to draw out relevant instances. However , neither accuracy nor 
replicability lived up to the bar of this volume (for example, Thomas et al. 2026). 
Ryan’s chapter shows how multi-word expressions are used at  narratological 
turning points in order to guide the reader’s attention. They are carefully 
chosen devices, selected for their semantico-pragmatic properties. Chapter 9 (by 
Hoffmann) takes a comparative perspective on the Greek and  Hebrew texts of 
the  Old Testament and the Greek and Latin texts of the  New Testament with a 
focus on  causative  support-verb constructions, such as German Angst machen 
“to scare” (dataset: https://doi.org/10.5287/ora-0zvrz5vnk). The chapter devises 
both a lexeme-based extraction method for relevant instances (i.e. focussing on 
structures with “to give” and “to make” as well as nouns referring to fearing) and 
a translation-focussed extraction method (i.e. focussing on German  causative 
constructions in the translation). The chapter is specifically interested in the 
incidence of multi-word expressions as compared to simplex verbs (for example, 
the  Hebrew Hif’il stem of and the Greek -ίζω -izō suffix on verbal roots) and how 
language-specific differences are dealt with in the translation setting (cf. Riel 
2017; Pontani 2023; Gray 2025). Chapter 10 (by Jiménez) takes its starting point 
from conceptual  metaphors. It traces the development of conceptual  metaphors 
that appear with the lexeme  dolor “ pain”, when used as a predicative noun in 
 support-verb constructions, through almost two millennia from  archaic Latin to 
 medieval Spanish (second century BCE to fifteenth century CE) (dataset: https://
doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19055091). It shows, on the one hand, the temporal 
depth of multi-word expressions with  dolor “ pain” and, on the other hand, their 
 diachronic variability including both continuities and changes over the two 
millennia of interest, with a specific focus on the semantico-pragmatic function of 
intensification. Together , the chapters illustrate the functioning of  verbal multi-
word expressions beyond the lexico-grammar and specifically in the semantico-
pragmatic sphere and thus illustrate their variability and polyfunctionality.  
Each chapter is accompanied by an abstract in English and a second, 
pragmatically preferred language by the author . As will become evident in 
the chapters of this volume, several corpora, methodologies, and analytic 
approaches seem to be attached to discourses in one modern language or the 
other . In the interest of enhancing  visibility across these research traditions, we 
have opted for multilingual abstracts.

1. Introduction
In this chapter , I introduce the  Herculaneum  papyri, a unique collection of 
primarily  Epicurean texts which were carbonised in the 79 CE eruption of Mt. 
Vesuvius. I explain how they might be useful as a dataset for the study of multi-
word expressions in Ancient Greek and describe their editorial situation and 
most common publication venues. But first, a few words about  Epicureanism, 
the  Herculaneum  papyri, and the history of scholarship on them.
I am a classicist, more specifically, a papyrologist and historian of ancient 
 philosophy, rather than a linguist; I approach these texts with an eye towards 
establishing their texts and meanings. They have never been part of the canon, 
and scholarship on them rarely circulates outside practitioners. Accordingly, 
this chapter is exploratory and illustrative and more than a little tentative: I 
hope to make an interesting, coherent group of texts, albeit perhaps a small, 
strange, and difficult one, more accessible to scholars beyond those who studied 
them in the past and to give one example of what might be interesting in them, 
with regard to the study of multi-word expressions. 
2.  Epicureanism
 Epicurus built his  philosophy on foundations laid by the shadowy Leucippus and 
the better-understood Democritus. In short, the  Epicureans argued that the only 
things to exist are atoms, the void, and combinations of these. There are no non-

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages14 
physical worlds or entities somewhere out there: the  Epicureans were rather 
strict materialists. This had wide-ranging metaphysical and ethical implications: 
the soul exists, but only temporarily, and it dissolves upon death. Consequently, 
it cannot be rewarded or tortured in an afterlife. The gods exist, but they live 
in isolated communities in the metakosmia, the spaces between worlds, and 
do not care about humans one way or the other . Their perfect happiness and 
peaceful lives are the goal of  Epicurean  philosophy, but  Epicureans engaged in 
conventional piety without believing that their prayers and sacrifices mattered 
to gods.
The non-existence of divine rewards and punishments frees the  Epicurean 
to pursue a life of pleasure and the kind of consistent happiness that they 
called  ataraxia—literally “freedom from disturbance”. The  Epicureans were 
hedonists. Because illegal and immoral actions can produce fear of discovery and 
punishment,  Epicureans are banned from committing them. Ataraxia is a long-
term goal, not the immediate pleasures of excessive food or drink—which bring 
future consequences—nor of any illicit gain. Consequently,  Epicurus advised his 
followers to weigh expected pleasures and pains, a process called the “hedonic 
calculus” by scholars. They must deliberate carefully and choose what to do and 
not to do. The terms for these decisions are αἱρεῖϲθαι haireîsthai “to choose” and 
φεύγειν pheúgein, literally “to avoid”, but idiomatically “to choose not to do”.1
3. The  Herculaneum library
In 79 CE, Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii,  Herculaneum, and other 
towns.2 Pompeii is the more famous, but Herculaneum turned out to be more 
important to the history of  philosophy.  Herculaneum was likely hit by an initial, 
fast-moving wave of hot ash (hotter than 510 degrees Celsius), before being 
buried by successive flows of volcanic mud. 3 The hot ash wave carbonised all 
the organic matter that it touched, such as wooden furniture.
In a gigantic seafront villa just west of town, hundreds of  papyrus rolls 
were found. They had also been carbonised in the ash wave and buried in the 
eruption, which had the remarkable effect of preserving them for posterity. 
Organic matter would normally simply decay, as the climate in southern Italy 
is sufficiently wet.  Papyrus normally survives only in very dry climates, such 
as the Egyptian desert, which is rainless and the source of most ancient  papyri.
The villa is now known as the  Villa dei papiri or “villa of the  papyri”, from its 
most famous find, but it was also the source of many important sculptures and

2. The Herculaneum papyri as a resource for discovering multi-word expressions 15
is architecturally interesting in its own right. An unknown number of  papyrus 
rolls were excavated—probably around 600–800. We do not know how many 
 papyri were destroyed before excavators realised what they were, nor how 
many are still buried, waiting to be discovered.
Initially, the rolls were cut into halves along the long axis, or into quarters, 
and sketches were made of the visible text. Then, the visible layer would be 
scraped out or , rarely, lifted out, and the new visible layer would be sketched. This 
continued until one layer was left, which was preserved. This procedure is called 
scorzatura, or “de-barking”, and the resulting pieces are called  scorze or “pieces 
of bark”. Later , only the outer layers were removed in this way, and the inner 
part, called the midollo, or “marrow”, was unrolled more or less continuously 
on a machine invented by Fr Piaggio, a former librarian in the Vatican. Sketches 
were also made of these. In both cases, bits or whole stretches of  papyrus 
frequently stick together and are scraped off or unrolled together , disrupting 
the clean series of columns that would have been legible in the original roll. 
When these are stuck below the main layer , they are called sottoposti (“placed-
unders”) and when they are above the main layer , they are called sovrapposti 
(“placed-overs”). Sometimes, it seems, entire columns or circumferences of 
the roll are sottoposto to the visible layer . Sotto- and sovrapposti can often be 
relocated correctly into their original positions: because they stuck out of place 
while the roll was in its cylindrical shape, they must always move by multiples 
of the circumference of the roll, i.e. one or more layers adjacent to their original 
position.4
Piaggio had intended for the midolli to be kept as continuous wholes, 
preserving their original roll-format. However , as this proved impractical, 
they were cut into smaller sections, attached to heavy paper and ultimately to 
wooden or stiff cardboard backers. When the Rev. Hayter took all the disegni 
(hand-drawn facsimiles of the  papyri) back to England in 1809, a second set 
was made. The first set is now stored in the Bodleian Library and called the 
Oxford disegni; the second set remained in Naples, in the Biblioteca Nazionale di 
Napoli, and are called the Neapolitan disegni. Because the  papyri were not well 
inventoried before many of them were cut up, the inventory reaches over 1800 
entries, but not every entry represents a roll. In many cases, one original roll 
must be reconstructed out of  papyri filed under several inventory numbers. For 
example, the work tentatively identified as  Philodemus’ On Providence consists 
of one midollo (PHerc. 1670) and four scorze (PHerc. 1100, 1577, 1579, and 1636).5
The  Herculaneum library contains primarily (ca. 90%)  Epicurean texts 
spanning the history of the school from its foundation by  Epicurus (341–270)

treatises, Latin literature, perhaps business or legal documents, and perhaps 
one or two historical works in Greek. Of the  Epicurean texts, the majority are by 
 Philodemus, followed by  Epicurus. 
Thus, the library presents a collection of related texts datable from the 
late fourth century down to at least the middle of the first century. This unity 
allows us to follow the development of the school’s prose, as well as providing 
interesting opportunities to study a language community unified by  philosophical 
commitments and by the study of the older texts of their own intellectual tradition, 
rather than by dialect or time period. But within the corpus of  Epicurean texts, we 
can also study differences by genre, for example, technical treatise, public-facing 
protreptic, school-internal polemics and letters by famous  Epicureans. Thus, the 
collection can be studied by genre,  diachronically, and potentially  diatopically: 
 Epicurus spent his career in Athens, along with the other early members of the 
school, and their texts were presumably composed there.  Philodemus, however , 
spent his career in the company of a Roman senator , and the evidence from the 
library suggests that he spent time in Southern Italy, in and around the partially 
hellenophone Naples.6 Other extant Epicurean texts add to this corpus: some 
letters by  Epicurus (to Menoeceus, Herodotus, and Pythocles) are extant via 
the usual route of manuscript tradition, and an extensive inscription outlining 
 Epicurean  philosophy was erected in Oenoanda by one Diogenes, probably in 
the second century CE.7
4. The difficulties of editing  Herculaneum  papyri and 
technological advances
Consequently, editing a  Herculaneum  papyrus is not easy or straightforward. 
Firstly, all parts of a roll must be identified. Handwriting and page-layout (i.e. 
features like the number of lines per column and the length of the lines of text) 
suggest that pieces may belong to the same roll, but ultimately the plausibility

to introduce him here.

2. The Herculaneum papyri as a resource for discovering multi-word expressions 17
of the resulting reconstruction confirms it. As a rule, each series of  scorze must 
be interleaved with another one (because each series is from half the roll) 
and they must be read in the opposite sequence of their numbers. Numbers 
were assigned in the order that disegni were created in, but the sketch-artists 
worked from the visible layer of the  scorze (the innermost part of the stack) 
outwards towards the beginning of the roll. The midollo, because it was 
continuously unrolled, can often be read in order , but the order of the pieces 
of  papyrus was open to confusion. The  papyri were also hung for a period on 
museum walls, and many of them had their backing material changed. 8 So, in 
some cases, the original order of the pieces that constitute the midollo must 
be recovered as well.
The number of sources of text for a particular column or fragment can vary 
widely. In cases of scorzatura, as a rule we have a single disegno made before 
the layer was destroyed. This makes the editor’s job easier , because she is not 
juggling many sources, but the disegni have various drawbacks. Their artists 
often omitted fragmentary or damaged material along breaks and did not 
usually preserve details about the physical condition of the  papyrus: this data 
can be useful for making joins and determining the sequence of fragments. They 
were also liable to fail to see or include marginal marks used for punctuation 
and line numeration, and to confuse similarly shaped letters.
The  papyri themselves, when extant, must be consulted. The basic difficulty 
is that the  papyrus itself is darkened, usually now black from carbonisation, 
so the ink is hardly visible. They are also delicate and liable to flake and crack 
and cannot be cleaned or conserved like non-carbonised  papyri are. They can 
be read with reasonable success under binocular microscopes with good light, 
but our ability to read them improved dramatically in the early 2000s, when a 
Brigham Young University team took infrared photographs of them. These were 
usually successful in making more text legible. New IR photos, including 3D 
ones, are being made by the EduceLab team at the University of Kentucky (see 
https://educelab.engr .uky.edu/).
Therefore, when the  papyrus itself is extant, there are usually four main 
sources for the text: the  papyrus itself, two disegni (Oxford and Naples), and 
an infrared photograph. 9 Simple rules cannot be given about the value of the

which took place during carbonisation. 
 The Vesuvius Challenge’s X-ray and  AI/machine learning results have made 
quite a splash in the news recently (see https://scrollprize.org/). The amount of 
published text from these sources is still small, and their editorial situation is 
simple: editors work from the images produced by processing the scan data in 
various ways.10 Sotto- and sovrapposti seem to be an issue even in the still rolled-
up rolls, either because the pieces are stuck out of place or because the process 
of digitally unrolling the rolls has not been perfected yet. Less heralded, but also 
important, is a new computer program, called  Maque-IT, which helps scholars 
rearrange pieces of papyrus, move sotto- and sovrapposti according to rule, and 
keep track of the page-layout (see https://recreate-maqueit.it/).
Familiarity makes all this easier , though perhaps never easy. It is important 
to keep the editorial situation of the  papyri in mind, especially the brackets that 
mark out the letters legible on the  papyrus. In (1) below, for example, both verbs 
that I study in this chapter are partially restored: αἱρο[ύ|μενοι ἢ φεύ]γοντεϲ 
hairo[ú]menoi ḕ pheú]gontes. Of these twenty letters, the editors only read ten of 
them (see below for details); the other ten are restored.
5. “Choosing and avoiding” and “choices and 
avoidances”
As mentioned at the end of Section 2, the concept of “choice” was important to 
the  Epicureans. Their technical vocabulary for this involves two related pairs of 
words: αἱρεῖϲθαι haireîsthai “to choose” + φεύγειν pheúgein “to flee”, literally, but 
in this context “to choose to pursue some goal or course of action” and “the choice 
to avoid or not to pursue one”, respectively. The nouns,  αἵρεϲιϲ  haíresis “choice” 
+  φυγή  phugḗ “flight”, literally, mean “choice to do something” and “choice not to 
do something”.11 These meanings have antecedents before the Epicureans (for 
10 The sole extensive text so far published can be found in Nicolardi et al. (2024).
11 I have not noticed that any verb is used commonly with the nouns, though they are frequently 
object of the preposition περί perí “about, regarding”.

example, in the orator Lycurgus, Plato, and Aristotle, and, contemporaneously, 
in Stoic authors), 12 but they occur often in Epicurean texts, even as the title of 
at least two treatises. These technical terms were not unique to the  Epicureans, 
but are very commonly found in their texts, and because of the  Herculaneum 
 papyri, we have a lot of  Epicurean texts. 
I have gathered the passages by surveying the texts (for details of the 
available resources, see below). What you see is what you get: I have included all 
passages that I found.13 Further , I have not limited the list to one part of speech 
derived from the root (for example, the noun or verb or one of the adjectival 
formations) but rather included all the pairs of the two roots I came across. In a 
highly inflected and morphologically flexible language like Ancient Greek, this 
procedure seems to make sense.14 It is worth noting that like is found with like: 
the noun  αἵρεϲιϲ  haíresis is found with the noun  φυγή  phugḗ, and so forth. Those 
who wish for a more limited set can prune as they see fit. 
I am agnostic about the terminology and definition for these phrases. They 
are pairs of frequently co-occurring words, whose exact grammatical/formal/
lexical realisations vary depending on context, but which are always built to 
the same pair of roots. These expressions may fall under Laporte’s (2018: 176) 
“non- lexicalised” multi-word expression (depending on how one understands 
“extra linguistic facts” and his example “salt and pepper”). Fellbaum (2015: 
778) uses the term “collocation” for phrases that have a certain “collocational 
strength”, though they are not necessarily fixed; they may be lexically and 
syntactically idiosyncratic but are semantically  decomposable (as opposed to 
idioms, which are not decomposable). The  Epicureans could talk about choices 
and avoidances separately from each other .  PARSEME seems to consider them 
a nominal idiom. 15 
In my view, the pairing can be reasonably classified as a collocation because 
the terms—at least within this corpus—cannot be replaced, they cannot be 
altered or added to, and there’s a good argument for understanding it to mean 
more than the sum of its parts, i.e. “ethical decision making”. Since every

In what follows, I give Greek texts and translations only when editions 
and translations might not be readily available or there is some other reason 
to quote them. Papyrological texts are laid out according to the  papyrus that 
preserves them, and I use lunate sigma (ϲ) in place of both Byzantine sigmas 
(σ, ς). Lunate sigma is normal in papyrological texts, but I have extended it 
to non-papyrological texts for consistency. I have preserved the orthography 
of the editions, which usually stands in the middle ground between the 
spellings found in the papyri and modern standards. 16 The papyrological 
texts are printed with the various signs and marks that papyrologists use 
to report what they see on the  papyrus. The most important of these are 
square brackets to mark lacunae (gaps in the  papyrus where nothing can 
be read), under-dots under letters (ξ̣̣ο ̣π̣, to mark uncertainly read letters, 
i.e. those that can be read as a different letter), and under-dots without 
letters (to mark either traces of a letter that cannot be deciphered or , when 
inside square brackets, to indicate space for one letter per under-dot:  
[  ̣  ̣  ̣]).17 Double square brackets and high tic-marks ( ⟦ηθι⟧ and ⸌κλμ⸍) mark 
deletions and additions by an ancient scribe. Curly and angle brackets ({αβγ} 
and ⟨δεζ⟩) mark deletions and additions by the editor .

dates and such geographic indications as are available, and works, with brief 
descriptions of genre and purpose, in which we find either the verbal version or 
the nominal version of the pair .

 Epicurus, founder of the  Epicurean school, lived from 341–270 BCE. He was born

a brief protreptic aimed at winning new converts to the school.24 The On Nature

of related topics. At least parts of it (books 28 and what has been identified 
as 10) were framed as dialogues, and another book (book 25) has dialogue-
like elements. 25 However , its overall compositional technique is not yet well 
understood.

7. Bibliographic guide and advice
The  Herculaneum library’s publication situation presents some difficulties for 
researchers. Texts are published overwhelmingly in the traditional print formats 
(book-length complete editions and journal article-length partial editions), and 
they are not reliably collected into conveniently digitised corpora. Many can be 
found in two databases, namely papyri. info and the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae. 
papyri. info is a hub for everything  papyrus-related; it incorporates a number of 
digital projects and includes texts of many papyri,  including many of those from 
 Herculaneum. The Thesaurus Linguae Graecae is a searchable database of Greek 
texts from the earliest alphabetic Greek texts (Linear B is not included) until the 
nineteenth century.
The online inventory Chartes is especially useful. It gives title and author 
identifications, language, conservation information, and notes about matches 
with other pieces, as well as a handwriting sample and bibliography. It also links 
to the Leuven Database of Ancient Books (LDAB) entry for papyri,  which makes it 
easy to find the papyri. info text.
The situation is made more complicated by the fact that there are many editions 
of parts of texts published in various journals, some of which are specialised 
and do not circulate widely. This makes it difficult to study a whole text. Take as 
an example PHerc. 831, thought to be a work by Demetrius the Spartan on false

The main venue for publication of  Herculaneum texts is the Bibliopolis series 
La scuola di Epicuro (“The School of  Epicurus”) which had a sub-series dedicated 
to the fragments of the early leaders of the  Epicurean school ( I frammenti dei 
Kathegemones “The Fragments of the Leaders”) and a supplement series (with 
editions of the Latin poet Lucretius and the Greek inscription of Diogenes of 
Oenoanda). The series has twenty-one volumes, with a twenty-second due out 
soon.40 The Society for Biblical Literature’s Writings from the Greco-Roman World 
series has four editions; the Les Belles Lettres’ Budé  series has two (with more 
expected), and Oxford University Press has published four fifths of Philodemus’ 
On  Poems and half of his  On Piety . A new series with Brill, Papyri Graecae 
Herculanenses has two titles. The most important journal is Cronache ercolanesi, 
the long-running home of  Herculaneum studies. Related material can be 
found in most papyrological journals (especially Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und 
Epigraphik) and the new journal Philosophical Papyri. Other journals dealing 
with papyrological and  philosophical topics occasionally publish  Herculaneum 
material.
The role of technology in editing the papyri  means that, as a rule, newer 
editions are overall better than previous ones. More recent editors simply 
have better equipment than older ones. However , this does not mean that their 
judgment in supplementing damaged traces and choosing conjectures is better , 
and older editors often saw the papyri  when they were in better condition than 
they are now. Ideally, a critical reader checks older editions for relevant material 
while keeping an eye on the sources (  papyrus, infrared photos, disegni) for the 
text. One must read the introduction of each text for details of reconstructions. 
Every  papyrus is different and presents unique problems. Likewise, though 
some uniformity has been enforced by the Leiden conventions, editors still use 
different conventions for material preserved in various sources and readings

8. Concluding remarks
Despite the difficulties, the number of surviving texts from a single library (and 
the fact that they mostly belong to the  Epicurean school) makes the  Herculaneum 
library an important resource for ancient philosophers. It could be important for 
other scholars as well. In this chapter , I hope to have demonstrated the interest—
and to have alleviated some of the difficulties—that these papyri  present.

 Victoria Beatrix Fendel and Matthew T. Ireland1
1. History versus anamnesis
The (post)classical Greek medical corpora, i.e. writings associated with 
Hippocrates (fifth century BCE) and Galen (second century CE), and the  
(post)classical historiographical corpora, i.e. the writings by Thucydides (fifth 
century BCE), Xenophon (fifth to fourth centuries BCE), and Polybius (second 
century BCE) here, pose difficulties for automated lemmatisation and part-of-
speech tagging due to their technical register . This register , however , makes them 
particularly interesting for the study of multi-word expression that are precise 
to the in-group, of medical or historiographical practitioners, and obscure to the 
outsider , i.e. the general public. What is anamnesis to the former is history to the 
latter .

speaking, “a large and principled collection of natural texts” (Biber and Reppen 
2015: 1). The writings by Thucydides, Xenophon, and Polybius on the one hand 
and by Hippocrates and Galen on the other hand are such large collections of

They are natural texts if we accept that the preservation history has shaped 
them, possibly in the sense of scribal edits, minor additions or deletions, and 
losses (Nicolai 2007: 18; Hoffmann 2005: chap. 8). They are the native speakers 
of a corpus language (Fleischman 2000: 34). They are principled in that they 
are associated with a specific discipline, and discourse, respectively. Medical 
practitioners focussed on physiological processes, historiographical authors on 
sociopolitical paradigms.3 
Both disciplines were emergent in the fifth century BCE. Medicine was a 
marketplace where practitioners were trying to attract patients (clients) and 
their language needed to be generally comprehensible, rather than highly 
technical, to drive, rather than prevent, sales (Lateiner 1986: 16; Willi 2003: 
95). Historiography was a classroom where “an author—assuming the persona 
of ‘inquirer’—took responsibility himself for giving an account of human 
affairs in the past” (Schepens 2007: 40) therein instructing and persuading a 
wide audience which required generally comprehensible, rather than highly 
technical, language (Nicolai 2007: 15 and 22; Schepens 2007: 42–43).

3. Technical writing across space and time  41
How did the historiographical and medical discourses emerge? Those 
working to shape the two emergent disciplines shared the approach of obtaining 
knowledge from empirical evidence (Lateiner 1986: 15; Schepens 2007: 48) and 
thus two discourses emerged. These are, in Michel  Foucault’s sense, “complex 
networks of statements that make knowledge possible; that delimit what can 
be said, or understood, within a particular discourse; and that determine who 
can speak (or at least speak with authority or be heard) within that discourse” 
(Lynch 2014: 121–122). Discourses emerge from groups of people that share 
experience and/or knowledge through interaction and/or practice, so-called 
communities of practice (Wenger 1999; Unwin, Hughes, and Jewson 2007). Such 
communities of practice can be externally recognisable, for example, schools by 
means of a location and possibly a type of dress code, but  visibility can also be 
limited to the insider perspective, for example, people sharing a specific interest 
who may only come together for events or in private social-media groups, to use 
a modern example. 
Crucially, “[d]iscourses can arise, be transformed, and disappear; they are 
fragmentary and incomplete” (Lynch 2014: 120–121). A strong case to this effect 
has been made for the Hippocratic corpus: “the CH [sc. Corpus Hippocraticum] 
did not produce a Hippocratic discourse; a discourse (Hippocratic or not is 
another matter) produced the Corpus. Changes in the Corpus are manifestations 
of how this discourse changed and evolved over time” (Nelson 2016: 126; see 
also Eijk 2016: 43 who wants to dismember the Corpus Hippocraticum; more 
generally Castro 2025: 317).4 The Hippocratic medical texts may have generated 
fierce debate in this regard as they would remain in use for about 2,000 years 
(Trenery 2020; Jouanna 2012: chap. 16; Paavilainen 2009: chap. 2). Conversely, 
with the rise of Christianity, historiography’s discourse fundamentally changed 
as “history became a part of a vision of the world and the destiny of man” 
(Nicolai 2007: 17).
Why are the medical and historiographical corpora so varied? Discourses may 
give rise to  subject-specific terminology, groups may give rise to  group-internal 
terminology, and items do not have to be monovalent. Due to the size of the corpora 
in question, Sheinfux et al.’s (2019: 41) observation pertains that in very large 
corpora even elements that otherwise seem fixed can show variation, innovation, 
and creativity. The size of the corpora further allows to take into consideration 
the co-text, i.e. the textual surroundings of an element and their cohesion (Lyons 
1995: 271; Crystal 2008: 109), the context, i.e. the discursive surroundings of an 
element and their coherence (Lyons 1995: 264 and 271; Crystal 2008: 119), and 
“the dynamics between default values and their discursive readjustments as well 
4 Part of such a discourse-driven corpus assemblage is that reworkings (cf. Roselli 2016) are 
a natural part of it. The starting point is the community of practice, the glue that holds it 
together is the shared knowledge and experience, and the visible trace is a corpus that may 
not have been perceived as one at all times.

as participants’ management of social relationships and identities” (Leitner and 
Jucker 2021: 705). Essentially, we are not only interested in the referential but also 
the social meanings and functions of elements (cf. Bentein 2019; Vieregge 2025). 
The chapter addresses the following three research questions with regard to 
(post)classical Greek medical and historiographical corpora: 
1. What is technical writing and what are the characteristics of its 
language?
2. How do technical writings pose difficulties for lemmatisation and part-
of-speech tagging?
3. Why are multi-word expressions in technical writings instructive?
The chapter takes a corpus-based approach.  Sketch Engine corpora for the 
relevant sub-corpora are built by means of reuse and modification of previously 
developed tools. These corpora are used to contextualise previous observations, 
put forward new observations, and propose avenues for the further investigation 
of less visible technical corpora in line with the  FAIR data principles.
After this introductory anamnesis, the chapter falls into five subsections. 
Section 2 introduces the reader to the corpora and tools. Section 3 addresses 
research question 1, Section 4 research question 2, and Section 5 research 
question 3. Section 6 brings together the results and offers conclusions and 
suggestions for future work.  
2. Adopt and adapt
In order to match  visibility, accessibility, and searchability of the five sub-
corpora—the writings by Thucydides, Xenophon, and Polybius as well as 
Hippocrates and Galen—,  Sketch Engine corpora were built by means of reuse 
and modification of previously developed tools. 
How do the historiographical and medical writings compare? The medical and 
historiographical corpora are comparable in terms of register , in that texts were 
written to be read,5 rather than, for example, performed like plays or speeches, 
and in that there was a need for comprehensible, rather than highly technical, 
language, in the fifth-century BCE beginnings of the two disciplines (Section 1, 
see further Section 3). The corpora are also comparable in terms of discourse, 
in that the texts reflect their authors’ approach of obtaining knowledge from 
empirical evidence (Section 1). Historiography is about “creating paradigms, 
predominantly politico-militaristic or ethical ones” (Nicolai 2007: 14; Rood 
5 The readership could be as small as the practitioner himself, e.g. personal notes (cf. Langholf 
1990: 184–185). The readership could have any number of intentions with the material they 
read, including the re-working and re-combining of passages (cf. Roselli 2016).

3. Technical writing across space and time  43
2014: 92; Nicholson 2021) with the historiographer taking on “the persona 
of ‘inquirer’” (Schepens 2007: 40), who has a keen interest in oral and visual 
testimony as primary sources (Schepens 2007: 47 on Thucydides; Rood 2014: 64 
on Xenophon; Schepens 2007: 51 on Polybius). Medicine is about understanding 
“the human body, its health and diseases” (Lateiner 1986: 15). The physician does 
an anamnesis and observes symptoms in order to treat the patient. Hippocrates’ 
writings were oftentimes so “compact and concise” that they would “require 
explanation to be understood correctly by the lay reader or beginner” (Boudon-
Millot 2018: 293). Galen did this in his commentary work. When Galen diagnoses 
and treats patients, he “not only gets things right; he can explain how it is that he 
does so” (Hankinson 2008: 9). Furthermore, the corpora match as regards their 
 diachronic potential, with the beginnings of both disciplines in the fifth century 
BCE and their development throughout the Hellenistic and Roman periods 
(Lateiner 1986: 16–17; Nicolai 2007: 16; Schepens 2007: 40), and as regards their 
potential for multi-word-expression research. Pilot studies on all sub-corpora 
have returned valuable results (for example, Fendel 2025c; Fendel Submitted-a; 
Rusten 2020; Fendel 2025d) (see further Section 5). This is why the five sub-
corpora have been selected, as despite their differing subject matter , they show 
a range of similarities ideationally and conceptually (see further Section 4).
The medical and historiographical corpora differ practically in terms of 
 visibility. The medical texts long remained  group-internal which was reflected 
also in the Latinate translation of terms for references to anatomy, diseases, and 
procedures, for example, German Keratitis as opposed to Hornhautentzündung 
“keratitis” (Doody, Föllinger , and Taub 2012; Durling 1993 on Galen; Karimullah 
2020; Maclean 2021 on Hippocratic reception; Bouras-Vallianatos and Zipser 
2019 on Galenic reception; Hunt 1999 on translation; Montalt and García-
Izquierdo 2025; Kalverkämper 2005 on layperson vs. professional since 
antiquity; Rochette 2005 on translating technical terms in literature; Fögen 2005); 
the historiographical texts became schoolbook models already in antiquity 
(Nicolai 2007: 20–22). This situation left traces in the physical and digital editing 
of relevant texts. Furthermore, the medical and historiographical corpora differ 
as regards the tailoring of the tagging tool. Thucydides’ and Xenophon’s literary 
classical Attic was part of the training data for the originally developed tool, 
whereas Hippocrates’ Ionic was not (Fendel and Ireland 2023). 6 We change 
this situation by producing  Sketch Engine corpora of all the sub-corpora and 
adapting the tagging tool to the technical language of the corpora. 
How can we reuse a tool developed for literary classical Attic historiography, 
oratory, and prose? The tool developed to tokenise, lemmatise, part-of-speech and

morphologically tag a corpus of classical literary Attic historiography, oratory,

for tokenisation 7 and the Perseus Digital Library  for lemmatisation, part-of-

form of a vertical table in .vert format along with an error .txt file which provides 
a log of all items for which lemmatisation, part-of-speech or morphological 
tagging failed. The output files can be implemented into  Sketch Engine by means 
of a modified corpus configuration file (cf. Fendel and Ireland 2023). By means 
of inspection of the error .txt files, the tool was fine-tuned for classical literary 
Attic historiography, oratory, and prose and the TEI .xml input format. In fact, 
Thucydides’ and Xenophon’ writings were part of the training data. 
We expected texts written in a different dialect (for example, Ionic in 
Hippocrates and some Galen), at a different time (for example, writings by 
Polybius and Galen), and/or belonging to a different genre and/or register (for 
example, medical texts) to cause issues. Technologically, the main adaptation 
related to handling the input format of the texts. The tool was built to operate 
on TEI .xml files but the digital version of the medical corpora was encoded 
in plain .xml. 8 Secondly, the tool’s functionality to output error .txt files after 
tagging a text was used to assess recurring issues to do with the digital encoding 
of the texts. For instance, we noticed issues with the encoding of hyphenation 
and missing whitespaces posing issues at the tokenisation stage and issues with 
punctuation being fused to the word end posing issues at the lemmatisation 
and part-of-speech-tagging stage. Finally, the tool draws for lemmatisation, part-
of-speech-tagging, and morphological tagging on the Perseus Digital Library , 
such that we expect technical morphology and lexis to cause issues (see further 
Section 4). The previously developed tool and corpus and the newly adapted tool 
and corpus conform to the  FAIR principles.
Why  FAIR data?   FAIR data limits the risk of containing texts within 
communities of practice and thus sentencing them to a Rapunzel sleep.  FAIR 
data is findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (Wilkinson et al. 
2016). The  Sketch Engine corpora for the medical and historiographical texts 
and the tools to build them described in this chapter are findable, in that a 
unique and stable identifier (DOI) has been assigned, accessible, in that all

We need to define what texts qualify as technical writing before asking what 
makes the language of technical writing distinctive and resolving the in-group 
paradox that is attached to any instance of technical writing.

“The following evils follow inevitably upon one another: if there is a chill, fever 
follows. If a cord is severed, it does not reunite, and a violent swelling supervenes. 
If the brain is shaken and suffers damage as the result of a blow, the patient 
immediately loses his speech, sight, and hearing; if the brain is wounded, fever 
and the vomiting of bile ensue, the patient becomes paralysed in some part of his 
body, and he dies. If a fold of peritoneum  becomes exposed, it must putrefy. If 
blood flows from a wound or a vessel into the upper cavity, it must turn to pus.” 
(Translation by Potter (1988), our emphasis)
The three extracts share at least three features. Firstly, they are highly specific 
regarding their subject matter . Secondly, they presuppose a background in the 
subject matter in the reader . Thirdly, they contain lexical items that are limited 
to the specific subject area. 
Observations one and two were made about medical language by Langslow 
(2000: 26–27), i.e. there is a contextual and a social parameter to the definition of 
medical language. However , the use of an item by a member of a specific group 
or community, such as physicians, would not qualify the item as technical as this 
use may be in an everyday context, like a supermarket (Willi 2003: 52). We thus 
land on “topic as the basic parameter of technical language” (Willi 2003: 52). 
The group of practitioners however shapes the topic and discourse (Nelson 2016 
on the Hippocratic discourse; Schepens 2007 on the persona of the inquirer; 
Nicolai 2007 on paradigm presentation). Physicians talk about “the human body, 
its health and diseases” (Lateiner 1986: 15) with the goal being diagnosis and 
treatment (if possible); historiographers talk about the “cultural and political 
achievements of noteworthy communities in the recent past” (Lateiner 1986: 
15) with the goal being the creation of paradigms (Nicolai 2007: 14–15).  
Conversely, “syntactic or stylistic features that are sometimes listed as 
‘technical’ […] are not technical-language features but register features” (Willi 
2003: 53). These features are often applied non-systematically in domain-specific 
technical writings (Eijk 1997: 101–106 on the Hippocratic corpus) and appear in 
non-technical contexts or different-domain technical writings too. For example,

3. Technical writing across space and time  47
aspects of medical language appear in oratory (Mader 2018 on imagery; Das 
2019 on similes and conceptual  metaphors), historiography (Lateiner 1986; 
Thomas 2000: chap. 2), tragedy (Clarke Kosak 2004; Jouanna 2012: chaps. 4 and 
5), and to a limited extent comedy (Willi 2003: 95). None of these text types deals 
with medical subject matter . 
One such syntactic or stylistic feature deserves brief comment, the so-called 
nominal style (Panagl 1982: 231; Mambrini 2019; Joho 2022: chap. 1; Ittzés 2024: 
93 n. 12; Marušić 2018: 103). The medical texts seem to be innovative in the 
creation of nominal formations (for example, in -ιτις -itis and -ις -is) to describe 
symptoms during anamnesis, diseases during diagnosis, and anatomical details 
(Eijk 1997: 101–102). Yet, these formations lack systematicity in formation and 
exclusivity to the medical domain (Eijk 1997: 102; Willi 2003: 67).
What is distinctive about the language of technical writing? Let us consider a 
modern example. One author recently took a multi-module course on  SEO offered 
by the University of California Davis. The  SEO community is an interesting case 
study as it is constantly engaging with the user , i.e. all of us, communicating 
with the user and trying to understand the user , but at the same time it has 
its toolboxes and tricks of the trade—in fact most of you will have wondered 
since sentence two in this paragraph what  SEO stands for or what it is. The 
community of practitioners is neither closed off nor secretive as a whole but it 
thrives on  group-internal,  subject-specific, and  ambiguous terminology (Fendel 
Submitted-a). A passage from a key manual is in (4) (repeated from above):
(4) “After you complete your initial optimization work, you will be able to more 
accurately assess the cost of optimization for your keyword list. This is a good time 
to drill down into long-tail keywords to look for the most efficient opportunities. 
Depending on the size and complexity of the  SEO project, this phase of keyword 
research can be the most labor-intensive.” (Enge, Spencer , and Stricchiola 2023: 
146, our emphasis)
A  group-internal term is “long-tail keywords”. In essence, while keywords such 
as “laptop” or even “gaming laptop” may be popular and mainstream, they are 
also highly competitive, i.e. they apply to many different products, companies, 
services, etc. that one may search for . Conversely, long-tail keywords such as 
“Lenovo gaming laptop 15 inch” are more specific, usually more niche, and at 
times even obscure, i.e. you may not think of the search term when you first 
start searching. A  subject-specific term is “  search engine optimisation” (  SEO), 
which in fact “is a bit of a misnomer” as  SEO is not about optimising search 
engines themselves but search results (Enge, Spencer , and Stricchiola 2023: 1). 
An  ambiguous term is “keyword”, which seems to stand for keyword proper and 
key phrase in this context. A keyword is “a word (usually one of several) chosen 
to indicate or represent the content of a larger document, text, record, etc.” or 
a word “entered as a search term in a database or search engine” (Mcarthur ,

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages48 
Lam-Mcarthur , and Fontaine 2018: s.v. keyword). While the original use of 
the term is anaphoric, the newer use is cataphoric. Furthermore, keywords 
in  SEO are selected not only for their contextual relevancy but also for their 
competitiveness and form part of the written text rather than functioning as 
metadata after the fact (see also Wright 2014). 
Every text is likely to have ingredients of all three in addition to general-
purpose items. For example, if we take a closer look at (3) above from Hippocrates’ 
Diseases, Thesaurus Linguae Graecae  statistics (for the eighth century BCE to 
third century CE) reveal that only three items in the passage may be  subject-
specific, as ≥70% of attestations of these appear in the Hippocratic and Galenic 
writings, see (5).

There is no item that is  group-internal, i.e. limited to the in-group of medical 
practitioners in this extract. There are several  ambiguous items, for example, 
πῦρ pur “fire” but also “fever” and κοιλία koilia “(any) cavity of the body” but 
also “cavity (in the earth)”. 12 The presence of group-internal and ambiguous 
items can cause obscurity; the presence of  subject-specific items contributes 
to precision. Medical and historiographical terminology could be considered 
 subject-specific. While medical terms, in their Latinate form, have long 
dominated in translations of medical writings (Doody, Föllinger , and Taub 2012) 
and created obscurity to the outside of the community of medical practitioners, 
historiographical terminology “even for key concepts of method, is largely made 
up of common words, which may then be used in a less familiar , more technical 
sense” to this day (Schepens 2007: 43). Thus, while medical terminology seems 
to be  group-internal, historiographical terminology falls into the  ambiguous 
category. 
Why is technical writing precise and obscure at the referential and social 
levels? While we initially may think of  group-internal items being very common 
in technical language, they are never the exclusive component and it crucially 
depends on the intended audience how much  group-internal terminology can 
be applied in order to avoid compromising comprehensibility (Ferreira 2025: 
50–51 on common ground). Consider (2) above. You notice many TLAs (three-
12 While for κοιλία koilia the medical meaning seems to have preceded the general meaning, for 
πῦρ pur the general meaning preceded the medical meaning.

3. Technical writing across space and time  49
letter abbreviations), such as CMS (content management system, for example, 
WordPress), CRM (a client management system, for example, Salesforce), USPs 
(unique selling points, of products), and KPIs (key performance indicators, 
for workers). To the uninitiated these may sound off-putting, initially possibly 
obscure—although ChatGPT and Google will surely assist you (Sabanés and 
Cunha 2025). The thus created language variety seems to be of the kind of 
Blake’s argot, i.e. a variety “designed to restrict communication to an in-group 
and exclude others” (Blake 2010: 227). However , the TLAs are not restricted to an 
in-group but are used, as in (2), in outward-facing job adverts. They are  subject-
specific and describe complex workflows, high-pressure environments, team 
dynamics, and sales targets precisely. This then seems rather akin to Blake’s 
slang, i.e. a variety that is “inventive, abounds in  metaphor and allusion, and 
is often more demanding or more opaque than the standard language” (Blake 
2010: 201). New TLAs appear daily, there is no lack of inventiveness. 
Inventiveness seems to have been a persistent feature of the medical and 
historiographical corpora. Polybius’s historiographical (second century BCE) 
and Galen’s medical (second century CE) writings illustrate the continuing 
inventive development of the discourses and their associated language. Polybius 
famously introduced a range of Latinate technical terms into his Greek and put 
on a reactionary tone towards the bookish Timaeus (Schepens 2007: 53–54), 
which shows how fundamental the transformation of Greek historiography 
at the time was. Galen explained, in the form of commentaries, the “compact 
and concise” Hippocratic writings referring to them “more than 2,500 times” 
(Boudon-Millot 2018: 293–294), which reflects the need for updated audience 
design (see Morison 2008). 
While both  subject-specific and  group-internal terminology is somewhat 
expected in technical writing,  ambiguous items are not. Langslow (2012: 102), 
for instance, called  polysemy and synonymy the “two arch-enemies of technical 
usage” and Willi (2003: 69) insisted that technical terms must be “standardised 
in usage and at least ideally monosemous” and “expressively neutral”. An 
interesting case is Polybius’ Latinisms, such as στρατηγός stratēgos for consul 
but also praetor. The consul is the highest magistrate in the Roman cursus 
honorum; the praetor was one level further down in the cursus honorum yet 
could carry out consular duties in the absence of the consul. Langslow (2012: 
104) resolves the issue by arguing in favour of audience design, which seems 
to align with what we see in earlier historians that Polybius likely wanted to 
emulate (Nicolai 2007: 24).
Furthermore, it may be that the terms are not expressively neutral nor 
equivalent as regards their  indexical value (Eckert 2008; Vieregge 2025). 
Linguistic indexes are “‘structures’ (lexemes, affixes, diminutives, syntactic 
constructions, emphatic stress, etc.) that have become conventionally associated

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages50 
with a particular situational dimension, and that invoke that situational 
dimension whenever they are used” (Bentein 2019: 123). Polybius’ στρατηγός 
stratēgos may have acquired a conventionalised association with a specific 
situational dimension and Polybius may have chosen it when he wanted to 
evoke this situational dimension. 
Finally,  ambiguous items may function akin to a bridge, not a sturdy one, but 
one that initially lets the audience feel drawn to the subject matter and community 
of practice. They may subsequently realise that they were mistaken in their 
interpretation. This may spark annoyance or curiosity, by the Goldilocks principle 
(cf. Pierrehumbert 2006: 525; Divjak 2019: 182). Which response it sparks may be 
a kind of initiation question that these  ambiguous items subtly ask. 
To resolve the paradox of obscurity and precision simultaneously (Elder 
1954), we must consider perspective. What is maximally precise to the in-group, 
possibly due to  group-internal conventions, is likely to be maximally obscure 
to the outside observer , who would not be privy to  group-internal conventions. 
However , we have noted that in addition to the items that are present for precision 
( subject-specific) and obscurity (  group-internal), there are also bridging items 
that function somewhat as a gatekeeping phenomenon. 13 Ambiguity is not 
coincidental but well-planned in order to keep a discourse alive.  
4. Lemmatisation and part-of-speech tagging

tables, for simplex items and combinations of items (lemmata, wordforms, tags)
