A noticeable difference exists between the ratio of total errors, i.e. the total 
number of tokens that resulted in any type of error during the tagging process, 
in the Attic historians and Polybius, Hippocrates, and Galen. This is expected 
given the training data the original tool was based on yet links to a broader 
ideational issue. Secondly, a noticeable difference exists between the ratio of 
unique errors, vis-à-vis the total number of errors, in Polybius, Hippocrates, and 
Galen as compared to the Attic historians. This is expected given the training data 
the original tool was based on yet also links to a broader conceptual issue. The 
below unpacks the broader ideational and conceptual issues before suggesting 
practical solutions. 
Ideationally, two long-standing beliefs have made the Attic historians 
visible and prominent and the later Polybius along with the medical writings 
comparatively invisible and marginal. The two beliefs are firstly the concept of 
the so-called  classical period, that is the fifth and fourth centuries BCE in Athens, 
which came to take its place at the heart of curricula (cf. Viti 2024: 20–21; Nicolai 
2007: 23), and secondly the concept of literature as implying a “certain  aesthetic 
shaping of a text which is not typically a central concern for authors of modern

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages52 
specialist and technical works” (Doody, Föllinger , and Taub 2012: 233), who 
may be more concerned with their writing as a “knowledge-constructing tool” 
(Montalt and García-Izquierdo 2025). This second belief is closely linked to the 
idea of topic as a key factor discussed in Section 3. While military and political 
paradigms were societally suitable and at times even fashionable topics, medical 
diagnoses and procedures were of interest only to a select few. Both beliefs 
have yielded to more inclusive views (Totelin 2012 on Galen; Langslow 2012 on 
Polybius) which have let non-classical and technical writings emerge from the 
shadows. However , the impact of these beliefs is still felt when it comes to the 
availability of resources, especially those in digital format, such as textbooks, 
grammar books, and dictionaries as well as language models and tools.
Conceptually, it is necessary to qualify the notions of hapax legomena , 
 group-internal features, and dialectal items. Hapax legomena are, traditionally, 
items that are attested only once in our extant texts. However , Section 3 noted 
that communities of practice, such as the medical or historiographical ones, 
develop discourses and as part of this are inventive in their language choices 
(Blake 2010: 201 on slang). Greek has a fully functioning system of derivational 
morphology, which is more or less productive, and a fully functioning system of 
lexical compounding (Fendel 2025e with further references). This means that 
inventiveness could be implemented in the form of minor formal modifications 
on an item, even if general systematicity is lacking (Eijk 1997: 102; Willi 2003: 
67). This explains the high number of unique errors in Hippocrates and Galen 
in particular . We may wonder whether such explicable modifications to an item 
should truly be considered hapax legomena. 
Group-internal features of any kind, including morphological, syntactic, 
and lexical ones, are pervasive in corpora produced and managed by the 
community of practice but do not feature outside of these corpora. They would 
thus only be considered relevant to include in resources, such as grammar 
books, textbooks, or dictionaries, which are specifically designed for relevant 
corpora. This observation is closely linked to the in-group paradox discussed in 
Section 3. However , fully  group-internal features are comparatively rare (Fendel 
Submitted-a) and relevant features may appear marginally or as one-offs in 
group-external corpora. This often earns them the label of “exception” or , in the 
worst case, “mistake”, a situation we gradually need to amend across resources 
as formerly marginal corpora are becoming more visible and accessible and 
thus allow for comparative work.  
Dialectal items are relevant especially to the Hippocratic texts written 
in the Ionic dialect. Ionic may have functioned as a kind of technolect in the 
fifth century BCE (Willi 2003: 95). Like any dialect, it contains areal features 
(here an “East Greek component”), contact features (here “analogies to Attic”), 
and unique features (García-Ramón and Binder; Colvin 2010: 206–207; Miller

3. Technical writing across space and time  53
2013: chaps. 13–15; Giannakis 2025). Areal features are unproblematic as 
the data sample available to examine these features, and train tools on, is 
relatively large. Furthermore, areal features are likely to be listed in standard 
dictionaries. For example, Liddell-Scott-Jones lists a “normal or default form”, 
that is a “form [which] could potentially occur in the widest range of Greek texts 
(with especial weight given to the kinds of texts that are widely read)” (Probert 
2019: 209). Contact features are unproblematic as the availability of data and 
focus of resources is skewed towards Attic, the contact variety in this case. This 
leaves only Ionicisms proper as a potential challenge. However , Herodotus’ 
Histories, written in Ionic, have long been canonical and have thus fed into 
tools and resources. The situation differs for Polybius’ language variety which 
is  diachronically and diastratically distinct from canonical texts (Langslow 2012 
on Latinisms; Briscoe 2013 on technical terms; Hutchinson 2025 on book 8). 16 
Furthermore, Polybius falls into the timeframe of the post-Koine dialects, that is 
the local diversification of the Koine due to language-contact scenarios (Bubenik 
1993; García Ramón 2020). This explains the high number of unique errors in 
Polybius.17       
From the ideational and conceptual issues discussed, two practical issues 
arise. Firstly, the  visibility of texts in digital form as training data for tools 
(such as the Universal Dependencies models) is limited outside of classical 
literary Attic.18 Secondly, the coverage of later and medical texts in open-access 
resources, including dictionaries that we rely on for lemmatisation, is limited.19 
A practical solution to the latter issue would be to draw on specialised 
dictionaries akin to Henderson’s (1991) Maculate Muse  on obscene language 
in Aristophanic comedy. Some such dictionaries exist for the medical and 
historiographic corpora, yet often still in formats that are not easily machine 
readable, for example, Durling collated 3,000 items from the Galenic corpora 
referring to the fields of anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacy, and 
surgery (Durling 1993: VII). However , he admits to have “excluded all those 
writings which have been rejected by modern scholarship” (Durling 1993: 
VIII), which is problematic if we approach the Galenic writings as the work 
by a community of practice developing a discourse rather than one man’s 
work (cf. Nelson 2016 on Hippocrates), as well as to have shortened lengthier

The issue concerning the availability of non-canonical texts in digital formats 
that allow for manipulation and development of tools could be addressed by 
the large-scale digitisation of relevant corpora, yet this is time-consuming and 
will initially render few highlight results.22 More realistic seems the incremental 
building of smaller corpora, such as the  Sketch Engine corpus for the fourth-
century CE Kellis  papyri (Fendel 2026) or the funerary inscriptions from Roman 
Sicily (Fendel 2024a). The  Sketch Engine corpora, and tools to build them, for 
the Galenic and Hippocratic texts as well as Polybius’ Histories are a step into 
this direction. These will eventually grow into a collection that enhances the

Specifically regarding multi-word expressions, there is the additional issue 
that the Universal Dependencies models for (post)classical Greek for instance 
currently do not operate with a language-specific xpos tag for multi-word

suitable for the study of multi-word expressions are ongoing, for instance in 
the form of the  PARSEME Ancient Greek corpus (Fendel, Squeri, and Platanou 
2026).23 Furthermore, a workable step forward may be resources like Temple’s 
Dictionary of Classical Greek Idiom and Syntax  (post-Homeric), which is open 
access and aims to make phraseological units more visible than they are in 
standard dictionaries, to learners, translators, and machines.24

A multi-word expression is a multi-lexemic unit that functions as a single 
unit at the part-of-speech level, for example, the preposition instead of  or the 
verb phrase to make a decision . Multi-word expressions lend themselves as a 
test case as they are  diachronically, distratically, and  diatopically variable in 
every way, i.e. lexically, morphosyntactically, semantically, and pragmatically 
(Fendel 2025b; Fendel 2025c). Thus, they provide “sociocultural, economic, 
and geographical coordinates in time and space” (Tagliamonte 2025: 3). 
Multi-word expressions are  ambiguous, at the lexicon-syntax interface, for 
example, ὀνόματα κατέχω onomata katekhō  “to have names” vs. (in GEMF 
30.77–81) “to hold names (written on twigs)” with a multi-word-expression 
as opposed to a verb-object reading (Fendel 2025a: 124), but also semantico-
pragmatically, for example, ἐν ἀπόρῳ ἔχομαι en aporō ekhomai “to be clueless” 
is used exclusively in historiography (Thucydides and later only in Lucian 
and Cassius Dio) and may thus signpost to the community of practice (Fendel 
2025d: 103–104).
In the medical corpora, the noun  κενεαγγεία  keneaggeia “lowering/evacuant 
treatment, evacuation by bleeding” has a  subject-specific meaning and seems 
to be a  group-internal term, or even coinage. The related verb κενεαγγέω 
keneaggeō “to have the vessels of the body empty, undergo lowering/evacuant 
treatment” and the noun in its Ionic form κενεαγγίη keneaggiē “lowering/
evacuant treatment, evacuation by bleeding” (without iotacism and with raised 
/a/) appear in Liddell-Scott-Jones as does κεναγγία kenaggia “emptiness of 
vessels” which however seems to differ in usage in that it refers to being without 
food, in Plato, Fragments, 156 “hunger” and in Aristophanes, Fragments, 608 
“to fast” with ἄγειν agein “to lead”.25 This latter item appears also in the Perseus 
Digital Library tools that underlie the tagging process.  κενεαγγεία  keneaggeia is 
noticeable because (i) it is not listed (in this form) in standard dictionaries, (ii) 
it is a  group-internal item (having the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae  Text Search 
tool operate on the wordform κενεαγγεί keneaggei returns hits from medical 
texts only), and (iii) it is an item that is frequent in medical texts, not a  hapax 
legomenon or an innovative coinage.

There are two main support verbs with  πορεία  poreia “journey”, that is ποιέω 
poieō “to do” and  χράομαι  khraomai “to use”, along with a range of largely one-

Verbs of realisation are “des verbes collocationnels qui ont le comportement 
syntaxique des Vsupp, mais qui, à la différence de ceux-ci, sont sémantiquement 
pleins” (translation: “collocating verbs which behave syntactically like Vsupp 
but, unlike them, are semantically full/heavy”) (Mel’čuk 2004: 208).
Generally, there is a strong preference for the singular form of the predicative 
noun. This may be linked to the fact that the plural of the predicative noun would 
be particularising whereas the singular seems to be treated like as a mass noun 
(Wittenberg and Levy 2017; Erbach 2025). The combination with ποιέω poieō “to 
do” tends towards invariability, especially morphosyntactically (for example, a 
determiner phrase is always present) and syntactically (i.e. the support verb-
predicative noun order appears in 99% of cases and only a mean of 0.25 items 
intervene between constituents). Where word-order changes, an attributive 
phrase, or the lack of a determiner phrase were contextually required, the 
alternative with  χράομαι  khraomai “to use” seems to have been used (see 
similarly Fendel Submitted-b). If flexibility with regard to the support-verb-
construction field was required additionally and thus usually also an additional

There are two main support verbs with  πορεία  poreia “journey”, that is ποιέω poieō 
“to do” and γίγνομαι gignomai “to happen” (cf. Jiménez López 2021), along with a 
range of one-off  verbs of realisation. There is overall a strong preference for the 
singular over the plural form of the predicative noun both with support verbs and 
with  verbs of realisation. The combination with ποιέω poieō “to do” tends towards 
invariability, especially morphosyntactically (for example, a determiner phrase 
is always present) and syntactically (i.e. the predicative noun-support verb order 
appears in 86% of cases). Where word-order changes or an attributive phrase

There are three noticeable differences between Polybius’ as compared to the 
classical historian’s use of the  support-verb constructions with  πορεία  poreia 
“journey”. Firstly, the word-order preference changes from predicative noun-
support verb in classical times to support verb-predicative noun in post-classical 
times. This may be due to systemic changes in Greek  word order (Horrocks 1990; 
Wahlgren 2024; Aresu and Cabriolu 2024). Yet the fact that these changes affect 
the internal order of the  support-verb construction suggests that the  support-verb 
construction was analytic enough to allow for this (cf. Fendel 2024b; Fendel 2023). 
Secondly, there is a numerical preference for the simplex verb over the  support-
verb construction in classical times which is fully reversed in post-classical times. 
This may be linked to the systemic change to the  middle voice (Gignac 1976: 321–
327; Mandēlaras 1973: 369–371; Vives Cuesta and Acero 2022). Yet it may also be 
that the  support-verb construction was advantageous for discourse coherence 
and cohesion (Fendel and Ireland 2023) or carried an  indexical meaning. Thirdly, 
the support verb  χράομαι  khraomai “to use” does not appear as an option in the 
classical historians but seems Polybius’ go-to option when increased flexibility of 
form was needed. Table 3.5 shows the distribution of πορείᾳ / (πορείαις)  χράομαι

“For they (sc. nerves) go deep (βύθια buthia) through the inner regions of the arm 
into the forearm, having come near the elbow joint, which is fleshless and made of 
bone (?) entirely, and are at risk, if they come to the surface under the naked skin 
on the bones with flesh, to make a journey  that makes one stumble , if nature 
had not found for safety such a solution as it is now.”
In (6), the  support-verb construction in question refers to the movement 
of nerves. The passage retains the conceptual  metaphor of PATH from the 
original meaning of the  support-verb construction. However , the  support-verb 
construction refers no longer to movement across geographical space but to 
movement more generally, in this case within the body (cf. Jiménez Delgado 
and Martínez Vázquez 2011). Noticeably, Galen uses the option with  χράομαι 
 khraomai “to use” when he requires the  support-verb construction to be variable 
enough to allow for an adjective qualifying the predicative noun (σφαλερωτάτῃ 
sphalerōtatē “very likely to make one stumble”). This aligns with Polybius’ use 
and the observation that the option with  χράομαι  khraomai “to use” was created 
in order to restore flexibility in a  support-verb construction that had lost it, i.e. 
the option with ποιέω poieō “to do”.31 While the option with ποιέω poieō “to do”

“I have written these things and (old translation:) made a digression in the 
narrative / (Rusten’s translation:) discarded the plan due to the fact that (...)”
Rusten’s re-interpretation rests on the meaning of λόγος logos in Thucydides 
(“content of speech, plan”) as opposed to other historiographers (for example, 
“unit of narrative” in Herodotus). The meaning of the event noun ἐκβολή ekbolē 
“tossing out” is  ambiguous between “tossing out for consideration” and “tossing 
out due to rejection”. The co-textually defined meaning of the dependent 
genitive pushes us towards the latter meaning (Rusten 2020: 234–235). However , 
noticeably, this metalinguistic remark is rather isolated in Thucydides’ writings 
as he rarely surfaces in his Histories as the narrator (Beasley 2023), unlike, for 
example, Herodotus in his Histories. 
Even if we adopt Rusten’s proposal, the ambiguity may have remained in 
place for a large proportion of the readership and may have been intentional in

the sense of the bridges mentioned in Section 3. Those readers who were part of 
the community of practice may have been familiar with Thucydides’ specific use 
of λόγος logos and his invisibility as a narrator , those who were at the outskirts 
of the community or were looking in from the outside may not have had this 
kind of knowledge. The ambiguity may thus serve as a  gatekeeper . 
6. Summary, conclusion, and outlook 
The chapter has discussed the building and use of  Sketch Engine corpora for the 
(post)classical Greek medical, i.e. writings associated with Hippocrates and Galen, 
and historiographical corpora, especially the writings by Thucydides, Xenophon, 
and Polybius, based on the digitised texts of the Digital Corpus of Graeco-Arabic 
Studies and the Perseus Digital Library .32 The medical and historiographical 
corpora have been considered orderly and principled collections of texts (i.e. 
corpora) from the perspective of a community of practice maintaining and 
curating a discourse which is reflected in their writings (Section 1). We adopted 
and adapted tools previously built and have provided a pipeline that allows for 
further modification and development (Section 2). The  Sketch Engine corpora 
enhance the  visibility of these technical writings, make them accessible and 
searchable, and offer insights especially from  verbal multi-word expressions to 
enhance existing resources and tools. 
We have taken topic as the key criterion to define what texts belong with 
each of the two technical discourses of interest. The texts of each discourse 
reflect a mixture of language features, including features that are specific to the 
in-group ( group-internal features), those that are specific to the subject matter 
discussed (  subject-specific features), those that are ambiguous between in-
group and generic readings (ambiguous features), and entirely generic features. 
Furthermore, it appears that technical writings align with Blake’s slang in being 
inventive and at times opaque while at the same time striving for precision. This 
apparent paradox resolves when we consider that what is maximally precise 
to the in-group, for example, in the form of  group-internal language features, 
may be maximally obscure to the outsider .  Ambiguous features adopt the role of 
 gatekeeping phenomena that can be interpreted correctly by the in-group and 
may appeal to but eventually deceive the outsider (Section 3). 
Such obscurity to the outsider is one factor that has had a far-reaching impact 
on the  visibility and coverage of technical writings in tools and resources. 
Conceptually, we identified the notion of a  classical period and the notion of 
literature as an  aesthetic ideal as critical to technical writings lacking  visibility

for a long time. Ideationally, this resulted in the misidentification of hapax 
legomena, features falsely being labelled exceptions or even mistakes, and 
features being considered marginal incorrectly. Practically, this explains the 
issues surrounding the  visibility of technical writings in digitised corpora and 
their coverage by available tools. Our  Sketch Engine corpora and the tools and 
pipelines to build them in line with the  FAIR data principles are a significant 
step towards addressing these issues (Section 4). 
 Verbal multi-word expressions are a language feature that lacks  visibility 
and coverage in corpora, resources, and tools despite recent advances (for 
example, Fendel and Ireland 2023; Fendel 2024a; Fendel, Squeri, and Platanou 
2026; Fendel 2025c). In the medical and historiographical corpora,  κενεαγγεία 
 keneaggeia “lowering/evacuant treatment, evacuation by bleeding” illustrates the 
necessity of comprehensive corpora in order to avoid omission and mislabelling 
of  group-internal and/or  subject-specific items in resources and corpora. In 
the historiographical corpora,  subject-specific  support-verb constructions of 
the type verb-object with  πορεία  poreia “journey” illustrate the synchronic 
and  diachronic variability in referential and social meanings of  support-verb 
constructions which can only be uncovered by means of large searchable and 
suitably annotated corpora, especially when comparatively rare structures are 
at issue. We should add that currently pragmatic and metatextual annotation 
is a desideratum in our corpora such that instances like Thucydides, Histories, 
1.97.2 remain difficult to discover . While their analysis by means of comparative 
evidence is facilitated by the corpora we have built, these  gatekeeping devices 
are still  gatekeeping.

4.  Old Egyptian multi-word 
expressions in  Unas’ and  Teti’s 
 Pyramid Texts (24th to 23rd c. BCE)
 Roberto A. Díaz Hernández
1. Introduction 
The  Pyramid Texts are a collection of spells recorded on the walls of the pyramids 
of the following Old Kingdom kings and queens:  Unas,  Teti, Pepi I, Merenre, Pepi 
II, Ankhenespepi II, Neith and Ibi. The earliest evidence of these texts is found 
in the pyramid of  Unas (ca. 2321–2306 BCE). The  Pyramid Texts were recited 
during the mortuary rituals carried out for the deceased and they are written in 
 Old Egyptian (ca. 2700–2000 BCE), the earliest stage of the Egyptian language for 
which extensive documentation exists. They have been edited by Sethe (1908–
1922) and more recently by Allen (2013).
Since Sethe’s edition, the  Pyramid Texts have been a valuable resource for 
studying  Old Egyptian, with Edel (1955–1964) using many examples from the 
 Pyramid Texts in his  Old Egyptian Grammar , and Allen (1984) carrying out 
thorough analyses of the verb forms used in the Pyramid Texts. Allen (2017) 
himself has recently begun publishing a grammar for each corpus of  Pyramid 
Texts.1 In addition, Hainline (2026) has conducted a study of linguistic variation 
in the  Pyramid Texts. A morphosyntactic annotation of the  Pyramid Texts 
has also been underway in the Universal Dependencies Egyptian-Pre-  Coptic 
treebank ( EPC treebank henceforth) since March 2024.2 This treebank currently 
contains 34,234 tokens and 3,089 sentences from the Pyramid Texts, 3 of which 
11,664 tokens are from  Unas’  Pyramid Texts and 8,648 are from  Teti’s  Pyramid 
Texts. This chapter provides a morphosyntactic analysis of the multi-word

expressions (MWEs henceforth) that appear in Unas’ and Teti’s Pyramid Texts. 
As part of a project devoted to the synchronic and diachronic use of Egyptian 
MWEs, the MWEs in the  Pyramid Texts of other kings are planned to be studied 
(Díaz Hernández 2024a: 31; 2024b: 112).
An MWE is a (continuous or discontinuous) sequence of words which should 
contain at least two  lexicalised component words and display some degree of 
lexical, morphological, syntactic and/or semantic idiosyncrasy (Savary et al. 
2018: 92), for example “to go bananas”, meaning “to become angry”. 4 Egyptian 
MWEs were identified and categorised according to the PARSEME 2.0 guidelines,5 
which distinguish four main types of MWE acting as specific parts of speech:
1. A  verbal multi-word expression ( VMWE henceforth), which consists of 
a verb as its head, for example to spill the beans.
2. A nominal multi-word expression (NMWE henceforth), which functions 
as a noun, for example hot dog.
3. An adjectival or adverbial multi-word expression (AMWE henceforth), 
which functions as an adjective or adverb respectively, for example 
ice-cold drinks and from time to time.
4. A functional multi-word expression (FMWE henceforth), which 
syntactically acts like a function word—i.e. a determiner , adposition, 
conjunction, or interjection—for example in front of.
Each of these categories comprises subcategories of MWEs which are presented 
at the beginning of each section below. The subcategories found in  Unas’ and 
 Teti’s  Pyramid Texts are explained using examples taken from the  EPC treebank. 
This treebank was recently used to annotate Egyptian MWEs during the 
 PARSEME 2.0 annotation campaign,6 which took place from March to April 2025. 
A total of 633 MWEs were identified in the  EPC treebank during this campaign 
(Savary et al. forthcoming: Table 2). Of these, 338 were found in  Unas’  Pyramid 
Texts and 235 in  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts. This chapter analyses the use of MWEs in 
these two textual corpora as a case study, based on the results achieved during 
the  PARSEME 2.0 annotation campaign.

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages76 
3.  Verbal multi-word expressions
According to  PARSEME guidelines 2.0, there are six types of VMWEs:
1. Verbal idioms ( VIDs), for example to go bananas;
2. Light-verb constructions (  LVCs), characterised by the use of a verb 
with a predicative noun.  If the verb contributes only morphological 
features to the meaning of the whole, it is a full LVC , for example to pay 
a visit. If the verb has a  causative meaning, it is a  causative LVC , for 
example to give a headache;
3. Inherently reflexive verbs (  IRVs). These can be classified into two 
types: those that are always used with a reflexive pronoun, such as 
the Spanish verb suicidarse (“to commit suicide”), and those that are 
occasionally used with a reflexive pronoun to express a different 
meaning to that of the original verb without a reflexive pronoun, for 
example to help oneself means to take something without asking, which 
is different from the meaning of the verb to help;
4. Idiomatic verb- particle constructions (  IVPCs), which can be full if the 
 particle changes the meaning of the verb, for example to do in, or semi 
non- compositional if the  particle adds a predictable meaning to the 
verb, for example to eat up;
5. Multi-verb constructions ( MVCs), for example to let go;
6. Inherently adpositional verbs (  IAVs), which are characterised by the 
use of a preposition that is either always required or , if absent, changes 
the meaning of the verb, for example to come across.
3.1 Verbal idioms
The use of  VIDs is common in  Unas’ and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, often consisting 
of a verb and a body-part noun,8 which may be: ꞽb (“heart”) (18x); ꜥw (“arm”) 
(7x); rʾ (“mouth”) (2x); rṭ (“foot, leg”) (2x); ḥꜣ.t(ꞽ) (“heart”) (3x); ḥr (“face”) (5x); śꜣ 
(“back”) (1x); and č̣̣r .t (“hand”) (1x), for example:

“Platz nehmen”, see Wb. IV 6, 6). Here, the verb ꞽri (“to make”) has little semantic 
content, in contrast to the predicative noun ś.t (“place, seat”) which expresses the 
action of sitting.
In contrast,  causative  LVCs are common in  Unas’ and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts. These 
can be classified according to the verb used as their head: those consisting of 
ꞽri̯  (“to do, to make”) (10x), wṭi̯  (“to put”) (1x) and r č̣ ̣i̯ (“to give, to cause”) (4x). 
Compare:
(4)  Pyramid Texts 500c  Unas (PT 500c W)
ꞽr ⸗f n ⸗k ꞽꜣ ꞽꜣ
make:sbjv =3sg.m for-prep =2sg.m adoration-m.sg adoration-m.sg
LT: “He shall make for you adoration (on) adoration.”
FT: “He shall adore you over and over .”
(5)  Pyramid Texts 302c  Unas (PT 302c W)
ꞽw (w)ṭ.n Wnꞽś n r. w ⸗f m ꞽb ⸗śn
aux put:pst  Unas-kn fear-m.sg =3sg.m in:prep heart-m.sg =3pl
LT: “Unas  has put his fear in the heart of them.”
FT: “Unas  has instilled fear in them.”

(6)  Pyramid Texts 197d Unas  (PT 197d W)
č̣ ̣i̯ ⸗č̣ mrw.t Wnꞽś pn
give:sbjv =2sg.f love-m.sg  Unas-kn dem:m.sg
LT: “You should give the love of this Unas .”
FT: “You should spread Unas’  love.”
In  causative  LVCs, there is a semantic difference between ꞽri̯  “to do, to make” 
and r č̣ ̣i̯  “to give”—the former emphasises the realisation of a fact, i.e. a factitive 
action, while the latter focusses on the cause of an action. This becomes clear 
when ꞽri̯  “to do, to make” and r č̣ ̣i̯ “to give” are used with the same noun. Compare:

FT: “It (the Eye of Horus) shall acclaim you before the gods.”

č̣ ̣i̯ ⸗č̣ kꞽ.t Wnꞽś pn

FT: “You should spread Unas’s  acclaim.”
3.3 Inherently reflexive verbs
As the verb ś:ms “to proceed” is only attested with the reflexive pronoun  św 
“himself” ( Pyramid Texts 10c Queen Neith (PT 10c N); see also Wb. V 141, 14), it 
can be considered as an IRV that is always formed with a clitic. Unas’  and  Teti’s 
 Pyramid Texts also contain the following  IRVs which have a different meaning

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages80 
to the original verb without a reflexive pronoun: ꞽ:ꜥbꜣ č̣w (“to make yourself 
ready”), cf. ꜥbꜣ (“to provide”); ś:mn św (“to establish himself”), cf. ś:mn (“to make 
firm”); ꞽ:ms kw (“to betake yourself”), Wb. II 135, cf. ms (“to bring”); and č̣s.y ⸗f św 
(“he may raise himself, i.e. get up”), Wb. V 406, cf. č̣si̯ (“to lift up”). For example:
(9)  Pyramid Texts 317c Unas ( PT 317c W)
č̣s.y ⸗f św
raise:sbjv =3sg.m 3sg.m
LT: “He shall raise himself.”
FT: “He shall get up.”
(10)  Pyramid Texts 294c  Teti (PT 294c T)
č̣s.y Ttꞽ pn nn
lift up:fut  Teti-kn dem:m.sg dem:sg
“This  Teti will lift up this.”
Comment: The literal meaning of č̣si̯  is “to lift up” something, as in (10). However , 
when used with a reflexive pronoun, it takes on the figurative meaning of “to lift 
oneself up” (i.e. “to get up”), as in (9).
3.4 Multi-verb constructions
There are no instances of multi-verb constructions in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid 
Texts. However , this type of MWE is used with verbs of motion in  Old Egyptian, 
for example:
(11) Siege et al. (2024: 80–82)
šm<.t> ꞽw.t
go:inf come:inf
LT: “Going and coming” (Fischer 1977: 115–119).
FT: “A visit.”

Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts also provide instances of inherently adpositional

original meaning, for example ꞽri̯  r (“ to act against (sb.)”), cf. ꞽri̯  (“to do, to 
make”), pẖr n (“to serve (sb.)”), cf. pẖr (“to turn round”), and śč̣̣m n (“to listen to 
(sb.), to obey”), cf. śč̣̣m (“to hear”):

ꞽr ⸗k ꞽr ⸗k
do:sbjv =2sg.m to:prep =2sg.m
LT: “You shall do to you.”
FT: “You shall act against yourself.”

4.  Nominal multi-word expressions
The  PARSEME guidelines 2.0 distinguish three types of NMWEs:

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages82 
1. Nominal idioms ( NIDs), e.g. hot dog;
2.  Pronominal idioms ( PronIDs), e.g. we love each other;
3. Deverbal nominal MWE ( NV), e.g. heart breaker, derived from the VID 
to break one’s heart.
Additionally, there are nominal idioms consisting of  nisba adjectives used as 
nouns in  Old Egyptian (see Section 4.4).
4.1 Nominal idioms
In Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts,  body-part nouns are usually used as modifiers 
in nominal idioms, for example:
(15)  Pyramid Texts 208b Unas ( PT 208b W)
šn č̣w ẖnw- ꜥw.w(ꞽ) mw.t ⸗k
enfold:sbjv 2sg.m interior-m.sg arm-m.du mother-f.sg =2sg.m
LT: “The interior of the arms of your mother shall enfold you.”
FT: “The embrace of your mother shall enfold you.”
Comment: The word ꜥw.w(ꞽ) is the dual of ꜥw (“arm”) and it cannot change its 
number when used with ẖnw (“interior”) in the MWE ẖnw-ꜥw.w(ꞽ) (“embrace”) 
(Wb. III 372, 6).
Other  body-part nouns are also used in  NIDs, for example: 
1.  tꜣ-rṭ(.w) (“ground (for) feet”, i.e. “stairway”) (PT 365a W);
2.  ś.t-ꞽb (“place (of the) heart”, i.e. “favourite place”) (PT 414c W);
3.  sꜣ n(.ꞽ) ẖ.t (“son of (my) belly”, i.e. “(my) bodily son”) (PT 1d T).
 NIDs without  body-part nouns also occur in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, for 
example: 
1.  mṭw-nč̣r (“god’s word”, i.e. “sacred writings”) (PT 333c T, 
see also Wb. II 181, 1);
2.  bw-mꜣꜥ (“the place of truth”, i.e. “correctness, justice”) (PT 4c T, 
see also Wb. II 14, 12);
3.  ś.t ḥtp.w (“place of peace”, i.e. “place of rest”) (PT 508b W, 
see also Wb. IV 5, 10).

4.2  Pronominal idioms
The following pronominal idioms occur in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts: pw-
nn (“this here”,10 i.e. “this one”); wꜥ pn (“one, this”, i.e. “this one”); wꜥ ⸗śn(ꞽ) (“one 
of both”, i.e. “one of them”); č ̣.t ⸗ś (“her body”, i.e. “herself”); and  č̣̣ś ⸗f (“his 
person”, i.e. “himself”):

son-m.sg =2sg.m cop dem:m.sg here:adv

FT: “Your son is this one.”

wꜥ ⸗śn(ꞽ) m pn gś
one-m.sg =3du on:prep dem:m.sg one-m.sg

4.3  Deverbal nominal MWEs
The head of deverbal nominal MWEs is usually a  participle used as a noun, 
for example, ḫśr-nč̣r (“one who repels the god”, i.e. “scorpion”) (  Pyramid Texts 
227b Unas ( PT 227b W)). However , it can also be an infinitive or a noun derived 
from a verb, for example, pr(.t)-ḫrw (“going out of the voice”, i.e. “invocation 
offering”) ( Pyramid Texts 59d Unas ( PT 59d W)) and ꞽꜥ.w-rʾ (“washing the mouth”, 
i.e. “breakfast”) ( Pyramid Texts 60a Unas (  PT 60a W)). There are three types of 
deverbal nominal MWEs in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts. Deverbal nominal 
derived from a VID ( NV.VID), for example:

be sweet:inf heart-m.sg

FT: “Happiness.”

4.4 Nisba idioms in  nominal function
An  adjectival MWE consisting of a  nisba adjective becomes a nominal idiom 
when the  nisba adjective is used as a noun, for example:
(24)  Pyramid Texts 211a Unas ( PT 211a W)
nꞽ ꞽm(.ꞽ)- rṭ ⸗k
not-neg one who is in-m.sg foot-m.sg =2sg.m
LT: “There is no one who is in your foot.”
FT: “You have no enemy.”
Comment: The  nisba adjective ꞽm(.ꞽ) (“one who is in”) derives from the preposition 
m (“in”). It forms a compound with the noun rṭ (“foot”). The idiosyncratic meaning 
of ꞽm(.ꞽ)-rṭ (“foot”) results from the Egyptian custom of decorating sandals with 
images of enemies to be trodden upon.
Nisba idioms in nominal function are common in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, 
especially those consisting of  body-part nouns used as modifiers, for example:

one who concerns-m.sg 3sg.m =2sg.m
LT: “One concerning him (relating to) you.”
FT: “Your relative.”
5. Adjectival and  adverbial MWEs
Three types of  adjectival and  adverbial MWEs can be distinguished in the 2.0 
 PARSEME guidelines:
1. Adjectival idioms ( AdjIDs), e.g. a bottom-up algorithm;
2. Adverbial idioms ( AdvIDs), e.g. by and large;
3. Deverbal  adjectival and  adverbial MWEs MWE (AV), e.g. a run-down 
apartment, derived from the IVPC to run down.
Additionally, there are adjectival idioms consisting of  nisba adjectives in  Old 
Egyptian. Deverbal  adverbial MWEs are unattested in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid 
Texts.
5.1 Adjectival idioms
The following adjectival sentence is used as an  adjectival idiom in Unas’  and 
 Teti’s  Pyramid Texts:
(27)  Pyramid Texts 195c Unas ( PT 195c W)
nfr w(ꞽ) ḥr ⸗č̣
good- m.sg ptcl face-m.sg =2sg.f

LT: “How goodly is your face.”
FT: “How nice it is to see you.”
5.2 Adverbial idioms
These  adverbial MWEs usually consist of a preposition and a noun, for example 
m-sp “at once”, (28), and n č̣̣.t “for ever”, (29):
(28)  Pyramid Texts 590c  Teti (PT 590c T)
ꞽn.n ⸗f n ⸗k nč̣r(.w) nb(.w) m- sp
bring:pst =3sg.m to:prep =2sg.m god-m.pl every-m.pl in:prep time-m.sg
LT: “He brought all the gods to you (certainly) in time.”
FT: “It is at once that he brought all the gods to you.”
(29)  Pyramid Texts 160c Unas ( PT 160c W)
sꜣ ⸗k pw n(.ꞽ) č̣ ̣.t ⸗k n č̣ ̣.t
son-m.sg =2sg.m dem:m.sg of-m.sg body-f.sg =2sg.m for:prep eternity-f.sg
LT: “Your son of your body is this for the eternity.”
FT: “He is your bodily son for ever .”
Adverbial idioms can also be noun phrases used as adverbs, for example rꜥw nb 
“every day”:
(30)  Pyramid Texts 123k  Teti (PT 123k T)
śč̣ ̣r Ttꞽ wč̣̣ꜣ(.w) rꜥw nb
lie down:sbjv  Teti-kn be healthy:ossc.3sg.m sun-m.sg each-m.sg
LT: “Teti  shall lie down being in good health each sun.”
FT: “Teti  shall lie down in good health every day.”
5.3 Deverbal adjectival MWEs
According to their morphosyntactic use in Unas’  and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, two 
types of deverbal adjectival MWEs can be distinguished: those consisting of 
a  participle as an adjectival modifier and those consisting of a  participle or a

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages88 
verbal adjective modified by a noun (i.e. a bahuvrīhi construction, also known 
as a “limitation” in Egyptology) (Peust 2008: 64–66).11 In the first type, the verb is 
used as a  participle to modify an antecedent, for example:
(31)  Pyramid Texts 511c Unas ( PT 511c W)
pśč̣̣.(w)t śč̣̣m.t mṭw ꞽtꞽ.w
Ennead- f.pl hear-ptcp.act(f.sg) word-m.sg monarch-m.sg
LT: “(...) The Enneads which hear the word of the monarch.”
FT: “(...) The Enneads which hear the case of the monarch.”
Comment: The AMWE śč̣̣m.t mṭw derives from the  VMWE śč̣̣m mṭw (cf. example 
(2) above).
A deverbal  adjectival MWE can also consist of a  participle or a verbal adjective 
derived from a verb used in a  VMWE, for example:
(32)  Pyramid Texts 507b Unas ( PT 507b W)
 (...)
Wnꞽś pꞽ Śbk (...) rś ḥr č̣s ḥꜣ.t
 Unas-kn cop Sobek-gn be watchful- 
ptcp.act(m.sg)
face-m.sg raised- 
ptcp.act(m.sg)
brow-f.sg
LT: “Unas is  Sobek (...), watchful of face, raised of brow.”
FT: “Unas is  Sobek (...), a vigilant and bold one.”
Comment: In this example, rś ḥr derives from the  VMWE rś ḥr (“watchful of face”, 
i.e. “vigilant”) (Wb. II 450, 17) and č̣s ḥꜣ.t from the  VMWE č̣si̯  ḥꜣ.t (“raised of brow”, 
i.e. “courageous” or similar).12
5.4 Nisba-adjective idioms
In  Old Egyptian,  nisba adjectives can be formed from nouns and prepositions by 
adding the ꞽ-ending. For example, the  nisba adjective n.ꞽ (“belonging to”) derives 
from the preposition n (“for”). An adverbial idiom consisting of a preposition 
and a noun can therefore be transformed into an  adjectival idiom, by using the 
 nisba adjective of the preposition. This occasionally occurs in Unas’  and  Teti’s

As is common in Unas’ and    Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, a compound preposition can

6.  Functional MWEs
According to the  PARSEME guidelines 2.0, there are four types of functional MWEs:
1. Determiner idioms ( DetIDs), e.g. every other day;
2. Adposition idioms ( AdpIDs), e.g. in front of the station;
3. Conjunction idioms (  ConjIDs), e.g. she was fortunate in that  she had 
friends to help her;
4. Interjection idioms ( IntjIDs), e.g. damn it!.
These types are all found in Unas’ and   Teti’s  Pyramid Texts.
6.1 Determiner idioms
Two determiner idioms are used in Unas’  Pyramid Texts, whereas this MWE 
category is not found in  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts:
(36)  Pyramid Texts 460b Unas (PT  460b W)
nn n(.ꞽ) rm.wt nč̣r
dem of-m.sg mourning-f.sg god-m.sg
LT: “This of mourning of the god.”
FT: “This mourning of the god.”
(37)  Pyramid Texts 264b Unas (PT  264b W)
nw n(.ꞽ) sšsš
dem of-m.sg lotus-m.sg
LT: “This of lotus.”
FT: “This lotus.”
Comment: The determiner idioms nn n (.ꞽ) and nw n (.ꞽ) show an idiosyncratic 
syntactic structure, consisting of the demonstratives nn and nw followed by the 
 nisba adjective n(.ꞽ) (“belonging to”, i.e. “of”) (Edel 1955–1964: 89 (§ 199)).

4. Old Egyptian multi-word expressions in Unas’ and Teti’s Pyramid Texts 91
6.2 Adposition idioms
In  Old Egyptian, adposition idioms are exclusively compound prepositions, i.e. 
fixed expressions which usually consist of a preposition followed by a noun, for 
example:
(38)  Pyramid Texts 735c Teti  (PT 735c T)
(...) m- ꜥb nč̣r(.w)
in:prep association-m.sg god-m.pl
LT: “(...) In association with the gods.”
FT: “(...) In company with the gods.”
(39)  Pyramid Texts 477c Unas (PT  477c W)
 
(...) mr ḳṭ ꞽ r. y n ⸗f ꞽm
according to:prep form-m.sg do-ptcp.pass(m.sg) for:prep =3sg.m there:adv
LT: “(...) According to the form which was done for him there.”
FT: “(...) In accordance with how it was done for you.”
The noun of a compound preposition is usually a  body-part noun. There are 
twelve compound prepositions  consisting of a  body-part noun in Unas’ and   
 Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, for example:
(40)  Pyramid Texts 270d Unas (PT  270d W)
(...) m- ṭp kꜣ
at:prep head-m.sg bull-m.pl
LT: “(...) At the head of the bull.”
FT: “(...) Before the bull.”
A compound preposition can occasionally be formed by the combination of 
a preposition, a  nisba adjective derived from a preposition and a noun, for 
example:

(41)  Pyramid Texts 582a Teti  (PT 582a T)
(...) m- ḥr(.ꞽ)- ꞽb ⸗f
in:prep one who is on - nisba.nom heart-m.sg =3sg.m
LT: “(...) In the one who is on his heart.”
FT: “(...) In his midst.”
Compound prepositions consisting of two prepositions are also used in the 
 Pyramid Texts of Unas and  Teti , for example: 
(42)  Pyramid Texts 130c Unas (PT  130c W)
ꜥꜣb.t ⸗f m- m ⸗č̣n
food-offerings-f.sg =3sg.m in:prep in:prep =2pl
LT: “His food offerings are in-in you.”
FT: “His food offerings are among you.”
6.3  Conjunction idioms
Two conjunction idioms with a causal meaning are attested in Unas’ and    Teti’s 
 Pyramid Texts: n-n.tt (three times in Unas and  once in Teti ), meaning “for that 
which is” i.e. “on account of the fact that” (i.e. “because”); and n-ꞽw.t (six times 
in Teti ), meaning “for which not” (i.e. “because not”). The former consists of the 
preposition n (“for”) and the substantivised form of the relative pronoun n.tꞽ, 
meaning “that which is” (Borghouts 2010: 123 (23.b.3); see also Schenkel 2012: 
337–338). For example:
(43)  Pyramid Texts 121b Unas (PT  121b W)
 
(...) n- n.tt śwt ꞽś kꜣ wr
for:prep that-which-is 3sg.m ptcl bull-m.sg great-m.sg
LT: “(...) On account of the fact that he is certainly the Great Bull.”
FT: “(...) Because he is certainly the Great Bull.”

4. Old Egyptian multi-word expressions in Unas’ and Teti’s Pyramid Texts 93
(44)  Pyramid Texts 659d Teti  (PT 659d T)
 
(...) n- ꞽw.t mw.t ⸗k mś.tꞽ č̣w m rmč̣(.w)
for:prep that-not mother-f.sg =2sg.m bear: 
prf-3sg.f
2sg.m in:prep man-m.pl
LT: “(...) For which no mother of yours bore you among men.”
FT: “(...) Because no mother of yours bore you among men.”
Comment: The conjunction idiom n-ꞽw.t is formed by combining the preposition 
n (“for”) and the negative  particle ꞽw.t (“that not”) derived from the adjective ꞽw.tꞽ 
(“who is without”) (Borghouts 2010: 124 (23.b.3); see also Schenkel 2012, 337 and 339).
6.4 Interjection idioms
There are two  common interjection idioms in Unas’ and    Teti’s  Pyramid Texts: 
m⸗k (“behold you!”, i.e. “look!”) and (ꞽ)r⸗f (“as to him”, i.e. “indeed”):
(45)  Pyramid Texts 333a Unas (PT  333a W)
m ⸗k Wnꞽś pr(.w)
behold:imp =2sg.m  Unas-kn go:ossc.3sg.m
LT: “Behold you! Unas has  gone up.”
FT: “Look! Unas has  gone up.”
(46)  Pyramid Texts 159b Unas (PT  159b W)
ꞽꞽ r ⸗f Wnꞽś pn
come:pst as for:prep =3sg.m  Unas-kn dem:m.sg
LT: “As for him, this Unas came.” 
FT: “Indeed, this Unas came.” 
Comment: The interjection idiom m⸗k consists of m, probably an obsolete  imperative 
meaning “behold!” (Gardiner 1957: 178 (§ 234)), and a second person suffix pronoun 
“you”. It is used to draw the listener’s attention. As for (ꞽ)r ⸗f, this is originally formed 
by the preposition (ꞽ)r (“as to”) and a suffix pronoun which varies depending on the 
context. This interjection idiom has an emphatic meaning (Gardiner 1957: 186 (§ 252)).

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages94 
7. Conclusion
This study has revealed that most  PARSEME categories of MWEs are used in 
Unas’ and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts. Multi-verb constructions and idiomatic verb-
 particle constructions are the only exceptions. In contrast,  Old Egyptian had two 
language-specific MWE types characterised by the use of  nisba adjectives (see 
Sections 4.4. and 5.4).
 Although MWEs are used uniformly in Unas’ and  Teti’s  Pyramid Texts, 
some differences have been found between the two textual corpora. For 
example, NMWEs are more common in Unas’  Pyramid Texsots than in  Teti’s, 
and determiner idioms are only attested in the former . These variations may be 
attributed to  compositional or stylistic factors rather than sociolinguistic issues, 
such as the use of dialectal expressions.
Finally, this work has paved the way for identifying  Old Egyptian MWEs, 
enabling us to find and categorise more of them in the rest of the  Pyramid Texts 
and other Egyptian texts once the morphosyntactic annotation of these texts 
in the  EPC treebank is complete. This will contribute to the development of 
synchronic and  diachronic studies on the use of Egyptian MWEs.

5.  Assessing verb- particle 
constructions through classical 
Greek  preverbation (8th to  
4th c. BCE)
 Elena Squeri
1. Background, methodology, and purpose
This chapter tests the possibility of treating classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs, for 
example, ἀπο-βάλλω apo-ballō “to throw away”, and verb- particle constructions 
(VPCs henceforth), for example, English to give away, as instantiations of a cross-
linguistic comparative concept (Haspelmath 2010). 1 It further aims to identify 
some first categories for a more thorough corpus study of classical Greek  pre-
verbed verbs while also employing the semantic and morphosyntactic data thus 
acquired to better define English VPCs. 
1.1 Verb- particle constructions,  phrasal verbs, and  preverbation
The descriptive category of  phrasal verb is peculiar to the English language 
(Dehé 2002: ch. 1; Thim 2012: ch. 2; Luo 2019: ch. 1). It refers to verb-  particle 
combinations achieving a shared predication, with different degrees of 
idiosyncrasy in meaning, for example, to go out  and to give up . The category 
of verb- particle constructions, considered sometimes synonymous (Dehé 2002: 
1; McIntyre 2015) sometimes more inclusive (Luo 2019: §1.2) than the one of 
 phrasal verbs, is well represented in Germanic languages (Thim 2012: §2.5), but 
is overall well attested typologically, also outside of the Indo-European family 
(Thim 2012: §3.1.1). The positioning of the  particle before or after the verb is

not a separating feature, being influenced by the  word order preferred by each 
(stage of a) language (Thim 2012: ch. 3).
The category of  preverbs on the other hand is a “descriptive notion in Indo-
European linguistics. It refers to morphemes that appear before a verb, and 
which form a close semantic unit with that verb. In many cases, the morpheme 
that functions as a  preverb can also function without a preverbal context, often 
as an adverb or an adposition” (Booij and van Kemenade 2003: 1). Classical 
Greek  preverbs occur before a verb but can also head prepositional phrases, 
their adverbial use being only attested in Homeric Greek. 
Therefore,  pre-verbed verbs instantiate in a single lexeme, while VPCs are 
realised as verb-governed multi-word expressions (MWEs henceforth), i.e. 
complex predicates (McIntyre 2015: §3). However , in older Indo-European 
languages,  preverbs and verbs could still occur separately, their cohesion 
increasing  diachronically (Pinault 1995). This stage is testified by Homeric Greek 
“tmesis” (McConnel 2025: ch. 5), often suggesting the parallel with “  phrasal 
verbs” (Horrocks 1981; Pompei 2014).
(1) Homer , Iliad, 1.437
ἐκ  δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ  βαῖνον  
ek  de kai autoi  bainon  
outside prt and them.nom.pl.m step.aor .ind.act.3pl
“And they all stepped outside.”
(2) Homer , Odyssey, 7.284–285
ποταμοῖο  ἐκβὰς  
potamoio  ekbas 
river .gen.m.pl step-out.aor .prtc.act.nom.sg.m
“Stepping out from the river .”
In Classical Greek, verb and  preverb are  univerbated, but can still be 
separated by the augment (pres. ἐκβαίνω ekbainō—impf. ἐξ̣ έβαινον ex-e-
bainon), which was by then a standardised tense marker (Willi 2018: ch.7), 
and by reduplication characterising perfect stems (pf. ἐκβέβηκα ek-be-bēka). 
Therefore, while escaping an interpretation as MWEs, classical Greek  pre-
verbed verbs represent a further stage in the evolution of VPCs from complex 
predicates to complex verbs (Booij and van Kemenade 2003), i.e. verbs whose 
meaning is still perceived as produced by two (or more) constituting elements, 
even though the possibility of identifying the exact contribution of each of 
them varies.

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 101
1.2 Objectives and theoretical framework
Much debate has surrounded the criteria for establishing if, in VPCs, the  particle 
is part of the predicate or an independent head. The  univerbation of classical 
Greek  pre-verbed verbs apparently ensures the inclusion of the meaning of the 
 particle into the predicate (Section 3.2), allowing us to address the problem from 
a different perspective and rather defining a range of effects triggered by such 
inclusion (Section 3.3) at the morphosyntax-semantics interface (van Valin 2005). 
The theoretical framework adopted here is the lexical  decomposition of 
predicates in event-structure patterns (van Valin and LaPolla 1997: §3.2; Rappaport 
Hovav and Levin 1998; Levin and Rappaport Hovav 2005). This representation 
highlights how the varying syntax of verb phrases reflects the distinguishing 
semantic trait of the lexical meaning of their head, the constant (Grimshaw 
2005: ch. 2), and the relative  Aktionsart (Vendler 1957; Dowty 1979). Therefore, 
it efficiently illustrates how the semantico-syntactic effects triggered by adding 
a  particle to the predicate also depend on the meaning of the verbal component.
In lexical  decomposition, a first distinction is drawn between verbs whose 
constant (in angle brackets) identifies a state (Section 1.2.1) or a specific way of 
acting (manner verbs (Section 1.2.2)). 
1.2.1 (Change-of-)state verbs
When verbs involving a state predicate are static, this state is predicated as a 
condition of the subject.
I. States
[x<STATE>]
e.g. stink
This apartment stinks
[apartment<STINK>]
If they are dynamic, as represented by the BECOME operator , the relevant  change 
of state is predicated, (II), of the subject or , (III), of the object, as the result of the 
action of the subject.
II. Intransitive achievements/accomplishments = unaccusatives/anticausatives 
(Perlmutter 1978; Haspelmath 1993)
[BECOME [x<STATE>]]
e.g. break [intr .]; melt [intr .], fall
The ice melted 
[BECOME [ice<MELTED>]]

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages102 
III. Causative achievements/accomplishments 
[[x ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [y<STATE>]]]
e.g. break [tr .]; melt [tr .]; expel [tr .]
The polar bear broke the ice
[[polar bear ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [ice<BROKEN>]]] 
The  change of state may also consist in a  change of position (fall, expel), involving 
a Theme rather than a Patient.2
1.2.2 Manner verbs 
The constant of manner verbs predicates how the subject acts, also as a manner 
of movement ( run). It is thus coded in the subevent representing the agentive 
role of the subject.
IV. Intransitive activities = unergatives
[x ACT<MANNER>]
e.g. run, eat [intr .], laugh, wipe [intr .] 
Tom ate (during the entire lesson)
[Tom ACT<EAT>]
Tom laughed (during the entire dinner)
[Tom ACT<LAUGH>]
This way of acting may secondarily entail a  change of state and/or position 
(wipe [tr .]) on another entity. Therefore, these verbs enter the so-called activity/
accomplishment  alternation (van Valin 2013: §4.2.1), between  transitive and 
intransitive uses. Differently from  causative alterations, (II) and (III), however , 
the subject remains the external  causer in both variants. These verbs can also 
be distinguished by the object they may take. Some involve Patient objects (eat), 
while others involve cognate objects of eventive value, doubling the constant of 
the verb in nominal form (laugh) and forcing a reinterpretation of the subject as 
producing a specific event rather than simply performing an action (see further 
Squeri 2026).
V. Transitive active accomplishments
[[x ACT<MANNER>] & CAUSE [BECOME [y<STATE>]]]
e.g. eat [tr .]; laugh [tr .]
Tom ate a bag of chips
2 The classification as Theme or Patient has the purpose of distinguishing between undergoers 
involved in either a  change of position or a  change of state (Levin–Rappaport Hovav 2005: §2.4).

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 103
[[Tom ACT<EAT>] & CAUSE [BECOME [bag of chips<EATEN>]]]
Tom laughed a scornful laugh
[[Tom ACT<LAUGH>] & CAUSE [BECOME [laugh<EXISTENT>]]]
These verbs lexically determine the way in which the subject acts to entail a 
 change of state or produce a specific product. Therefore, the type of  change of 
state the object undergoes or the type of produced event is bound by the verb 
meaning. This guarantees the consequentiality of the subevents, represented by 
“&” (van Valin and LaPolla 1997: 109). Weren’t these blocks logically implicated, 
we would be facing two separate actions, represented by two verb phrases. 
2. Defining the syntax and semantics of verb- particle 
constructions
The criteria for labelling VPCs vary especially in terms of inclusiveness (Dehé 
2002: §1.2; Thim 2012: ch. 4; Luo 2019: §1.2), as results from the large array of 
theoretical frameworks applied to their study (Luo 2019: §2.1–2) and from the 
variety of languages analysed. Differently from  phrasal verbs, for instance, German 
 separable verbs allow for the  particle to be both  univerbated and separated from 
the verb. To start from a language-unspecific definition, this chapter adopts the 
one elaborated by the  PARSEME initiative (Savary et al. 2018), which studies VPCs 
as a category of  verbal multi-word expressions (VMWEs henceforth), annotated in 
a corpus of more than thirty varieties. VMWEs are predicates surfacing as (more 
or less regular) verb phrases rather than as single verbal lexemes, for example, 
to take a nap, to take the bullet, and to take off. They can thus be considered the 
lexical representation of complex predicates, “predicates which are multi-headed; 
they are composed of more than one grammatical element (either morphemes or 
words), each of which contributes part of the information ordinarily associated 
with a head” ( Alsina, Bresnan and Sells 1997: 1; see also Amberber , Baker and 
Harvey 2010; Nash and Samveilan 2016).
2.1 Criteria for identifying verb- particle constructions
 PARSEME’s definition of VPCs combines two key characteristics: (a) the 
combination of verb and  particle in forming a single predicate, and, (b) the 
idiomaticity of the resulting meaning (Dehé 2002; Thim 2012; Luo 2019).
As for criterion (a), the guidelines insist on the need for the  particle to be 
part of the  VMWE rather than the head of an autonomous prepositional phrase: 
verbs and  particles would not be annotated in (3), (4) and (5).

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages104 
(3) Tom sang (loudly) in his room (for the entire afternoon). 
(4) Tom composed a song in his room.
(5) Tom took his hat off his head. 
In (3) and (4) the preposition introduces an adjunct, and, thus, it is not part of the 
internal representation of the predicate (van Valin and LaPolla 1997: §4.4.1.1).
(3a) In his room [Tom ACT<SING>]
(4a) In his room [[Tom ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [song<EXISTENT>]]]
In (5), however , the preposition introduces an argument, and, therefore, is a 
constituting element of the predicated event (Jackendoff 2002: §4). 
(5a) [[Tom ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [hat<OFF-HIS-HEAD>]]]
In (3) and (4) the full prepositional phrase can be omitted, but the  particle 
cannot be left in the sentence. In (5), on the other hand, one can omit the phrase, 
provided that the  particle is left, showing that it is part of the predicate, (6).
(6) Tom took his hat off.
The  particle (not) taking up a role in the predicate does not depend on the 
(in) transitivity of the verb: both compose and put are  transitive, with a shared 
event template. What is relevant is the lexical meaning of the verb: compose 
predicates a  change of state from non-existence to existence, while put predicates 
a  change of position, whose characteristics need to be specified. The content 
introduced by the  particle does not represent the element undergoing the 
predicated  change of position but rather qualifies it, either alone or by heading 
an argument.
The fact that, once its argument is omitted, the  particle can raise to direct 
adjacency to the verb, (7), demonstrates its inclusion in the predicate (see Dehé 
2002: §1.1 and ch. 4–5; Luo 2019: ch. 4 on the unstable  word order of English 
VPCs and the pragmatic reasons triggering the different configurations). 
(7) Tom took off his hat. 
When separated from the verb, the  particle maintains its predicative position, 
following the element of which the state it represents is predicated (Los et al. 
2012: §2.4). In (6), off occupies the same position as red in we painted the room red.
It remains to be established if verb and  particle combine in a compound or 
a phrase (Goldberg 2016). English is a (partially) satellite-framed language, i.e. 
a language in which the direction of movements predicated by verbs tends to 
be expressed externally from the verbal lexeme (Talmy 2007: §2.6), contrarily 
to what happens in verb-framed languages, like Romance ones. Italian would 
render (5) as (8) and (6) and (7) as (9).

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 105
(8) Tommaso si è tolto il cappello dalla testa.
(9) Tommaso si è tolto il cappello.
Take off surfaces as a phrase, but, semantically, is equivalent to the Italian 
lexeme togliere. Off having an autonomous lexical representation, though, also 
allows for its use as the head of the argument it governs, whereas Italian needs 
to introduce it with a new preposition (dalla). 
Structures like take off , therefore, cannot be excluded from VPCs because 
they do not meet the conditions for being classified as VMWEs. Their exclusion 
follows from the  compositionality of their meaning: they do not meet criterion 
(b), establishing for VPCs a (partial) idiosyncrasy in meaning (Luo 2019, 7). This 
is why  PARSEME relabelled VPCs as I(diomatic)VPCs. (10) and (11) would qualify 
as such, idiomaticity being guaranteed by the impossibility of the  particle to 
head a prepositional phrase.
(10) Tom turned down the offer/turned the offer down. 
(*Tom turned the offer down the drain.)
(11) Tom ate up the cake/ate the cake up.
(*Tom ate the cake up his nose.)
 PARSEME further distinguishes between cases, like (10), in which idiomaticity is 
so strong that one cannot compute what element of the  VMWE contributes what 
part of the overall meaning (IVPC.full), and cases, like (11), in which one can still 
identify what part of the overall meaning is contributed by the  particle (IVPC.semi), 
even though different from the meaning the  particle would have outside the IVPC.
In  IVPCs.semi, the verbal head does not shift from its original meaning, and 
the  particle alone loses its locative value. Therefore, one can still distribute the 
meaning represented by the lexical elements of  IVPCs.semi between the blocks 
of the event. It suffices to allow a different meaning to the  particle, specifically 
a  telicising one ( up = completely). This is why  IVPCs.semi are also labelled as 
aspectual VPCs (Dehé 2002: §1.2; Luo 2019: §1.3): the type of  change of state is 
still identified by the lexical meaning of the verb, to maintain consequentiality, 
but the  particle insists on its completeness.
(11a) [[Tom ACT<EAT>] & CAUSE [BECOME up [the cake<EATEN>]]] 
The increase in  telicity triggered by the  particle also affects the  transitivity of 
the verb: eat can also occur intransitively, with a null object ( Tom already ate; 
Section 1.2.2). This is impossible for eat up, since the  particle needs to predicate 
over something. 
On the other hand,  IVPCs.full could only be represented by encoding the 
meaning represented by the full  VMWE in a single portion of the event, (10a):

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages106 
(10a) [[Tom ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [the offer<TURNED-DOWN>]
2.2 Issues in identifying verb- particle constructions: A grayscale
Between the two poles represented by (3) and (4), in which the  particle is not 
part of the predicate and only acts as the head of a prepositional phrase, and 
(10) and (11), in which the  particle is part of the predicate and cannot head a 
prepositional phrase, one finds many other options. Some involve cases, like 
(5), whose exclusion from VPCs can at least be justified by the fact that the 
predicated  change of position is fully identified by the  particle, given the under-
specification of the verbal head. Semantically, predication is thus not shared 
by the verb and  particle but headed by the  particle alone. One cannot measure 
the difference in meaning or  telicity between the structure with and without 
the  particle, since the verb needs the  particle to project correctly. This section 
discusses other options under the provisional label of verb- particle combination. 
Equivalent examples in classical Greek are provided in Section 3.3.
2.2.1 Locative  telicising  particles with  manner-of-motion verbs 
The combination with a  particle can turn unergative manner verbs expressing 
motion into unaccusative verbs of  change of position. It does so by profiling an 
endpoint of the movement. Endpoint refers here to the point in space which 
measures the end of the predicated action, it might be the Target of an allative 
movement, (13), or the starting point of an ablative movement, (14). 
(12) Tom ran for three hours.
(12a) For three hours [Tom ACT<RUN>].
(13) Tom ran to the store in three hours.
(13a) [[Tom ACT<RUN>] & in three hours [BECOME [Tom<AT-THE-STORE>]]]. 
If the  particle can predicate alone an identifiable position (see Section 3.3.5 for 
ablative  particles being more effective in this respect), it need not to be combined 
with lexical content and builds a more compact unit with the verb, (14).
(14) The burglar ran off in a few seconds.
(14a) [[The burglar ACT<RUN>] & in a few seconds [BECOME [burglar<OFF>]]].
Differently from eat up (11), the  particle  telicises the predicate by keeping its 
locative meaning, either by heading a prepositional phrase or autonomously. 
Differently from take off  (5) the verb could project without the  particle. 
Nevertheless, the  telicising effect of the  particle can only be justified by it 
entering the predicate (Borer 1994), as in (11) and (5).

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 107
2.2.2 Locative  telicising  particles with (non-motional) manner verbs
Particles telicise manner verbs which do not only express motion. By combining 
with the  particle, however , the manner of acting of the subject is forced into 
causing a  change of position, (15). 
(15) Tom wiped the crumbs off the table.
(15a) [[Tom ACT<WIPE>] & CAUSE [BECOME [crumbs<OFF-THE-TABLE>]]].
The  particle can also be deprived of its argument and move to verb adjacency, (16). 
(16) Tom wiped the crumbs off/Tom wiped off the crumbs. 
(16a) [[Tom ACT<WIPE>] & CAUSE [BECOME [crumbs<OFF>]]]. 
The  particle, thus,  telicises the action, as in eat up, but keeps its locative meaning 
and can (but does not have to) head a prepositional phrase (see also Luo 2019: 81).
2.2.3 Locative  telicising  particles with manner verbs in locative 
 alternations
Particles may shift from locative to  telicising meaning if combined with verbs 
involved in locative  alternations. In (15), the  particle heads an argument position. 
This argument becomes a constituting member of the event, affected by the 
predicated action. (15a) should thus be more thoroughly presented as (15b).
(15b) [[Tom ACT<WIPE>] & CAUSE [BECOME [crumbs<OFF-THE-TABLE>]] & CAUSE [BECOME 
[table<WITHOUT-CRUMBS>]]].
Being involved in the outcome of the predicated action, the endpoint can raise 
to the object position, in a locative  alternation (Levin 1993: §2.3; van Valin and 
LaPolla 1997: §7.3.2.1; McIntyre 2015), (17). 
(17) Tom wiped off the table.
In this restructuring, however , the  particle off loses its locative value in favour 
of a  telicising one, as up does in eat up. If we stick to the criterion of idiomaticity, 
paradoxically, the same verb- particle combination should fall within or without 
the category of VPCs based on the section of the same event brought in focus by 
the  alternation. The shift in meaning, however , is provoked by the  alternation of 
the verb- particle combination as a whole, as it happens with simplex verbs (cf. 
load the truck with hay  in which load ≈ fill and load hay on the truck , in which 
load ≈ put on), and not by a shift in the semantic intake of the  particle. 
Such  alternations are not possible for  telic verbs as put off in 3 (* Tom put 
off his head [of the hat] ). With these verbs, the  particle (and the lexical content

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages108 
it may head) must be encoded within the  change of state undergone by the 
argument and does not project an additional argument position whose content 
could compete for the direct-object slot. The head verb is not a manner verb: it 
only projects a  change of state and the  particle is thus included in that  change 
of state. Particles  telicising  manner-of-motion verbs (Section 2.2.1), on the 
other hand, theoretically introduce a new argument slot. Differently from the 
alternating verbs here analysed, though, such verbs are intransitive unergatives 
turning into intransitive unaccusatives. Therefore, the argument coded in the 
prepositional phrase could not be raised to the object slot, but rather to the 
subject position, the key characteristic of unaccusatives being the encoding of 
the Patient as a surface subject, rather than as an object. A sentence like (18), in 
which the  particle has a full localistic value, can be analysed as in (18a). 
(18) Gas was running out of the tank.
(18a) [Gas ACT<RUN>] & [BECOME [gas<OUT-OF-THE-TANK>]] & [BECOME [tank<WITHOUT-GAS>]]].
If we raise the content of the prepositional phrase to the argument position, as 
table in (17), but represent it as the subject of an unaccusative rather than as 
the object of a  transitive verb, we get the idiomatic meaning of run out in (19) 
(McIntyre 2015).
(19) The tank was running out of gas.
Again, the (non)-idiomatic meaning of a verb-  particle combination depends on 
the section of the event brought in focus by argument selection.
2.2.4 Prepositional verbs
There exist verbs whose only argument is introduced by a  particle, as look at (Tom 
looked at Mary), as well as verbs which can draw a second participant into the 
action by combining with a  particle, as laugh at (Tom laughed at Mary). The  particle 
maintains its localistic value and cannot be separated from the verb (*Tom looked/
laughed Mary at, see further Thim 2012: 2.3.2). The argument is not understood 
as undergoing any  change of state which can be predicated by the  particle, 
it simply represents the Target. The lexical meaning of the verb is, thus, low in 
 transitivity and  telicity (Hopper and Thompson 1980). Nevertheless, the  particle 
draws another participant into the action (*Tom looked/laughed Mary) and does 
not head an adjunct with locative meaning (Tom laughed loudly at the party), it can 
thus be considered part of the predicate.  PARSEME proposes a tentative category 
of inherently adpositional verbs (IAV henceforth) for verbs whose combination 
with a  particle is either always mandatory or mandatory if one aims at producing 
a specific meaning (cf. come and come across). However , verbs fall under this 
definition only if they bear an idiomatic meaning, unlike look at and laugh at.

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 109
2.2.5 Secondary idiomatic meanings
Verb- particle combinations with  compositional value can develop secondary 
idiomatic meanings. The degree of idiomaticity can vary and is triggered by 
different factors. The verb phrase take out, which is fully  compositional in Tom 
took out the rubbish, has a particular nuance in Tom would love to take Mary out. 
A specific lexical content can become so standardised for the prepositional 
phrase headed by the  particle of a verb-  particle combination that it may be 
omitted, in a semantic specialisation (Squeri 2023). The meaning of take off in 
(21) and (21a) could be interpreted as the anticausative version of (20) and (20a), 
in which the content of the prepositional phrase is omitted. 
(20) The commander took the plane off land at 6 AM.
(20a) at 6 AM [[The commander ACT] CAUSE [BECOME [plane <OFF-LAND>]]].
(21) The plane took off (land) at 6 AM.
(21a) at 6 AM [BECOME [plane <OFF-(LAND)>]]].
Finally, the idiomatic meaning of verb- particle combinations can vary due to the 
varying content of their arguments (Dixon 2022: §1.3). 
(22) Tom looked up the chimney.
(23) Tom looked up the word. 
The meaning of chimney allows for up to combine with it in a prepositional 
phrase and maintain its the localistic value. The meaning of word disallows the 
combination with up in a prepositional phrase. Word is thus interpreted as the 
object of the idiomatic VPC look up. 
2.2.6 Summary
Idiomaticity grants the interpretation of verb- particle combinations as VMWEs, 
since the unpredictable semantic intake of the  particle prevents from assessing 
the pair as a standard combination at phrase level. The opposite, however , 
is not true: combinations which are not idiomatic can still be interpreted as 
VPCs.  Idiomaticity is thus one parameter among others, and, as observed in 
this section, is more a graded than an exclusive feature (Luo 2019: 127). In 
other instances, the  particle needs to be taken as part of the predicate since it 
represents a constituting element of its event structure, even when keeping its 
localistic value (Goldberg 2016). By paralleling the variables analysed in this 
section with classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs, the next section shows how the 
degree of idiomaticity of VPCs correlates to the need of accommodating the 
 particle in the event structure headed by the  base verb, by keeping the necessary 
consequential link with its lexical meaning.

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages110 
3. Particle-induced changes in the morphosyntax and 
semantics of classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs
3.1 A working hypothesis
The idea of deriving the idiomatic meaning of VPCs from the one produced by 
combining the localistic meaning of the  particle with the lexical meaning of the 
verb is not new, and has become widespread after the recognition of the human 
tendency to reconceptualise non-spatial aspects of reality in spatial terms 
(Lakoff and Johnson 1980; Luo 2019: §2.1.2 for an overview). 
This chapter rather insists on how the addition of the meaning represented 
by an originally localistic  particle to a simple predicate might shift its event 
template to one which is typical—but not exclusive—of predicates expressing 
a  change of position (Luo 2019: ch. 3; Goldberg 2016). Non-locative meanings 
of VPCs would not be derived from locative ones via a purely  metaphorical 
shift. The activation of either a locative or non-locative meaning would rather 
be linked to how the new portion of meaning represented by the  particle is 
accommodated into the event template activated by the lexical meaning of the 
verb. The high degree of variability of lexical meanings of verbs will then better 
account for the grayscale between full  compositionality and full idiomaticity 
observed in Section 2.2 for VPCs.
We assume that, as observed in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, when the  particle enters the 
predicate, its meaning is accommodated into the event either within an already 
available  change-of-state subevent, or by being assigned to a new one, whose 
presence becomes mandatory (hence the mandatory  transitive use of eat up with 
respect to eat, (11) and (11a). In both cases, the type of  change of state headed by 
the  particle must adapt to the lexemic content provided by the meaning of the 
verb: with  change-of-state verbs (Section 1.2.1), the type of  change-of-state headed 
by the  particle must combine with the type of  change-of-state already identified 
by the verb meaning. With manner verbs, it must follow from the way of acting 
performed by their subject. If there were not a consequential link between the 
subevents headed by the verb and the  particle, they could not be thought of as 
constituting blocks of the same event, and  monoclausality, a characterising feature 
of complex predicates (Baker and Harvey 2010, Butt 2010), would be missing. A 
bi-clausal interpretation might be perceived as impossible, since the structure 
has a single verbal head, but some interpretations of VPCs have supposed that 
they actually involve a small clause (for example, Tom saw [Mary play the piano]) 
with an unrepresented verbal head (Dehé 2002: §2.2; Goldberg 2016: §3.4). 
The difference between small clauses and subevents is that the arguments of 
subevents are governed by the main verb, while the arguments of small clauses 
are governed by the predicative element in the small clause.

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 111
3.2 The lexical status of  pre-verbed verbs
The hypothesis put forward here (Section 3.1) rests on three assumptions: (A) In  pre-
verbed verbs,  particles enter the predicate and, thus, (B) a bi-clausal interpretation 
is prevented, and, (C) when  particles enter the predicate, the projected event 
structure needs to involve a (change of) state. Assumption (C) has been proven by 
Tenny (1994: §1.2.7 for modern languages) and Romagno (2022 for pre-modern 
Greek and Latin), but, along with (B), it depends on (A) being validated.
By instantiating in a single verbal lexeme, classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs 
strongly testify for (A), and exclude the phrase interpretation in favour of the 
compound one. According to Pompei (2014), the evolution from the free co-
occurrence of verbs and localistic adverbs to compounds stored in the lexicon—
through an intermediate stage of complex verbs—is already accomplished in 
Classical Greek, previous stages being testified by Homer . This is why classical 
Greek texts were chosen to build the dataset of the examples provided in Section 
3.3, with a strong preference for prose, less prone to the tendency to imitate 
Homeric diction.
One piece of proof of  pre-verbed verbs having raised to word status is that they 
serve as the base for further  preverbation, for example, προκαταλέγω prokatalegō 
← [πρό + καταλέγω pro + katalegō] (Zanchi 2019), and derivation, for example, 
κατάλογος katalogos ← καταλέγω katalegō, and they bear a single stress (Giannakis 
2023). Horrocks and Stavrou (2007) have argued that, having a grammaticalised 
way of predefining aspect via stem selection, “ancient” Greek prevents  telicity 
or perfectivity (see Bertinetto and Delfitto 2000 on the differences between the 
two; Rodríguez Adrados 1992: 442–449 on the relationship between stem selection 
and  preverbation in “ancient” Greek) to be further triggered at sentence-level. 
The telicisation provoked on run by its combination with to the store  (Section 
2.2.1) cannot be triggered on Greek verbs by the same means. It can, however , be 
triggered by  preverbation (Section 3.3.2), a fact which confirms that the  preverb 
is a constituting element of the verb, which is only afterwards marked for aspect.3 
Other data, however , support the interpretation of classical Greek  pre-
verbed verbs as early forms of  univerbation, occupying an intermediate stage 
of  phrasal compounds before reaching the stage of fully-fledged compounds. 
Phrasal compounds still display, in synchrony, recognisable internal structuring 
respecting the rules of the productive syntax, but can also be treated as 
standard lexical entries (Lehmann 2020), and act as productive bases for further 
 preverbation and derivation. The perception of the constituting elements of  pre-
verbed verbs as partially autonomous is shown by (A) the fact that morphological 
material marking tense or aspect, i.e. the augment and reduplication, can still

Classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs thus represent a special case in which the 
constituting elements of what is semantically perceived as a lexeme are partially 
autonomous and functional morphemes at syntax level. This allows us to interpret 
 pre-verbed verbs as complex predicates and, only functionally, as VMWEs.
This assumption has some noteworthy entailments: 
1.  Preverbs are not simple prefixes. This aligns with Indo-European words 
being resistant to prefixation (Pinault 1995: §2) and classical Greek verbs 
never being otherwise prefixed by elements which can autonomously 
function as adverbs (forms like εὐλογέω eulogeō “to praise” are 
denominals/deadjectivals drawn from compounds built with adverbs 
[εὔλογος eulogos ← εὖ eu “well” + λόγος logos “speech”], see Duhoux 2000: 
§24).  Preverbs are words with two alternative sentence positions:  heads 
of prepositional phrases or verb-adjacent lexemes. When verb-adjacent, 
they do not simply bring a semantic addition to the verb, but head their 
own argument position and, thus, represent an independent subevent 
(Rappaport Hovav and Levin 1998), with the relevant “selectional” 
restrictions (Resnik 1996), as they would do when heading prepositional 
phrases. When that position is not saturated, (16), as in structures with 
null objects licensed by the restrictions provided by the meaning of the 
head verb (Cennamo 2017), the restriction provided by the  preverbs 
is taken as a sufficient semantic information, and the valency of the 
predicate is reduced. 
2. The fact that  particles represent a subevent explains why they can 
telicise the predicate in which they are included even though they do 
not display any  telicising meaning when used as adverbs or as heads 
of prepositional phrases, for example, there is no autonomous use of 
ἀπό apo which has the meaning of “completely” it takes up in ἀπο-
θνῄσκω apo-thnēskō “to die” (see Luraghi 2003: §3.1; Bortone 2010: ch. 
2; Beekes 2011: §17.5.1) This would be paradoxical if we understood 
 preverbation as a simple semantic addition to the verb meaning.

3. The maintenance of the perception of the word boundary between

heads of  change-of-state subevents (Section 3.3.5). This function might 
have been attributed to them in analogy with the one they have when 
they truly represent an endpoint in space, if combined with verbs 
expressing a  change of position or a  manner of motion. 
3.3 From endpoints to  telicity-markers: How  preverbs interact 
with verb meanings
The present section analyses how the varying impact of  preverbation can be 
connected with two interrelated aspects: the internal structuring of the event 
projected by the verb and the distinguishing semantic trait of its lexical meaning, 
with special reference to its capacity to express—or be forced to express—
motion. The relevance of the lexical meaning of verbs on their belonging to the 
core or to the periphery of the classes in which they are organised with respect 
to  Aktionsart and  transitivity (Section 1.2) has indeed been shown for modern 
languages (Sorace 2000).
The different effects of  preverbation here analysed for classical Greek align 
with the ones observed for verb- particle combinations in English candidates for 
a VPC interpretation (Section 2.2).
