The  change-of-state subevent cannot be headed by the simplex verb and is thus 
headed by the  preverb alone, autonomously projecting an argument position. 
If that position is left unsaturated, the semantic information projected by 
the  preverb-head in the form of “selectional” restrictions is the only element 
characterising that subevent, or recalling anaphorical information. Moreover , 
specific content can be assumed to be included in that subevent, even though 
left unexpressed, triggering a (partially) idiosyncratic meaning. The  pre-verbed 
verb καταπλέω katapleō for instance, develops the meaning of “to sail back 
home“ from the  compositional one of “to sail back”.

second argument 
At the border between  change-of-state verbs and manner verbs, there are verbs 
predicating a specific way of acting of the subject, (41), which may also entail a 
 change of state over another element, (42) (see Sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3).

The characteristics of this  change of state must follow from the way of acting 
encoded in the verb meaning and may also involve a  change of position. If they 
do, the object can be understood as both a Patient and a Theme, altered both 
in condition and position. There is no example of simple καθαίρω kathairō “to 
clean” with a prepositional phrase defining the spatial endpoint of the action in 
Attic prose, but this structure is frequent in the contemporary Ionic prose of the 
Hippocratic Corpus, (43).

5. Assessing verb-particle constructions through classical Greek preverbation 121
(43a) [from her uterus [Suppository ACT<CLEAN>] & CAUSE [BECOME [blood<CLEANED>]]].
The content of the prepositional phrase can take scope over the whole event, 
(43a): it qualifies the way in which the subject acts, and, thus, the consequential 
 change of state undergone by the Patient. 
A different interpretation is however possible, (43b), in which the endpoint 
is drawn into the event, as a secondary affected element involved in the chain 
of subevents. The Patient is reinterpreted as a Theme, whose movement allows 
the interaction with the element representing the endpoint. All the subevents, 
however , must still logically follow from the manner of acting predicated of the 
subject.
(43b) [[Suppository ACT <CLEAN>] & CAUSE [BECOME [blood <OFF-HER-UTERUS>]] & CAUSE 
[BECOME [uterus<WITHOUT-BLOOD>]]]
When a  preverb is added, (44), the endpoint it expresses is fixed within the event. 
Therefore, differently from the simplex verb, the  pre-verbed verb is mandatorily 
 transitive: a Theme is needed for the endpoint to be reached and the action to 
end (Tenny 1994: §1.2.7; Romagno 2022). If the argument slot headed by the 
 preverb is saturated, an interpretation like (43b) is mandatory, (44a).

[BECOME [murex<WITHOUT-MOISTURE>]]].
If the position is left unsaturated the  preverb can be understood as simply 
adding a  change of position to the  change of state undergone by the Patient, 
(45a), or to anaphorically retrieve a more specific reference point, (45b).

“The phlegm not being cleared away (from the body).”

(45b) [[BECOME [phlegm<OFF-THE-BODY>]] & [BECOME [body<WITHOUT-PHLEGM>]]].
The semantics of manner verbs do not allow the  preverb to simply qualify the 
 change-of-state subevent involving the object. That  change of state must follow 
from the lexical meaning of the verb which need not be conceived as involving 
motion, (41) and (42). The endpoint represented by the  preverb needs to be 
added in an additional argument slot, in order to force an interpretation of the 
object as also undergoing a  change of position. The action is thus understood 
as involving two arguments: the Patient, reinterpreted as a Theme, and the 
endpoint reached by/deprived of the Theme. The fact that both are coded as 
arguments in autonomous subevents is shown by their competing for the direct-
object slot, in a locative  alternation, compare (45) with (46) (de la Villa 2017). 
(46) Aristotle, Problems, 958b
τὸ  ἀποκεκαθάρθαι  τὰ  ὄμματα 
to  apokekatharthai  ta  ommata 
the.nom.sg.n clean-off.prf.inf.mid the.nom.pl.n eyes.nom.pl.n
“The fact that the eyes are cleaned up.”
(46a) [BECOME [eyes<CLEANED-UP>]].
Most of these verbs can already alternate in the simplex form, but the addition 
of a  preverb helps in aligning syntax with semantics, providing two semantically 
different types of heads for two semantically different types of arguments. 
However , in the alternated form, (46), the value of the  preverb moves from 
locative, and  compositional, to  telicising, and idiomatic.
3.3.4 Manner verbs with eventive meaning:  Preverbs heading a first 
argument
Many manner verbs predicate a type of performance of the subject which 
cannot involve a Patient or Theme. The action is identified by the type of event 
produced while acting: one can tell laughing apart from crying by the type of 
produced event (see Section 2.2.4), (47).

gelōntes   […] oligou  paretathēsan

“Laughing […] until they nearly fainted.”

and (49a).

3.3.5 Change-of-state verbs, and manner verbs not implying motion
In the previous cases,  preverbs are coded in a subevent of  change of state which, 
semantically, represents an endpoint in space, but, functionally, represents the 
end of the action. 
This ambivalence is clear in alternating verbs. In two cases, however , 
 preverbs take up an exclusively  telicising function (see Section 2.1). Firstly, when 
combined with  change-of-state verbs without a  change of position implied, as 
κτείνω kteinō “to kill”, they overabundantly mark the  telicity of the  change of 
state, (52) and (53).

By not blending into the verb meaning and being still identifiable as autonomous 
heads within complex predicates,  preverbs might have been functionally re-
analysed as simple telicisers, abstracting their function of endpoints from 
their semantic value of endpoints of motion events (Horrocks 1981: §3.E). This 
reanalysis might have been helped by (i) their ambiguous role with alternating 
verbs and (ii) their combination with verb-framed predicates of  change of 
position (πίπτω piptō “to fall”), when the endpoint they profile doubles the one 
already profiled by the verb (ἐκπίπτω ekpiptō “to fall off”). In this latter case, 
the  preverb could have been interpreted exclusively as a  telicity marker to 
avoid redundancy, for example, “away” in (34b) shares the same position as 
“completely” in (53a) and (55a). The redundant effect, though, is only perceived 
if the  preverb does not head an argument providing a more specific reference 
point. Pragmatically, the reference points which are more likely to be omitted,

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages126 
being thematised by what precedes or by the contingent situation, are the ones 
representing the starting points of the movement, rather than its Target. This 
might explain why  preverbs acquiring  telicising function are mostly ablatival 
(ἐκ- ek-, ἀπο- apo- “from”, ἀνα- ana- “up from”, κατα- kata- “down from”). This 
reinterpretation of  preverbs as purely functional telicisers also explains the 
idiosyncrasy of their choice and the apparent synonymity that they display 
when used as such, which they could not display when used as prepositions (cf. 
ἀπο-κτείνω apo-kteinō “to kill” with κατ-εσθίω kat-esthiō “to eat up”). A reuse 
of  particles in composition with noun-morphemes with which they display an 
idiosyncratic meaning due to the compound being constructed in analogy with 
an existing one with a fully combinatorial meaning is also attested for nouns 
and adjectives (Rousseau 2016: §3.b.1–2), for example, in ὑποταρτάριος hypo-
tartarios “in the Tartarus”, ὑπο- hypo- “under” occurs with the idiosyncratic 
meaning of “in”, its choice being analogical with its use in ὑποχθόνιος hypo-
khthonios “under the earth”, in which it displays a fully combinatorial value.
5. Conclusion and outlook
Being  univerbated, classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs elude by definition the label 
of VPCs, if understood as VMWEs, as in the definition of  PARSEME. Univerbation 
of  pre-verbed verbs, on the other hand, guarantees the inclusion of the  particle 
in the predicate. All English borderline cases explored in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, 
excluded from the category of VPCs due to the lack of idiomaticity, can be 
paralleled to classical Greek  pre-verbed verbs, semantically and functionally. 
Idiomaticity turns out to be a sufficient, but not a necessary parameter to assess 
the inclusion of a  particle into the predicate, and, thus, classify a verb-  particle 
combination as a VPC. 
Coherently with their original localistic value,  preverb- particles profile the 
endpoint of motion events or events whose interpretation as involving motion 
can be forced. All motion events expressed by  pre-verbed verbs are  telic since 
the  preverb gets coded in a subevent of  change of position: the action ends when 
the Theme changes its position according to the endpoint profiled by the  preverb. 
When combined with verbs not involving motion,  preverbs are reanalysed 
as telicisers, generally profiling the  change of state which marks the end of an 
action. Therefore, in both  phrasal verbs and  pre-verbed verbs, the idiomaticity of 
the verb- particle combination, and the consequent (in)capacity of the  particle to 
head a prepositional phrase, cannot be taken as proof of the  particle (not) being 
part of the predicate. These aspects simply depend on the type of final state which 
can logically follow from the meaning of the verb combined with the  particle.
The claims made here should be fully substantiated by a  diachronic analysis 
of the function of pre-modern Greek  particles as well as a typological analysis of

the outcome and function of  particles of the same stem in other Indo-European 
languages. The  telicising function of  particles profiling an endpoint should also 
be contrasted to the one of  particles profiling a path, for example, περί peri 
“all around” (see Cappelle and Declerck 2005 for English), or a non-locative 
information, for example, σύν syn “with”.

6. The pragmatic development of 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn as 
an  intersubjective marker in post-
classical Greek (4th to 6th c. CE)
 Lucía Madrigal Acero
1. Introduction
Languages employ a range of mitigation strategies (Brown and Levinson 1987; 
Caffi 2005). From  politeness markers to indirect speech, to forms of address, each 
speaker , language, and culture has its own way of maintaining social harmony, 
addressing uncertainty, or managing communicative contexts. In this chapter , 
I address one of the linguistic formulae that pre-modern Greek developed for 
attenuating interrogative and directive speech acts: ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson 
agápēn “(literally) do [me] a favour > please.”1
Cross-linguistically, there are several different sources for phrases meaning 
please, that is, phrases that are typically used to downplay commands or direct 
questions. Where some languages choose to use verbs of begging or asking in the 
first person (Latin precor > Italian prego, Standard Modern Greek (SMG henceforth) 
παρακαλώ parakalṓ, German bitte), others prefer to address the interlocutor more 
directly with the use of an  imperative form (Italian scusi, French excusez-moi, 
Spanish disculpe). Some expressions may be tracked back to  verbal multi-word 
expressions (English please < if it please (subjunctive), French s’il vous plaît), or to 
simpler adverbial multi-word expressions (Italian per favore, Spanish por favor, 
see Ben Khelil et al. 2022). Even at a semantic level, there are similarities in their 
origins. When addressing a second person, it is common to use verbs of excusing,

i.e. verbs that are aimed at freeing the speaker from the guilt of disturbing the 
addressee (English excuse me, French excusez-moi, Spanish disculpe, Italian scusi, 
German entschuldigen Sie). Another common source are nouns meaning favour 
(Italian per favore, Spanish por favor, Arabic من فضلك min faḍlak), which may also 
appear in different formulae, such as SMG κάνε μου την χάρη káne mou tin khári 
“do me a favour .” The phrase that I look into in this chapter is also semantically 
related to the notion of favour (ἀγάπη agápē), but differs from these examples, in 
that it has its origin in a support-verb construction (see Section 2).2 
These strategies and phrases are typically used in oral exchanges, and it is 
difficult to guess what communication strategies were used in everyday Greek 
from the literature that has been preserved. For instance, we are uncertain of 
the formulae used to say please (but see La Roi 2025) or thank you in spoken 
language (Denizot 2022). At best, we can guess through parallels with SMG or 
the formulaic forms of address found in letters. However , it is unlikely that we 
date these utterings correctly, given the complexity and the turnabouts in the 
historical development of SMG, and the archaising and literary character of 
forms of address in ancient letters. 
The aim of this chapter is to explore the development of the phrase ποιέω 
ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn into a marker of  politeness in post-classical Greek. Other 
research has explored the development of specific verbs or verbal phrases in 
Greek into pragmatic markers (La Roi 2022, 2025; Fendel 2024). This chapter is, 
to my knowledge, the first inquiry into the use of a  support-verb construction, 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn, as a  politeness marker that reduces the  illocutive 
force of the following command or question. The phrase ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson 
agápēn may have been overlooked in literary texts as a pragmatic marker due to 
its short life and its similarity to the realisative construction ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō 
agápēn “to do a favour .” However , previous work on  support-verb constructions 
in Greek  papyri already noted its prevalence in non-literary texts, which may 
push back the date for the beginning of the  pragmaticalisation of ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn. For instance Fendel (2022: 142) provides a reference for 
the phrase ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn in a fourth-century  Christian  papyrus. 
The  Christian context of this finding is relevant in view of the kinds of texts in 
which our literary examples are found, which are also  Christian (see Section 2).  
This chapter intends to explore three research questions: 
1. What is the meaning of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn?
2. What are the indicators of the  pragmaticalisation of ποίησον ἀγάπην 
poíēson agápēn? 
2 Research on pre-modern Greek pragmatic markers is an ongoing process. Before ποίησον 
ἀγαπήν poíēson agápēn, which is a late formula, there were different means to ask for a favour 
or for information, such as parenthetical ἱκετεύω hiketeúō “I beg.” This and other formulae for 
“please” in archaic and classical Greek have been discussed by La Roi (2025).

3. To what extent is ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  a  pragmaticalised 
phrase, adopting a gradient rather than categorical view of 
 pragmaticalisation? 
In the following sections, I describe my working data (Section 2) and the 
changes undergone by ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn in its progressive acquisition 
of pragmatic functions. Firstly, I describe the semantic changes (Section 3). 
Secondly, I provide a syntactic analysis (Section 4), focussing on the (absence of) 
ossification of  morphological number in the expression ποίησον ἀγάπην poiēson 
agápēn (Section 4.1), the syntactic position in which it tends to appear (Section 
4.2), its degree of  syntactic integration in the clause (Section 4.3), and its main 
pragmatic functions (Section 4.4). Lastly, I provide a synthesis of the main points 
of this chapter and make some concluding remarks (Section 5). 
2. Research data
The data that I have analysed are the results of searching for ποιέω poiéō in 
co-occurrence with ἀγάπην agápēn in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae (https://
stephanus.tlg.uci.edu/).3  This allows to track the semantic and syntactic 
development of the different meanings and contexts of use of the  polysemic 
multi-word expression ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn: “to love; to perform an act 
of love; to make love; to make peace; to celebrate a banquet; to do a favour” 
or “please” (see Section 3). Originally, ποιέομαι ἀγάπην poiéomai agápēn was 
used as a  support-verb construction. Support-verb constructions are semi-
 compositional verb-noun phrases in which the noun has predicative properties, 
that is, it governs its own arguments, and the verb performs the function of an 
operator , which provides the nouns’ arguments with the syntactic slots that they 
need for their realisation in a sentence. This makes  support-verb constructions 
a peculiar kind of multi-word expressions as defined in the  PARSEME Universal 
Annotation Guidelines for Multi-Word Expressions. 4 Multi-word expressions 
are non- compositional combinations that include at least two different lexemes. 
However , non- compositionality is a scalar property and, because  support-
verb constructions are only semi-  compositional, they behave somewhat like 
prototypical multi-word expressions, but also like free constructions in certain 
aspects. A strict definition of prototypical  support-verb constructions, which is 
the approach that I take in this chapter , includes only collocations formed by a 
semantically empty and syntactically  transitive verb and its object ( to throw a 
tantrum, to give a hug, to make a request ) (Jiménez López 2016; Mel’čuk 2023;

4 See https://parsemefr .lis-lab.fr/parseme-st-guidelines/2.0/

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages134 
Fendel 2025).5 One of the features that distinguishes support-verb constructions 
from other phraseological units is that they show, to a certain extent, some 
syntactic flexibility (Gross 2004; Fendel 2023). For example:
(1) I don’t have a clue.
(2) I have no clue.
(3) Jane did a brilliant job.
(4) Jane did her job brilliantly.
(5) Mary took a walk down the riverside.
(6) The walk that Mary took down the riverside was very pleasant.
Examples (1) and (2) evidence the mobility of negation in  support-verb 
constructions (Fendel 2023; 2025). Since the verb and the noun form a semi-lexical 
unit, the whole phrase is negated whether negation lies within the scope of the 
verb, (1), or the noun, (2). A similar phenomenon affects the complementation 
of  support-verb constructions, (3) and (4). The same complement can be 
formulated as accompanying the verb, i.e. as an adverb, (4), or the noun, i.e. as 
an adjective, (3). Since the  support-verb construction functions as a lexical unit, 
the modification of the verb or the noun affects the whole phrase, rather than 
just one of its component lexemes. Other evidence of this syntactic flexibility 
includes the possibility of extracting the noun from the phrase and replacing it 
with a relative pronoun, (6). 
When syntactic flexibility is lost, one must consider whether the  support-
verb construction has experienced some degree of ossification—hence moving 
into the category of idioms—or whether another factor is driving changes in 
the phrase. This decrease in syntactic flexibility indicates that, at least from the 
fourth century CE onwards, ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn no longer behaves as a 
regular  support-verb construction, but rather as a pragmatic marker (Section 3). 
The current study is corpus-based and focusses on the analysis of Greek 
texts extracted from the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae . The selection process 
has been manual. I have carried out a proximity search in the whole corpus 
of the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae  in order to find all the instances of ποιέω 
poiéō and ἀγάπην agápēn within a seven-word range, discarding false positives 
which were generally cases in which ποιέω poiéō and ἀγάπην agápēn appear in 
separate clauses or cases in which ἀγάπη agápē is used in a case other than the 
accusative. The search intended to also look into other uses of ποιέω ἀγάπην 
poiéō agápēn in different contexts. The findings allow for the identification of at

The first time that  pragmaticalised ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn appears 
in Greek literary texts—i.e. in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae—is in the fourth 
century CE. After that point, its use becomes widespread until the sixth century 
CE, when its decline begins. However , ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn remains 
present in the literature in later centuries, probably because of the conservative 
character of written Greek and its liking of the imitation of previous literary 
models. The full list of works which contain the (partially)  pragmaticalised phrase

Most of the instances of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn appear in texts written

in texts that rework or even quote the information from earlier sources. These

later uses are to be considered remains of a receding phrase that peaked in the 
literature of the period from the fourth to sixth centuries CE, and which was 
already in use in documentary  papyri (see Fendel 2022: 142). However , I have not 
found examples of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn in documentary  papyri dated 
prior to the fourth century CE. I have not excluded the more recent examples 
(from the seventh century CE onwards, see Table 6.1) from my analysis because 
not all of them are secondary in this sense, and it is important to see the whole 
picture, where older phrases keep being brought into later texts or speech due to 
the use of earlier sources or due to the Greek diglossia (Toufexis 2008; Horrocks 
2014). Furthermore, the decline of this phrase may be linked to the prevalence 
of different  politeness strategies in post-classical Greek. For instance, in Greek 
 papyri collocations with the noun χάρις kháris ‘grace’ are very productive (Fendel 
2022). Nevertheless, the question whether the gradual disappearance of ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is due to lexical substitution with another phrase or with 
other expressions of  politeness is beyond the scope of this chapter . 
Apart from chronology, another factor has proved relevant in the distribution 
of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn: sociocultural context. The texts in which it 
is found are  Christian—with very few exceptions, such as the Erotopaignia—
which aligns with Goutsos’ (2017) findings that sociolinguistics impacts greatly 
the distribution of certain pragmatic markers. Most of the examples are found in 
hagiographical or ecclesiastical texts. Even the documentary  papyri that include 
this phrase belong to a  Christian context. The example cited in the introduction 
(Fendel 2022: 142) comes from the archive of Apa Paeious, who was the head of 
a fourth-century Meletian community.

integration and pragmatic function. All of them are discussed in depth in Section 4. 
The next sections develop the semantic and syntactic changes that ποιέω 
ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn underwent on its path to  pragmaticalisation. The way I 
understand  pragmaticalisation in this chapter is as a process involved in language 
change which shares a lot of properties with grammaticalisation and is, in fact, 
part of the process of grammaticalisation. It is not the purpose of this chapter to 
discuss the distinction between grammaticalisation and  pragmaticalisation, for 
which I refer to the chapters that I have used (Degand and Evers-Vermeul 2015; 
La Roi 2022). More importantly, Degand and Evers-Vermeul (2015: 68) sum up 
the semantic and syntactic processes undergone by  pragmaticalising units. The 
semantic changes include: 
(i) the evolution from referential to discourse-orientated and/or interpersonal 
meaning including semantic bleaching through pragmatic strengthening, (ii) 
persistence of the original lexico-grammatical meaning, (iii) subjectification, and to 
a certain extent (iv) intersubjectification (Degand and Evers-Vermeul 2015: 68–69).

(iii) syntactic optionality” (Degand and Evers-Vermeul 2015: 69). These are some 
of the characteristics of  pragmaticalisation that affect the change in ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn.
The next section starts with a description of the semantic uses of ποιέω 
ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn that I have identified within the corpus and ends with an 
introduction to ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn as a pragmatic marker .
3. Semantic changes
The phrase ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn can be used in several different ways, 
which are, on the one hand, due to the  polysemy of the noun ἀγάπη agápē and, on 
the other , to its progressive recruitment of pragmatic properties. In this section, 
I introduce the eight main meanings of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn present in 
the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae  and trace the semantic relationship between 
them. There are three major sets in which all these meanings are articulated. 
The first one includes the only  support-verb construction in the group (Section 
3.1). The second set includes the instances in which ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn 
is used as a realisative construction with different meanings (Sections 3.2 to 3.6). 
The last set is formed by the  pragmaticalised uses of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson 
agápēn (Sections 3.7 and 3.8).
3.1 ποιέομαι ἀγάπην poiéomai agápēn “to love” (≈ ἀγαπάω agapáō)
The verb ἀγάπάω agapáō “to love” is morphologically derived from the noun 
ἀγάπη agápē, whose core meaning is “love” (LSJ, DGE, Bailly, s.v.). Therefore, 
the first meaning of the phrase ποιέομαι ἀγάπην poiéomai agápēn is “to love.” 
Example (7) illustrates this by creating a parallel sentence with the synthetic 
expression in the first clause and the analytic form in the second one.

construction and the simplex verb include the greater syntactic flexibility of 
the  support-verb construction and its use of the  middle voice. Firstly, the noun 
in the  support-verb construction in (7) is determined by the article την tḕn and 
modified by the adjective δικαίαν dikaían and the  participle μὴ συνκεχυμένην mḕ

expression. If anything, it is possible to modify the simplex verb with an adverb, 
but it seems difficult to adverbialise a complex expression such as a participial 
clause. Secondly, the support verb ποιέομαι poiéomai needs to be used in the

ἀγάπην agápēn and the syntactic subject of the verb ποιεῖσθαι poieîsthai (Cock 
1981; Jiménez López 2016; Fendel 2025). In this specific case, the clause is in fact 
impersonal, which gives the statement general validity.

Still related to the core meaning of ἀγάπη agápē, there is a different phrase: 
ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn  “to practice love or charity”. Morphologically, 
this phrase differs from the  support-verb construction in that it is used in the 
active voice. This is an indication that the phrase is not used as a  support-verb 
construction, but rather as something else: a realisative construction. The 
definition for realisative constructions varies from author to author and we 
are still far from a consensus on the matter (Alonso Ramos 2004; Mel’čuk 2023; 
Fendel 2025). The definition I follow in this chapter is that of Alonso Ramos 
(2004: 113–114), which focusses on the semantics of the verb. Whereas a support 
verb is semantically empty, meaning that it adds no meaning to the construction

6. Development of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn as an intersubjective marker 139
and performs the function of a syntactic operator , in a realisative construction 
the verb retains a part of its original semantics, and conveys the notion that the 
purpose of the existence of the noun has been fulfilled. A realisative verb can 
be glossed as to-carry-out-the-purpose-of-the-noun. There are different ways 
to understand this definition, which becomes clear through the examples that 
each author gives. For instance, Alonso Ramos (2004: 114) gives the examples 
to fulfill/keep a promise . The goal of a promise is not to be broken, but rather 
to be fulfilled or kept. Hence, there is an obvious semantic difference between 
the prototypical  support-verb construction to make a promise , where the verb 
is semantically empty, and the realisative-verb constructions to fulfill /keep 
a promise, where it is not. 7 In the case of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn , ποιέω 
poiéō retains its meaning of “making, manufacturing”, as in “creating a physical 
reality that materialises the abstract concept of ἀγάπη agape” and implies that 
the objective of said ἀγάπη agápē is fulfilled, that is, helping another person 
such as to make them feel taken care of and loved. Therefore, there is a syntactic 
explanation for the verb being used in the active: the subject of ποιέω poiéō is 
not an Experiencer of ἀγάπη agápē—i.e. the first argument of the noun—but 
rather an Agent that carries out an action. So, while there are other models that 
define  support-verb constructions and realisative constructions differently, how 
I use the distinction between realisative and support verbs is especially relevant 
in Greek because it is supported by the voice  alternation. While  support-verb 
constructions use poiéomai in the middle due to the co-referentiality between 
the first argument of the predicative noun and the subject of the support verb, 
realisative constructions use ποιέω poiéō because the active voice implies that 
the subject is more Agent-like and not necessarily coreferential, and that the 
verb is semantically closer to the core meaning of ποιέω poiéō “to create” than 
to the semantically empty support verb ποιέομαι poiéomai “to do”.8

Also related to the core meaning of ἀγάπη agápē “love” is another sense of 
ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn “to make love.” Morphologically, semantically and 
syntactically, this phrase behaves almost like (ii), but refers exclusively to having 
intercourse, which may be considered a specific “act of love”. The difference 
between (ii) and (iii) is clear from the contexts in which they are used. (ii) is 
used to refer to the  Christian notion of “charity” or “love towards other human 
beings,” whereas (iii) is used in a sexual sense. Example (9) condemns the action 
of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn as being a shameful act, whereas (10) shows its 
use in erotic poetry.
3.4 ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn “to make peace, to make an 
alliance” (realisative construction)
Another construction is ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn  “to make peace”. This 
construction also takes the active voice, which is a clue that it is in fact a realisative 
construction. Example (11) addresses politics, so a political interpretation of the 
term ἀγάπη agápē is required.
(11) Collatio quinta. Novellae constitutiones annorum 1204–1453, 6.28
ἵνα μετὰ τὸ συνδεθῆναι αὐτοὺς εἰς ἀγάπην μετὰ τῆς βασιλείας μου οὐ μὴν ποιήσωσιν

hoûtoi metà állou génous agápēn katà tē̂ s basileías mou
“So that, after having begged for peace with my kingdom, they will not make an 
alliance with another people against my kingdom.” 
Kingdoms do not have the ability to experience love, so the closest thing to love 
between two kingdoms is friendship or an alliance between them, analogous to two 
people who show ἀγάπη agápē to one another . The first argument of ἀγάπη agápē 
“alliance” is the entity who makes or holds the alliance, in this case, the people 
referred to by αὐτούς autoús “them,” which is the logical subject of ποιήσωσιν 
poiḗsōsin. In other words, the first argument of ἀγάπη agápē and the subject of 
ποιέω poiéō are coreferential, yet the verb is used in the active because this is not 
the  support-verb construction ποιέομαι ἀγάπην poiéomai agápēn “to love”, which 
refers to an emotion. Here, the subject has more agentive characteristics: rather 
than experiencing something, the subject is making something, i.e. a new political 
situation which requires negotiation and active involvement. 
It seems, however , that there is a historical instability in other similar phrases. 
For instance, ποιέομαι συμμαχίαν poiéomai symmak hían and ποιέομαι φιλίαν 
poiéomai philían “to make an alliance” were widely used collocations in classical

In  Christian Greek, a new meaning of ἀγάπη agápē emerged which can also be 
traced back to “love.” Thayer (1887, s.v.) defines ἀγάπαι agápai, in the plural, as 
love-feasts, feasts expressing and fostering mutual love which used to be held by 
Christians before the celebration of the Lord’s supper , and at which the poorer 
Christians mingled with the wealthier and partook in common with the rest of 
food provided at the expense of the wealthy.
So, in certain cases, ἀγάπη agápē is used to refer to a ritual which was used for 
the expression of mutual affection and solidarity in a religious context. As in 
(ii) to (iv), the noun refers to a specific realisation of ἀγάπη agápē, and the verb 
is used in the active to indicate that the subject is not an Experiencer of ἀγάπη 
agápē, but rather a more prototypical Agent. Furthermore, this meaning is more 
typically used in the plural, (16) and (17), which also leads to interpreting the 
predicate as an iterative activity, i.e. a ritual that is repeated consistently over 
time. However , when the speaker refers to a specific ἀγάπη agápē, rather than 
the performance of ἀγάπαι agápai in general, the noun may also be used in 
the singular , (15). Typically, the context provides the necessary information to 
identify this value of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn. In (15), the text speaks about 
how a monk takes care of a garden where he grows the food with which he is 
then able to provide for his guests at an ἀγάπη agápē. In (16), there are specific 
signals that the text talks about the religious ritual, such as the specific mention 
of ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις taîs ekklēsíais “the churches” or the verb ἐσθίειν esthíein “to 
eat.” Example (17) provides a synonym for ἀγάπαι agápai, which is συμπόσια 
sympósia.

Another meaning that can be derived from “perform an action to show

is common from the fourth century CE onwards, when it appears in literary texts 
for the first time.11 It seems that the phrase was also common in the papyri of the

ἀγάπην agápēn here does not refer merely to any other kind of act of love, but 
to a specific favour , is the following sentence, where the author details that the 
favour consists of a man lending his horse to a friend. In (19), the favour that the 
speaker is asking for is for the addressee to buy him a rod.
In both examples, ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn is used in the active voice. Early

but examples such as (18) and (19) display how it could also be used as the main

by a prepositional phrase, (19). This is an indication that the  pragmaticalised

with the realisative construction (ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn “to do a favour”). 
However , the (partially)  pragmaticalised phrases are more frequent than the 
regular  support-verb construction. 
3.7 Pragmatic marker (“please” + request)
The sense of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn “to do a favour” is the source of the 
semi- pragmaticalised expression ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  “do [me] a 
favour; please.” There are certain indicators of an ongoing  pragmaticalisation 
process, such as its acquisition of  intersubjective meaning and, in most cases, 
its syntactic optionality. It is used in only two contexts: either to introduce a 
request (typically another  imperative) or to introduce a question (typically a 
direct question, see Section 3.8). The syntactic changes undergone by ποίησον

The main reason for separating uses (vi) and (vii) is that, despite semantics

phrase. Whereas in (vi) the verb could appear in different parts of the sentence, 
in (vii) it can only appear in the left periphery introducing a demand in the

And, whereas in (vi) it could be conjugated in other moods and coordinated 
with other nouns, in (vii) it can only be used in the  imperative with no noun 
co-ordination. The following examples evidence that, despite the semantic 
persistence, the phrase ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is not used freely within 
the clause anymore, but rather as a satellite, with an ossified morphological 
form and a fixed  word order:

The formulation of the clauses is very similar to the ones in (vii): ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  in the left periphery, followed by a vocative and, 
optionally, the phrase διὰ τὸν Κύριον dià tòn Kýrion “for the lord’s sake”. 
In (22), the question is introduced directly after the vocative, but in (23) 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  is coordinated with the  imperative εἰπέ eipé 
“speak”, which in turn introduces the question. In both examples, the aim 
of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  is to soften the illocutionary strength of 
the direct question, so as to introduce it more politely. In this context, the 
semantics of ἀγάπη agápē as “favour” is less clear: the speaker is not asking 
the addressee to carry out any specific action—if anything, the action of 
speaking in (23)—but rather to provide a certain piece of information. In (22), 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  does not introduce any other verb, but rather 
just a direct question. This evidences that it is not at all integrated into the 
main clause but used as an attitudinal satellite. It indicates that the speaker 
does not wish to be overly invasive with their question, and that they will 
be thankful if the addressee decides to provide the requested information. 
In other words, this is the context in which  pragmaticalisation, and more 
specifically intersubjectification, is the most evident. By intersubjectification, I 
understand the recruitment of pragmatic functions that focus on the reception 
of the message by the addressee, rather than the speaker . Intersubjectified 
expressions such as ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  are intended to re-shape

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages148 
a message from the speaker considering the addressee’s possible reaction to 
said message, more specifically, to try to make the addressee’s response more 
favourable. 
In this section, I have rearranged the  polysemy of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn 
according to semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic criteria. Despite the variation 
that it displays, ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn has in fact only three basic values: 
 support-verb construction, realisative construction, and pragmatic marker . The 
biggest  polysemy can be found within the group of realisative constructions. 
However , the meanings of all the constructions discussed can be reduced to 
“to carry out a [specific kind of] act of love”. This could help to simplify and 
re-organise the lexicographical entries of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn  across 
dictionaries. 
In the following section, I focus on the evidence for the  pragmaticalisation 
of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn in the cases of (vii) and (viii). I address the 
morphological and syntactic parameters that prove a higher or lower degree of 
 pragmaticalisation and explain the specific pragmatic contexts in which ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is used.
4. Syntactic changes
Together with the semantic development of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn  
explored in Section 3, some syntactic changes became apparent that point to its 
progressive acquisition of pragmatic properties (see Section 2). Below, I explore 
the degree of ossification of the categories of number ,  word order , and  syntactic 
integration of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn as a pragmatic marker . Lastly, I 
describe the pragmatic contexts in which it is used. 
4.1  Morphological number and number of addressees
The first hypothesis that I tested was whether there were phrases where 
number was used inconsistently with the context in which they are used, 
namely texts in which ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  occurs in the singular 
with a plural addressee or texts where ποιήσατε ἀγάπην poiḗsate agápēn in the 
plural occurs with a singular addressee. If the phrase ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson 
agápēn were fully  pragmaticalised, it could also be used to address a plural 
addressee. However , no such incoherences were found, which speaks for a 
lower degree of  pragmaticalisation. When the singular is used, it addresses a 
single interlocutor , (24), whereas the plural is used when speaking to groups of 
two or more people, (25).

4.2 Syntactic position
Despite being a longer phrase, ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  behaves 
similarly to other  imperative  particles, such as φέρε phére, ἄγε áge, ἴθι íthi ( ≈ 
“come on!”), etc. Zakowski (2018: 64) indicates that these  imperatives appear 
preferentially in the first position of the sentence, which he links to their 
acquisition of pragmatic meaning. La Roi (2022: 182) counter-argues that this 
correlation is not to be taken lightly, since another  imperative, ἀμέλει amélei 
“don’t worry”, gradually acquires a higher syntactic mobility as it recruits 
 intersubjective functions. In short, different values of ἀμέλει amélei tend to 
take different syntactic positions: where non-  intersubjective uses of ἀμέλει 
amélei mostly take a first position,  intersubjective uses show a higher degree 
of positional mobility. 
Another issue that La Roi (2022: 180, n. 31) raises is the difficulty to define 
first, second, and other syntactic positions in Greek. For instance, there may 
be several first or second positions, depending on how we define a position. 
In this chapter , I understand that the first position of a sentence is its first

prosodic item. If ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is preceded by a  particle such 
as ἀλλά allá, then it is not in the first position, (26). However , if ποίησον ἀγάπην 
poíēson agápēn is the first item of a sentence in direct speech, no matter how it 
is inserted into the text, it takes the first position, (27). In this chapter , I only look 
into whether ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is used in the first position or any 
other position (see Table 6.1).

In these cases, I have tagged ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn as occupying the 
first position, since it is the first prosodic item of the sentence, despite its syntactic 
discontinuity. This is how I have obtained the results that ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson

Bybee 2015: 124). This aligns with La Roi’s (2022: 166) statement that
the fact that the  imperative  particles do not reveal the effects of all changes 
associated with grammaticalization (Zakowski 2018: 63-65) is not problematic, 
since grammaticalizing constructions do not need to undergo every change 
associated with grammaticalization (e.g. phonetic reduction).
The development of this more complex pragmatic  imperative supports the 
notion that not all the changes associated with grammaticalisation need to be 
completed for a linguistic item to progressively acquire new pragmatic functions. 
The contexts in which ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is coordinated by means 
of καί kaí “and” with another verb phrase, (21), (23), and (26), show a lower 
degree of grammaticalisation, since the implication is that ποίησον ἀγάπην 
poíēson agápēn still retains some of its properties as an independent  imperative 
 support-verb construction, despite its acquisition of certain pragmatic functions 
( politeness, attenuation of  illocutive force).
4.3 Syntactic integration
Since the phrase ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is only partially  pragmaticalised, 
it is possible to trace in the texts the process of syntactic detachment that 
accompanies its acquisition of pragmatic properties. For example, in older texts, 
it is used as the main verb of the clause, still with the full meaning of “do me a 
favour” and taking other complements, (30). This represents only 6 examples 
out of the 122 that have been analysed.

4.4 Pragmatic function: Requests and demands
The core pragmatic function of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is the expression 
of  politeness. Whether it precedes a  request, (34), or a  question, (35), it is used to 
downplay the  illocutive force of the speaker’s statement. 
(34) Joannes Moschus, Pratum spirituale, 79.2929
τί κελεύεις, κύριε; Τότε λέγω αὐτῇ· Ποίησον ἀγάπην, ἐλθὲ ἕως ὧδε 
tí keleúeis, kýrie? tóte légō autē̂ i· poíēson agápēn, elthè ʰéōs ʰō̂ de
“‘What do you command, lord?’ Then I tell her: ‘Please, come here.’”
(35) Joannes Moschus, Pratum spirituale, 123.2985 (= 22)
ποίησον ἀγάπην, καλόγηρε, πόθεν με οἶδας; 
poíēson agápēn, kalógēre, póthen me oîdas;
“Please, Reverend, whence do you know me?”
However , examples such as (35) in which ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  
introduces a direct question are more obviously  pragmaticalised than examples 
such as (34), in which the distinction between the  support-verb construction 
and the pragmatic marker is blurrier . In a way, (34) is rather similar to those in 
which ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn retains its full meaning “to do a favour” 
and introduces a description of the favour with an infinitive clause, (31), or 
a coordinated καί kaí “and”-clause, (32). It might even have been possible to 
paraphrase (34) as ποίησον ἀγάπην ἐλθεῖν poíēson agápēn eltheîn. But this is not 
the case with (35), where ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn is neither syntactically 
nor semantically linked to the interrogative clause. It seems clear that ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn in (35) does not convey any meaning related to a favour , 
but that it is used to politely catch the attention of the addressee and prepare 
them for a positive outcome of the interaction, whose purpose is to obtain a 
specific piece of information. Out of the 20 examples of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson 
agápēn introducing a question, thirteen are juxtaposed, whereas only six are 
coordinated by καί kaí “and”. The examples that show juxtaposition introduce 
direct questions, (35), whereas the examples that show coordination introduce 
indirect questions, (23). Furthermore, the use of ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn 
introducing questions is chronologically restricted, since most examples appear

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages154 
in the sixth century CE (see Table 6.1). From the chronological distribution of the 
examples, it can be stated that there is not a chronological directionality from 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn + request to ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn + 
question, but rather a functional specialisation of the phrase. However , from 
a sociocultural perspective,  pragmaticalised ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn 
is restricted to  Christian texts, both in content and origin, and is particularly 
common in hagiographical texts. 
5. Conclusions
In this chapter , I have discussed the  pragmaticalisation of the phrase ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  according to three research questions: (i) What is the 
meaning of ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn , (ii) what are the indicators of the 
 pragmaticalisation of ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn , and (iii) to what extent 
is ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  a  pragmaticalised phrase? First, I have 
presented an overview of the 122 examples of semi-  pragmaticalised ποίησον 
/ ποιήσετε ἀγάπην poíēson/poiḗsete agápēn (see Table 6.1), which show that the 
expression peaked in use by the fourth to sixth centuries CE, in  Christian and 
more specifically in hagiographical texts, and declined afterwards, even though 
it did not completely disappear . Secondly, I have explored the different meanings 
with which ποιέω ἀγάπην poiéō agápēn is used in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae, 
where I have identified six  unpragmaticalised meanings, the first one of which 
is a  support-verb construction, while the rest are realisative constructions (i. “to 
love”, ii. “to perform an act of love”, iii. “to make love”, iv. “to make peace”, v. “to 
celebrate a banquet”, vi. “to do a favour”) and two pragmatic uses (vii. “please” 
followed by a request, viii. “please” followed by a question). 
Next, I have studied the pragmatic uses (vii and viii). I have found that 
 morphological number is coherent with the number of addressees of the request 
or question, which is an indication that the  pragmaticalisation of ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn  is only partial. Then, I have discussed the position of 
ποίησον ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn in the left periphery of the clause, which is the 
typical position for the codification of  intersubjective information. Regarding 
the  syntactic integration of ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  in the clause, 
coordination with καί kaí “and” is the most common form of linking ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poíēson agápēn to the main clause. However , καί kaí “and” is used to link 
another  imperative, which means that direct questions may only be introduced 
by ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  without καί kaí “and”. The last conclusion 
permeates all the points of the discussion: ποίησον ἀγάπην  poíēson agápēn  as 
a pragmatic function is only used in two contexts within  Christian literature, 
one of which is the introduction of requests and the other is the introduction of 
questions. In both cases, its function is that of catching the addressee’s attention,

softening the  illocutive force of the statement, and predisposing the addressee 
to a positive outcome of the interaction.

7. Between word and phrase: 
The puzzle of  Coptic  light-verb 
constructions (2nd to 5th c. CE)
 Nina Speransky
1. Introduction1
 Coptic represents the final documented stage of the Egyptian language, an 
independent branch of the Afroasiatic family that was spoken in the northern 
Nile Valley. It is attested from around 300 CE (Richter 2023), 2 and remained in 
use as a living language of written communication until the eleventh century 
CE, when it was gradually replaced by Arabic following the Arab conquest of 
Egypt in the seventh century CE. Today, it survives as a liturgical language of the 
 Coptic Orthodox Church. 
Early  Coptic already exhibits substantial dialectal variation (Richter 2023). 
Of these dialects,  Sahidic (southern) and  Bohairic (northern) are by far the best 
attested.  Sahidic alone accounts for ca. 90% of the  Coptic textual corpus. For 
this reason, the present study primarily draws on  Sahidic data, occasionally 
comparing  Sahidic and  Bohairic  light-verb constructions (  LVCs henceforth). 
Examples are marked with the conventional sigla, ( S) for  Sahidic and ( B) for 
 Bohairic.
The issue of  LVCs is briefly treated in two recent descriptive grammars of 
 Sahidic (Reintges 2018; Layton 2011).3 The present chapter builds on their data, 
but attempts to situate  Coptic  LVCs within general typology. Addressing the

inventory of  LVCs in both dialects and investigating their argument licensing 
strategies, the chapter shows that they function primarily as a derivational 
strategy while remaining accessible to syntactic operations such as agreement 
and indexing. 
Unless otherwise specified, the data for the study are drawn from the  Coptic 
Scriptorium corpus ( https://data.copticscriptorium.org), a digitally annotated 
collection of  Coptic texts. The translations are mine. Given the canonical 
nature of the biblical material that resists any changes and the uncertainties 
surrounding the dating of individual manuscripts, the corpus does not allow 
for a detailed  diachronic investigation. The present study therefore adopts a 
primarily synchronic perspective. 
The chapter is organised as follows. Section 1 argues that not all 
combinations of bound verb forms with nominal objects can be analysed as 
 noun incorporation or  lexical affixation and proposes a set of criteria correlating 
with  LVCs. Section 2 presents a survey of the inventory of  LVCs in  Sahidic and 
 Bohairic. Section 3 examines argument assignment strategies associated with 
 LVCs. Section 4 addresses the relationship between  LVCs and their synthetic 
counterparts arguing that attributing a uniform grammatical function (such 
as  telicity marking) to  Coptic  LVCs is implausible. Finally, Section 5 considers 
the implications of the  Coptic data for the  Lexical Integrity Principle pace Booij 
(2009).
2. Separating  light-verb constructions from 
morphologically bound complementation
The elementary units of  Coptic are not words—the notion of “word” can hardly 
be meaningfully defined for  Coptic (Haspelmath 2015)—but rather stress groups, 
also known as “bound groups” (Layton 2011). These groups mostly consist of 
a nominal or verbal root preceded by a series of phonologically dependent 
grammatical morphemes. Synthetic constructions with postposed person and 
tense-aspect markers (TAM henceforth), characteristic of earlier stages of 
Egyptian, underwent  periphrasis in a pre-  Coptic stage, followed by secondary 
synthesis in  Coptic. This development resulted in structures with preposed 
person and TAMs (Haspelmath 2015). 
 Coptic employs two verbal clause patterns: the TAM–subject–verb eventive 
pattern, and the subject–predicate durative pattern. In the eventive pattern, 
the verb may appear either in a free form (the so-called status absolutus) or in 
a bound form. Transitive 4 verbs typically exhibit two bound forms: one used

The combination of status constructus  forms with nominal objects in  Coptic 
remains in need of a morphosyntactic interpretation that is meaningful from 
a typological perspective. A morphological merger of the bound verbal form 
with an internal object noun may resemble two distinct phenomena:  noun 
incorporation understood as a verbal compound of a nominal and a verbal 
stem (Mithun 1984) and  lexical affixation, whereby bound morphemes with 
root-like meaning attach to host (Mithun 1997). Since  lexical affixes are 
regarded as a step in the evolution of  noun incorporation (Mithun 1997: 366), 
the difference between the two constructions amounts to their semantics. In 
incorporation, the verb is semantically specified by the  incorporated noun, 
while in  lexical affixation, the affix typically contributes a highly generalised 
meaning. 
One could argue that  Coptic exhibits verb–noun constructions of both types. 
The combinations ⲥⲕ-ⲙⲟⲟⲩ sk-moou “to draw water” and ⲣⲉⲧ-ⲧⲛϩ ret-tnh “to 
grow wings” in (2) and (3) resemble Mithun’s type I of  noun incorporation, that 
class reveals additional symptoms of  transitivity, such as sensitivity to the predicate aspect or 
the referentiality status of the object (see Speransky 2022).

Conversely, some accounts (for example, Grossman 2023) propose interpreting 
bound verbs in bound verb-noun combinations as  lexical affixes, based on 
their strict adjacency to the nominal object, the syntactic contiguity of the 
combination (notably, its resistance to the insertion of Wackernagel clitics), 
and the alleged association of the object noun with the lower end of the 
referentiality scale.
However , neither  noun incorporation nor  lexical affixation provides a fully 
adequate model for the  Coptic data. Each analysis captures certain properties 
of  Coptic verb–noun combinations while failing to account for others. First, in 
these combinations the noun occupies the usual position of a nominal argument; 
this does not comply with the strict definition of  noun incorporation proposed 
by Haspelmath (2025). 5 Further , in canonical incorporation constructions, 
nouns are typically non-referential or unmarked for specificity and definiteness 
(Mithun 1984: 849ff.). Similar restrictions apply to  lexical affixes, with additional 
diagnostics:  lexical affixes form a closed class (Mithun 1997: 369), and verbal 
prefixes undergoing  lexical affixation are subject to significant semantic 
bleaching, combining with another root to form a word expressing a single 
5 According to this definition, noun incorporation is a compound in which “the noun […] occurs 
in a position where nominal patient arguments cannot occur” (Haspelmath 2025: 2).

primary concept.  Coptic construct verb phrases do not consistently conform to 
these diagnostic criteria.
a) Verbs exhibiting construct forms do not constitute a closed lexical class. On 
the contrary, nearly all  transitive verbs in the native verbal inventory possess a 
construct form that cliticises to nominal objects.
b) The construction is not restricted to low-referentiality nouns. Examples 
(4) to (7), which are by no means marginal, demonstrate that the object position 
may be occupied by definite nouns with possessive modifiers, demonstrative 
pronouns, or even proper names. Rather than correlating with low referentiality, 
the construction is associated with low informational status (Speransky 2022), 6 
a property compatible with the third type of  noun incorporation identified by 
Mithun (1984).

semantics and do not merge into a single lexical concept, as illustrated in (4)

To sum up, none of the usual diagnostics for  LVCs, such as membership of 
the verb in a closed class, its semantic bleaching, or non-referentiality of the 
complement noun, consistently applies to the whole class of  Coptic construct 
predicates. Hence, treating all the instantiations of bound verb forms under the 
umbrella terms “ noun incorporation” or “ lexical affixes” seems to misrepresent 
the situation in  Coptic. 
However , there exists in  Coptic a class of construct verb phrases easily 
recognizable by the sheer frequency of specific verb-noun collocations, 
where the verbs are best analysed as  light verbs or even as affixes. However , 
the concept of a  light verb has to be modified for  Coptic. The usual, more 
or less intuitive idea of a  light verb is based, in most general terms, on the 
division of labour between the verb and the complement noun: the verb 
carries the grammar of the combination (tense and agreement in Jespersen 
(1954), aspect in Sobolak (2023), etc.), whereas the noun defines the semantics 
of the combination. In  Coptic, this concept only applies at the semantic 
level, since the tense-aspect-mood and person inflection is the property 
of a clause pattern as a whole (see above) and is not marked on the verb, 
anyway. Therefore, the essential criterion identifying this class appears to 
be a semantically  light verb combined with an inherently (as with nomina 
actionis ) or contextually non-referential object noun. The criterion of verb

The tight link between the verb and the noun can also be manifested in the 
following:
1. Non- compositionality/idiomaticity of the combination;
2. In cases where the verb-noun phrase takes arguments, the verb-noun 
phrase can be further expanded: argument licensing by the verb-noun 
combination as a whole, rather than by the verb or the noun alone; in 
the extreme case, the ability to take an argument identical to the object 
noun;
3. Non-modifiable object noun.
Non-modifiability of the object noun is not a decisive criterion for  Coptic: several 
 LVCs index their A[gent]- or P[atient]-argument as a possessor on the object noun 
(for example, ⲡⲉϥ-ⲟⲩⲟⲓ pef-ouoi “his course” in (9)). Importantly, such possessive 
indexing does not render the noun referential: as in English take one’s leave, the 
nominal component does not denote a discourse entity, and the construction 
still qualifies as an  LVC.

The constructions examined here only partially align with the cross-linguistic 
profile of  light-verb constructions as defined in annotation frameworks such 
as those developed within the  PARSEME initiative. In particular , the nominal 
element in  Coptic does not denote an action or event and, in most cases, does 
not license syntactic arguments (see Section 4). Furthermore,  Coptic  light-
verb constructions seem to appear as one (phonological word), also in many

lexical inflexibility, semantic non-  compositionality, and tolerance of so-called

frozen parts.
An idiomatic construction whose arguments are licensed not by any of its 
members, but by the construction as a whole is effectively a univerbation. 7

3. The inventory of  light-verb constructions and their 
components
The overall number of the light-verb phrases corresponding to the above criteria 
in  Coptic is difficult to estimate, because various dialects and even various 
corpora within the same dialect differ considerably in this respect. Thus far , 
no cross-dialectal description of  Coptic  light verbs has been undertaken. Even 
the most authoritative reference work, Crum’s dictionary, does not contain all 
such compounds. It is clear , however , that there are several dozen such forms in 
the  Sahidic and  Bohairic biblical corpora, which means that these constructions 
constitute a notable part of the verbal lexicon. Some of them are common to 
both dialects: they consist of the same lexical elements, and the contexts of 
 Sahidic constructions consistently match those of  Bohairic ones. Examples

As these examples show, the core of the light-verb inventory consists of the verbs 
(ⲉ)ⲣ- (e)r- “to do; to be”, ϯ- ti- “to give”, and  ϫⲓ- č̣i- “to take”, with significantly 
fewer examples of other verbs, for example, ϭⲛ- cn- “to find”, ⲕⲁ- ka- “to put”, ϥⲓ- 
fi- “to lift”, ϣⲉⲡ- šep- “to receive”, ϫⲉ-, ϫⲓ- č̣e-, č̣i- “to say”, ϩⲓ- hi- “to throw”. This set 
looks similar to those attested in many other languages, such as (post-)classical 
Greek (Fendel 2023), modern European languages of the  PARSEME sample, for 
example, Irish (Bloch-Trojnar 2010), to some extent Salishan Bella Coola (Mithun 
1997), and Chinese (Zhu 1985, Feng 2016). 11 A considerable body of research 
explores the possibility of a shared semantic or grammatical function among 
 light verbs as a lexicogrammatical category. On different accounts,  light verbs 
do (Butt 2003, Seiss 2009) or do not (Sobolak 2023) assign theta-roles. At least, 
in some languages, they create the effect of boundedness, ascribing  telicity to 
the event in question (Sobolak 2023). Finally, they are semantically selective, 
being not totally devoid of the semantics of their own (Cetnarowska 1993, Butt 
2003, Sobolak 2023). In English (Cetnarowska 1993) and in Irish (Bloch-Trojnar 
2010), the choice of the  light verb is shown to depend, among other things, 
on the  theta-role orientation of the predicated event (i.e., whether the subject 
referent is construed as an agent, a patient, or an experiencer of the event) 
and, accordingly, on the encoded meaning of (un)intentionality. Interestingly, 
construing the subject as a patient or experiencer of the complex predicate 
would still be compatible with the  telic aspect of the predicate:  telicity, in this 
case, results from the  transitivity of the  light verb itself.
In Coptic , synthetic predicates and synonymous  LVCs do not display aspectual 
preferences. This must stem from the fact that the Coptic   verbal system does

not support any aspectual ambiguity; aspects are encoded in the conjugational 
morphology. On the other hand, there is some correlation between a  light verb 
and the  theta-role of the subject, at least, in as much as give-compounds usually 
introduce a  causative event, and take-compounds do not. More precisely, the 
three main  light verbs differ in how much control or volitionality the subject 
referent has over the resulting event. Give-compounds are +controlled/volitional, 
take-compounds, as a rule, are controlled/volitional, do-compounds are neutral 
in this respect. 
Though in a very few tokens, Coptic   also manifests a phenomenon that is, 
to my knowledge, unattested in other languages, that is, secondary affixation, 
when a  light verb is attached to a stem that already consists of a  light verb and a 
noun.12 The Bohairic Bible contains examples, such as ⲉⲣ-ϭⲓ-ϥⲉⲛⲧ er-č̣i-fent “to be 
worm-eaten” (Acts 12:23), ⲉⲣ-ϭⲓ-ⲛⲓⲟⲟⲣ er-č̣i-nior “to ford a river” (Gen.31:21 and 
passim), and ⲉⲣ-ϭⲓ-ⲥⲁⲛⲓⲥ er-č̣i-sanis “to have doubts” (Psalms 118:39), while in a 
fragment of the  Sahidic Shepherd of Hermas, the compound ⲣ-ⲡ-ⲙⲉⲉⲩⲉ er-p-meeue 
“to remember” is nominalised by the definite article ⲡ- p- and further expanded 
by another ⲉⲓⲣⲉ eire “to do” ( ⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ-ⲡ-ⲣ-ⲡ-ⲙⲉⲉⲩⲉ ⲙ-ⲡⲉϥ-ⲙⲟⲩ eire m-p-r-p-meeue 
m-pef-mou “to remember his death” (Lefort 1940)).13 The diachronic development 
of such  LVCs can be reconstructed as follows: Coptic  had a productive zero-
derivation from verbs to nouns, so the verbalised expressions ϭⲓ-ϥⲉⲛⲧ č̣i-fent “to 
take worms” and ϭⲓ-ⲥⲁⲛⲓⲥ č̣i-sanis “to take doubt” became  univerbated and in 
their turn nominalised, which prompted the second-order verbal derivation. To 
appreciate this phenomenon in the larger context of Coptic  morphology, we have 
to remember the specifics of Coptic  word-formation. Coptic  can simultaneously 
be termed an analytic (Funk 1978, Reintges 2011) and a synthetic (Haspelmath 
2015) language due to the dual nature of its morphology. On the level of 
lexical units, Coptic  is a root-and-pattern language. It almost completely lacks 
concatenative inflectional morphology and has a very restricted derivational 
morphology (Jernstedt 1986: 169-176, Richter 2023: 13). On the level of prosodic 
units, Coptic  is an agglutinative language; its verb-containing unit can consist 
of two to five morphs. Light-verb doubling points to the fact that, at least, the 
primary  light verbs in these lexemes came all the way from being a part of a 
syntactic construction (verbal phrase) to being an affix capable of further 
morphological integration. Thus, similarly to the abstract-deriving prefix ⲙⲛⲧ- 
mnt- and the privative prefix ⲁⲧ- at-, it can signal a transition from the root-
and-pattern morphology inherited from earlier Egyptian to a concatenative

4. Valency of  light-verb constructions
As distinct lexical units, light-verb compounds establish a valency pattern of 
their own. However , the semi- lexicalised nature of these constructions raises the 
question of which component ultimately determines the valency of the whole 
compound. Depending on the language, all four logically possible answers 
can be found in the literature. For Japanese, it is argued that a  light verb is 
just a licensing host for the theta-roles assigned by the semantic head of the 
compound (Grimshaw and Mester 1988). Elsewhere, different  light verbs can 
assign distinct valencies with one and the same semantic head thereby affecting

Kettnerová and Bejček (2016) claims that in Czech, both the  light verb and the 
object noun contribute to the valency pattern of the compound.
Finally, in a study dedicated specifically to  LVCs with lexemes of Greek origin 
in  Bohairic Coptic,  Zakrzewska claims that the use of prepositions other than the 
default marker ⲛ/ⲙⲙⲟ= n-/mmo= with the second argument “is limited to certain 
semantic classes of verbs, such as verbs of perception and cognition and verbs 
denoting contact-by-motion, whose second argument is marked by the allative 
preposition [ⲉ-/ⲉⲣⲟ=] e-/ero= or verbs of ritual behavior and speech actions, which 
occur with [ ⲛ-/ⲛⲁ=] n-/na=” (Zakrzewska 2017: 233). In Zakrzewska’s opinion, 
therefore, theta-roles are not assigned by the  light verb or its complement, but 
stem from the semantic class of the resulting verbal lexeme.
As can be seen already from Zakrzewska’s description, Coptic  LVCs are 
not homogeneous with respect to their  theta-role licensing. Rather , they form 
classes depending on the degree of  univerbation. Some  LVCs are fully or almost 
fully analysable and more construction-, than word-like. The valency in such 
compounds can be seen as determined by one element, less often the noun (as 
in ϭⲛ-ϩⲙⲟⲧ ⲙⲡⲉⲙⲧⲟ ⲛ- cn-hmot mpemto n- “to find grace before”), more often the 
verb, as in various compounds with ϯ ti “to give” (for example, ϯ-ⲥⲃⲱ ti-sbô “to 
give knowledge” = “to teach”).

of take-compounds represents patient or beneficiary, or experiencer , while the 
subject of give-compounds refers to agent or stimulus. This class includes, for 
instance, ϯ-ⲃⲉⲕⲉ / ϫⲓ-ⲃⲉⲕⲉ ti-beke / č̣i-beke “to pay; to be paid”, ϯ-ⲙⲕⲁϩ / ϭⲓ-ⲙⲕⲁϩ

the complement noun, give has three arguments and take has two), which makes 
the give-compounds bivalent, and the take-compounds intransitive. Typically, in 
such cases, ϯ ti “to give” assigns dative case (marked by the preposition ⲛ-/ ⲛⲁ= 
n- /na= in Coptic)  to the second argument. 
However , the parallel derivation of ϯ-/ϫⲓ- ti- / č̣i- as inducing thematic roles of 
stimulus/(in)direct  causer and experiencer/patient, respectively, is not regular 
or pervasive, thus does not reach the extent of a full-fledged grammatical device. 
So, the subjects of ϯ-ⲟⲥⲉ ti-ose “to lose” (literally “to give loss”), ϯ-ⲟⲩⲃⲁϣ ti-oubaš 
“to grow white” (literally “to give white”) do not denote either a stimulus, or 
a  causer , while the subjects of ϫⲓ-ϫⲛⲓⲧ č̣i-č̣nit “to test, to examine” (literally “to 
take test”) or ϫⲓ-ⲙⲟⲉⲓⲧ č̣i-moeit “to lead” (literally “to take way”) do not refer to 
patients.
What happens in those less easily analysable cases is a certain  metaphorical 
reinterpretation of the compound which can be more or less remote from the 
sum of the literal meanings of the parts, as, for instance, in ϫⲓ-ⲥⲙⲏ č̣i-smê “to hear” 
(literally “to take voice”), ϫⲓ-ϩⲟ č̣i-ho “to favour” (literally “to take face”), ⲙⲉϩ-
ⲣⲱ= meh-rô= “to bite” (literally “to fill mouth”), ϫⲓ-ⲏⲡⲉ č̣i-êpe “to count” (literally 
“to take number”), ϫⲓ-ϣⲟϫⲛⲉ č̣i-šoč̣ne “to advise” (literally “to take decision”). In

by the complement noun. Rather , it mirrors the argument structure of synthetic 
verbs with similar meanings and thus, in line with Zakrzewska’s observations, 
is determined by the semantic class of the verb. The semantic gradations are 
subtle, so I shall limit myself to pointing out only a few regularities or particularly 
curious cases. The addressee of a speech act is typically coded with the dative ⲛ- 
/ⲛⲁ= n- / na= preposition, so this is the valency of ϫⲓ-ϣⲟϫⲛⲉ č̣i-šoč̣ne “to advise”,

5. Light-verb constructions vs. synthetic verbs
Although the existence of a synthetic verb with a similar or equivalent meaning 
is often proposed as one of the criteria for identifying  LVCs, to my knowledge, 
relatively few studies have systematically compared synthetic and analytic 
counterparts. Sobolak (2023) undertakes such a comparison for English and 
Korean, concluding that  LVCs re-organise the event structure making it  telic. 
Cetnarowska (1993: 41–42) assumes that the choice of an  LVC in English may be 
influenced by discourse principles of end-weight and end-focus (as suggested in 
Quirk et al. 1972) or by the relative ease of modification (as claimed by Jespersen 
1954 and Halliday 1985).
In Coptic,   relatively few  LVCs have a synthetic equivalent. In most cases, 
 LVCs introduce entirely new concepts by verbalising nouns—for example, 
ⲣ-ⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ r-khreia (“to need”) or ϫⲓ-ⲙⲁⲧⲟⲩ č̣i-matou (“to be poisoned”). When a close 
synthetic synonym does exist, in some cases,  LVCs seem to be associated with a 
particular type of participants or situation. Thus, the verb ⲱⲡ ôp “to count” is 
consistently applied to inanimate/non-human entities, such as time units, stars, 
or cattle, (30) and (31).

6. Coptic  light-verb constructions and the Principle of 
Lexical Integrity
Let us consider again the  LVCs in which the  light verb and the complement noun 
can be separated by a possessive prefix referring to the P[atient]-argument, such

or ϭⲙ-ⲡⲉⲥ-ϣⲓⲛⲉ cm-pes-šine “to visit her” (literally “to find her seeking”).

The prefix ⲙⲛⲧ- mnt- is a fully grammaticalised, bound derivational morpheme; 
it does not carry independent lexical meaning but functions as the morphological 
head of the derived lexeme assigning it feminine gender , so functionally it is 
equivalent to an abstract-deriving affix in European languages. Yet, we saw that, 
similarly to LVCs  with an internal inflection, ⲙⲛⲧ- mnt-nominalisations remain 
accessible to agreement and indexing operations, revealing a mismatch between 
syntactic and morphological processes. Clearly, the lexical units, such as LVCs 
 and ⲙⲛⲧ- mnt-nominalisations, occupy some middle field between constructions 
and words, pointing to the  univerbation tendency which in time could change 
the morphological type of Coptic  to concatenative.
7. Conclusion
Though the majority of native verbal vocabulary have bound  transitive 
allomorphs, only a closed set of verbs can also function as  light verbs, or in 
other words, verb-deriving affixes. Defined by a priori  criteria, such as non-
referentiality of noun objects, semantic voidness of the verb, and idiomaticity 
of the combination, some LVCs  show additional properties testifying to the 
complete  univerbation of the initial affix-noun combination: the ability to take 
arguments cognate to the object noun, the phonological assimilation of the verb, 
the generation of stative allomorphs to the verb-noun complex as a whole, and 
finally, occasional secondary derivation of an  LVC from another  LVC.
The core of the set of verb-deriving affixes consists of the verbs meaning 
do, give, and take; the last two frequently derive  causative-passive pairs. 
The inventory of verb-deriving affixes has many cross-linguistic parallels. A 
promising line of inquiry would be to examine whether the lexical meanings 
of the verbs that become verbalisers are systematically associated with specific 
semantic effects in derivation—for instance, in Coptic,  give tends to correlate 
with volitionality/agency, whereas take predominantly yields non-volitional/
non- causative verb phrases. 
As for the inventories of derivations,  Sahidic and  Bohairic differ: an  LVC 
in one dialect often corresponds to a synthetic verb in the other . Yet in both 
dialects, this type of derivation represents a productive mechanism, applying 
to both native and borrowed nouns. Both examined dialects also exhibit the 
 diachronic residue of this mechanism in the form of LVCs  containing nouns that 
are not used outside these constructions. Synchronically, these function as semi-
analysable  lexicalised compounds. 
 Valency is rarely determined by the noun; more often it is imposed by the 
verb, and even more often, it matches the theta-roles defined by the meaning of 
the derived verb. In a few cases, the argument is morphosyntactically realised 
as a noun modifier (possessive prefix or suffix). The occurrence of an inflected

1. Introduction
 Luke opens his gospel with a prefatory declaration to Theophilus about his 
storytelling mission, which alerts his readers to a potential curation of and sensitivity 
to the ways in which Greek is able to tell stories. As we read the gospel, we are 
taken on a journey, from Nazareth to Jerusalem, and through Jesus’ teaching. This 
journey, I suggest, is partly scaffolded by  Luke’s idiosyncratic use of the  imperfect 
tense, and the multi-word (sometimes  periphrastic)  imperfect construction in 
particular . In this chapter , therefore, I compare and contrast the use of the multi-
word  imperfect as opposed to the synthetic  imperfect in the  gospels of  Mark and 
 Luke.2 A fuller analysis including at least Acts of the Apostles and the other gospels 
would be interesting for the sake of contextualising the argument. Given that Acts 
deals with different kinds of materials, however , and  John’s gospel is very different 
to the synoptics, a comparison of  Mark and  Luke offers a useful and manageable 
starting point for the kind of analysis which can be undertaken in a short chapter .
The first section of this chapter outlines my methodology and approach. I 
define my understanding of the multi-word form of the  imperfect, within an 
understanding of what does or does not class as “  periphrastic”, acknowledging 
where some disagreement lies. I then introduce my data and its limitations.
Before analysing the different constructions further , I then outline and explore 
the standard uses of the  imperfect. I move on to use this to formulate a specific 
argument about how the multi-word version of the  imperfect tense, however

categorised, plays a specific  narratological (and consequently exegetical) role in 
 Mark and  Luke, exploring key similarities and differences. Previous research has 
focussed primarily on understanding the  imperfect in general, or on discerning 
what a  periphrastic construction is, and for the  New Testament, how this relates 
to the language of the  Septuagint (for example, Rundgren 1965; Bentein 2011; 
Bentein 2013).3 In this chapter , I blend these approaches to assess how multi-
word formulations of the  imperfect differ from their synthetic equivalents in 
meaningful ways. I argue that the difference triangulates an aspectual and 
indeed literary/ narratological approach that is present in  Luke’s gospel, but only 
emerging in  Mark’s, offering three different ways to set up the background action 
in a scene. 
 Luke states his historiographical approach directly and also signals it with 
his specific phrasing. He opens the gospel with an unusual  particle, ἐπειδήπερ 
(epeidēper) “when”.4 As Thrall (1962) documents, the New Testament writers make 
very little use of the richness available through Greek  particles. Compounding 
 particles is particularly weak, with even  Luke using a statistically very low number 
of combinations (Thrall 1962: 8–9). Using such an unusual word, therefore, to 
open the text, sets our scene for a work that could be expected to be linguistically 
deliberate and rich. In verses 1-4, a preface dedicated to Theophilus, he establishes 
himself as wanting to write the story clearly, that is, to being in some sense a 
historian. Even phrases such as ἔδοξ̣εν κἀμοὶ (edoxen kamoi) ”it seemed a good 
idea to me” are reminiscent of Herodotus’ ὡς ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ (hōs emoige dokei) ”so 
it seems to me”, casting  Luke as an engaged and deliberate narrator , unlike in the 
other gospels.5 Where Herodotus, however , uses this phrase to excuse himself from 
criticism over implausible content,  Luke will do the opposite: take the thoroughly 
implausible story of Jesus’ life, and commit to its veracity. With this deliberate 
positioning, it is appropriate to probe other ways in which  Luke uses language 
to structure expression. Moreover , Herodotus (and other historians), themselves 
make specific, notable use of  periphrastic constructions, highlighting the specific 
linguistic feature under discussion in this chapter (for example, Gonda 1959).6
