2. Methodology
Classifying what is, or indeed is not, a  periphrastic construction, is itself not 
uncontested.7 Nardi (2025: 34), as a recent summariser , describes εἶναι einai “to 
be” +  participle as the most studied and contested  periphrastic construction. 
Nardi and Romagno (2025: 45) discuss “prototype” categories for these multi-
word expressions, removing the focus on ascertaining precisely what kind of 
 periphrastic construction may be present. I take such a broad view in this chapter . 
For the purpose of this chapter , I work within some specific parameters. My 
primary focus is on exploring the potential  narratological impact and exegetical 
usefulness of a specific kind of multi-word expression in the  imperfect. The 
impact of this is that precise classification of  periphrasis is not essential to the 
argument. I use the term “multi-word expression” as the umbrella category of 
which  periphrastic constructions are an example. When engaging with secondary 
literature, I echo other author’s uses of the term  periphrastic. This is, however , an 
argument about multi-word expressions broadly conceived, and their impact on 
understanding, not on the narrower category of  periphrastic constructions and 
their definition. I explore these categorisation differences further below.
I include almost all  imperfect verbs in the Greek  New Testament. I use the 
term  periphrastic with regards to the basic data as a shorthand to refer to any 
example of εἰμί (eimi, “I am”) used with a  participle in the same clause, that is, to 
any multi-word formulation with εἰμί (eimi) as the auxiliary verb. Bentein et al. 
(2012) discuss how existential uses of εἰμί (eimi) may be combined with  participles, 
leading to a lack of clarity over whether an εἰμί ( eimi) +  participle combination 
is in fact  periphrastic; their example is  Luke 1:10. As they demonstrate, it is 
possible to read some examples in multiple ways (they categorise  Luke 1:10 
as both existential-progressive and  periphrastic). In a separate study, Bentein 
(2013: 174) notes that 3/4 of his durative progressive examples from  Mark and 
 Luke are ambiguous; precise classification remains elusive. The scope of this 
chapter is not all  periphrastic constructions in  Mark and  Luke, but all multi-
word expressions using an  imperfect auxiliary verb.
For the purpose of this chapter , I restrict discussion to εἰμί ( eimi) as an 
auxiliary verb. Given my focus on the  imperfect rather than  periphrasis per se, I 
exclude examples with other tenses of εἰμί (eimi) from my main analysis but do 
comment briefly on these.8 I include all participle tenses used with the imperfect 
of εἰμί (eimi); these are predominantly present or aorist, with occasional perfect 
 participles.9 Where more than one participle depends on the same auxiliary verb, 
in either  Mark or  Luke, I count it as “1.5” for multi-word-expression purposes.

4. Uses of the  imperfect in Greek
To help understand what the multi-word  imperfect phrases are doing differently 
to their synthetic counterparts, I first summarise some of the (relatively) agreed 
uses of the  imperfect in Greek, especially in the  New Testament Koine. Discussions 
over tense and aspect in Greek continue, with consensus yet to be agreed, but 
functional roles for the  imperfect, however classified, can be broadly accepted. 
Siebenthal (2019: 321–323) categorises the key difference between the 
 imperfect and aorist (indicative) as aspectual, citing it as durative, and linear . 
Wallace (1996) describes the  imperfect in the  New Testament as giving an internal 
aspect, akin to a motion-picture experience from within the action, that is not so 
concerned with its beginning or end. This reflects Smyth’s categorisation of it as 
representing an action as still going on, or a state still existing in the past (Smyth 
and Messing 2013: §1889). This progressive/descriptive sense, which also gives a 
vividness or simultaneity with other actions is what people often consider to be 
the  imperfect’s main role.13  
13 See also Du Plooy (1991: 163) on uses of the imperfect. He gives six: progressive/durative/linear ,

This is the usual “was doing” kind, or as Smyth writes: “The  imperfect is 
often used to describe an action or state that is in progress in past time from 
the viewpoint… of the speaker …. It speaks either of vividness or simultaneity 
with another action” (Smyth and Messing 2013: §1898). 14  While the sense of 
being in medias res  is clear , the inchoative force of the  imperfect should not 
be dismissed, and remains relevant to the New  Testament. 15 As Robertson 
(1914: 885) notes, the inchoative (or inceptive)  imperfect is particularly useful 
for describing the ‘beginning of an action’ rather than its mere occurrence, a 
feature that aligns with the introductory nature of Jesus’s teaching in the early 
chapters of Mark  and Luke. 
 There are also times when the  imperfect will be instantaneous, that is, similar 
to the aorist. These mainly involve ἔλεγεν ( elegen) as “he said”, particularly in 
Mark ( 46 uses), but also for example, Matthew 9:24, Luke 23:42  , John 5:19. The 
 imperfect can, with ἔλεγεν (elegen), be a stylistic tool to keep a narrative flowing, 
while still marking points of action and change in the narrative akin to the aorist 
(see Smyth and Messing 2013: §1908; Siebenthal 2019: 323).
The  imperfect may also be used iteratively (where Wallace’s standard 
examples do not include Mark  or Luke), or  conatively, to suggest attempted 
action which may or may not have been completed (for which Wallace suggests 
Matt 3:14, Mark 15:23, Acts 26:11, Luke 1:59,   Rom 9:3.). 16 It can be used in a 
customary or habitual way, for which Wallace offers Matt 26:55, Mark 4 :33, Luke 
2:41,  Acts 3:2, Rom 6:17, Gal 1:14. It may also be used pluperfectively, to indicate 
antecedent action relating to a main narrative expressed in the past. Wallace 
(1996) suggests that this is more common with ἔλεγεν (elegen), offering Mark 5 :8 
and 6:18, and Luke 8:29 as examples (see also Smyth and Messing 2013: §1906).17 
In summary, the imperfect  is a versatile verb form which was used in a broad 
range of ways to describe actions within both tense and aspect frames. Reducing 
this to a simple guide has eluded grammarians. We can complicate the picture 
further by considering the multi-word, or  periphrastic version.

5. The multi-word imperfect
 The synthetic imperfect,  for example, ἐδίδασκεν (edidasken) “he was teaching”, 
is also accompanied, throughout the New   Testament, by a multi-word version, 
for example, ἦν διδάσκων (  ēn didaskōn ) “he was teaching”. This multi-word 
expression formulation of the imperfect,   pairing an auxiliary verb (εἰμί eimi) 
with a  participle, is relatively frequent in the gospels. In his dissertation on 
the grammaticalisation of time and use of the imperfect  in the New  Testament, 
Ortner (2019: 62) makes only one passing reference to  periphrasis (as a specific 
form of multi-word expression. Johnson (2010) gives an extensive account, but 
makes only one reference to Luke. He  suggests that the  periphrastic imperfect 
 has a discourse function, but is limited to narrative sections of the gospel, and 
that its use is over-reported. He argues that it has been under-investigated 
because of its assumed grounding in Semitic grammar , but that it represents, 
instead, a more marked form of Koine. 18 His analysis is limited, and while I 
return to it, I acknowledge Bentein’s (2013: 170) criticism of the narrowness, 
and in this chapter use a broader definition of multi-word expression. 
Daniel (2021: 729) explores how frequent ἦν ( ēn) with a present  participle 
is in the  Septuagint (see also Bentein 2013). Bentein (2016: 248) observes that 
as many as 82% (146/178) of the examples of what he identifies as  periphrastic 
constructions in the New   Testament are, consequently, structurally influenced 
by their  Hebrew parent text. 
Perhaps the best-known example of the  periphrastic/multi-word imperfect 
 in the gospels is ἦν διδάσκων ( ēn didaskōn) “he was teaching”. This occurs seven 
times in the New   Testament, five of which are in Luke. 19 It becomes a stylistic 
quirk of Luke’s, but  in this chapter , I suggest that it is more than idiolectical. It 
is to some degree intentional, contrasting with both the aorist and the synthetic 
imperfect  as a way to introduce scenes. I turn now, therefore, to compare its use 
with the synthetic equivalent, ἐδίδασκεν (edidasken).
ἐδίδασκεν (edidasken) is used 14 times in the New  Testament. Six are in Mark 
( 1:21, 2:13, 4:2, 9:31, 10:1, 11:17). Three are in Luke-Acts (  Luke 4:15,  5:3, and 
Acts 2:14). This weighting reverses when we consider the multi-word version 
ἦν διδάσκων ( ēn didaskōn), used once each in Matthew and Mark ( Matthew 7:29, 
Mark 1 :22), but five times in Luke. The  sole use in Mark  comes just one verse 
after its synthetic equivalent, (2).

There is a sense in Luke’s  gospels, of an undercurrent of constant dialogue 
with the Pharisees, of which only small elements “break through” into the text 
to be witnessed in a narrative. This accords with a further sense in Luke that 
 central chapters represent an ongoing dialogue/debate between Jesus and the 
Pharisees, only some of which is captured in the text. 21 The use of ἀποκρίνομαι 
(apokrinomai) “to answer , to reply” is important here.22 Both the aorist participle, 
ἀποκριθείς (apokritheis), and indicative, ἀπεκρίθη ( apekrithē) occur frequently. 
ἀποκριθείς (apokritheis) is particularly Lukan, with 34/94 uses of the  participle 
in the New  Testament being from Luke-Acts; the  relational quality of his writing 
is made clear . Sometimes this is in genuine reply to someone, for example Luke 
10:27,  where Jesus replies to the lawyer . At other times, it is to a situation, for 
example at Luke 11:14  where the high priest responds to Jesus healing on the 
Sabbath. 
There remain times, however , where the provocation for response is less 
clear; at Luke 14:3  there is an assumption that Jesus will heal the man, and cause 
consternation as a result. His reply is almost pre-emptive of what we have seen 
in places like Luke 11:14.  The use of ἀποκρίνομαι ( apokrinomai) “to answer , to 
reply” provides a way to show that the gospel is not the whole teaching, and 
the ongoing murmuring against Jesus is a constant conversation. This point is 
reinforced by Luke’s use of  διαγογγύζω (diagogguzō) “to murmur”, used only 
twice in the New  Testament, both by Luke, in the  imperfect,  of the Pharisees 
and those suspicious of Jesus (Luke 15:2, 19:  7). Luke is the  only author to use

enquire” (and 9/12 total uses are Luke-Acts).   Similarly, although there are 56 
uses of ἐπερωτάω (eperōtaō) “to ask” in the New  Testament, only Mark  and Luke

indicative of a pattern which is hinted at in Mark,  particularly with his frequent

5.1 καὶ  ἐγένετο kai egeneto: Aorist scene-setting as a contrast
Example (7) includes not only an imperfect  setting, but an aorist opening: 
καὶ ἐγένετο ( kai egeneto ) “and it happened”. The grammar of scene-setting is 
relevant to both pericopes and chapters. Half of the chapters in Luke open with  
an imperfect (  as opposed to only a third in Mark,  and only two chapters in 
Matthew).23 Luke, however ,  uses ἐγένετο ( egeneto)/ καὶ ἐγένετο ( kai egeneto) 68 
times. Although it is often seen as a Markan phrase, it occurs only 17 times in 
Mark.
 Luke’s use is  copious, and not purely formulaic. Reilig (1965: 159–160) suggests 
that Luke is using  it not as a marker of a majestic or hieretic style, reflecting the 
 Hebrew phrasing of the  Old Testament, but as a development of the Greek of the 
 Septuagint. While the  Septuagint is itself a reflection of the  Hebrew, it is also its 
own form of Greek, with Atticising tendencies, and other cultural influences. 
Luke is  primarily a Hellenist, rather than a Semiticist. His use of καὶ ἐγένετο (kai 
egeneto) is distinctive within Greek, with its own “scene-setting” impact. Five 
of Luke’s uses  include specific time references (Luke 1:5, 1:59 , 2:1, 17:26, 17:28), 
while 22 are followed by an articular infinitive to give a durative background. 
This includes both Luke 9:18 and  9:28, (8).

kai egeneto en tōi proseuchesthai auton
“and it happened that while he was praying...”

this difference to suggest that there is no functional difference between the 
synthetic and  periphrastic forms. I suggest that the two uses are, instead, not 
intended to be comparable, and there is a distinction; as Nardi goes on to 
discuss, “difference” may come in different categories, including pragmatic,

5.2 Multi-word imperfects in Luke
This  sense that there was teaching taking place in a generic but important way 
helps explain other observations made about the clause, and integrate some 
apparent differences of opinion. Gonda (1959: 97) opens by countering Rosén’s 
(1957) argument that  periphrastic clauses occur when the idea of a verb is not 
the predicate of a sentence, but the subject, and the logical predicate is not the 
agent, but a complement. As Gonda explains,  verbal sentences have tended to 
be used for actions, while nominal/semi-nominal ones are used for description. 
With this development of  periphrastic clauses, we see a move towards more 
nominal sentences being used to set up action. Gonda (1959: 99–100) suggests 
that whereas the predicate of a verbal sentence focusses the hearer’s thoughts 
on what happens, the predicate of a nominal sentence directs their attention to 
what is (i.e. more existential). With  ἦν διδάσκων ( ēn  didaskōn), the important 
issue, on this model, would be that teaching were taking place, moreover in 
the synagogue, and on a Sabbath, rather than necessarily it being Jesus himself 
doing the teaching. Jesus’ agency can be assumed; this is, after all, his story. The 
novelty of what he is doing (where, when, how), cannot. By using the multi-
word imperfect,  therefore, on Rosén’s model, we shift the focus onto the novelty 
of the teaching, and see this borne out in the unusual linguistic use of other 
terms around it. This does not require it to be a “true”  periphrastic construction 
in any of the defined senses; the multi-word expression still stands in contrast 
to the synthetic equivalent.
σαββάτῳ ( sabbatōi “on the Sabbath”), is another irregularity demarcating 
difference. It appears in both the singular and plural.  When singular , as quoted 
above, it is often without a definite article, giving a generic sense of “on a 
Sabbath, any old Sabbath”. When plural, it would usually be construed of as 
“week” (i.e. seven days), but clearly refers to the Sabbath, and so seems to carry 
a sense, again, of “pick a Sabbath, any Sabbath”, because it is not the date that 
matters so much as the context of what teaching in a synagogue on a Sabbath 
means, as opposed to anywhere else, at any other time (cf. Levinsohn 2016b: 
313). Luke has both  maintained the novelty of Jesus’ Sabbath teaching, and the 
ongoing undercurrent of teaching and enquiry to which I suggest the imperfect 
 points.
Rosén’s approach, however , is not the only way to understand the multi-
word (and sometimes  periphrastic) imperfect,  particularly with reference 
to ἦν διδάσκων ( ēn  didaskōn ). Gonda (1959: 107) sees Rosén as overreaching 
himself, and the emphasis of one participant in the construction over another 
as too subtle. I suggest not that Rosén is overreaching/overly subtle, but that his

8. Roundabout ways of setting up scenes in the Greek New Testament 203
understanding of difference between synthetic and  periphrastic construction 
is in part grounded in both aspectual and narratological differences.25 Bringing 
in other perspectives, and both literary and lexical arguments gives Rosén‘s 
analysis a role integrated with the work of others, notably Björck, Bentein, and 
Johnson.
Björck (1940) takes a very different approach, with specific reference to the 
New  Testament. He identifies improper  periphrasis, where the  participle is 
not a predicate, and εἶναι ( einai) “to be” is not a copula, adjectival  periphrasis, 
where the participle has the character of an adjective, and “real” periphrasis.26 
Björck (1940) cites Luke 9:47 and ἦν  διδάσκων (ēn  didaskōn) as characterising 
“real”  periphrasis, where the process is being conceived as a temporal frame 
encompassing something else which may be expressed but may also be 
understood from the context (see also Gonda 1959: 104). It becomes about the 
relative duration of processes. The imperfect in   general establishes ongoing 
background contextual action across which specific moments are overlaid. 
Levinsohn’s (2016b: 312) variation on this, wherein what he calls the ”copular 
imperfect”  presents iterative events, portraying an actor as performing an 
action from time to time during a period rather than continuously may also 
point towards the reading I am giving; the multi-word imperfect  helps to set 
up a situation wherein what is represented in the text is a ”breakthrough” 
from a background situation, with iterative but distinct examples of an action, 
such as teaching. Taking Rosén’s view, the multi-word version of it may help 
shift attention from agent to action. Blending these together , we see how the 
multi-word imperfect  focusses our attention not only on action, but on the 
durative or progressive nature of that action. Every ἦν διδάσωκν ( ēn  didaskōn) 
therefore also becomes a cumulative contribution to the overall “didache” 
(teaching).

(Bentein 2013: 189).
Luke’s use of the  construction is more varied and nuanced than any other New 
 Testament writer , including within the specific realm of the imperfect.  Levinsohn 
(2016b: 314) summarises the imperfect  periphrastic as describing ongoing 
states, presenting iterative events, and background scene-setting events at the 
beginning of pericopes. In what I have presented, I have suggested a way in 
which these functions blend in Luke, and become  dependent on lexical context 
(verbs of enquiry/teaching etc.), offering a specific  narratological function 
grounded in historiographical awareness.
5.3 Comparing Mark  and Luke
There are  places where Mark  and Luke tell the same  story, for example the 
healing of the Gerasene (Gadarene) Daimoniac (Matthew 8:28–34, Mark 5  :1–20, 
Luke 8:26–39).  Matthew omits the detail, but both Mark  and Luke include a 
 description of herd of pigs grazing on a mountain, (11).

8. Roundabout ways of setting up scenes in the Greek New Testament 205
In both cases, the  participle is separated from the auxiliary verb by a considerable 
distance (Bentein 2011: 14, refuting Porter 1992). The extent to which this matters 
is debated, but it may suggest that we should read the ἦν ēn “there was” more 
existentially, with the  participle βοσκομένη ( boskomenē) “grazing” adjectivally, 
rather than within a periphrastic context.29 Two differences between Mark and 
Luke’s versions may  be important, however . In Mark’s  version, the  participle 
follows closely after the noun ἀγέλη agelē “herd”, the genitive describing it 
(χοίρων choirōn “of pigs”) and an adjective μεγάλη megalē “big”. It reads as 
part of that noun-phrase. In Luke, however , the  removal of μεγάλη megalē 
“big” breaks that sense of continuity and leaves the  participle more exposed. 
In addition, the phrase ἐν τῷ ὄρει en tōi orei “on the mountain” appears after 
the  participle, rather than between the auxiliary verb and the  participle, as in 
Mark.  This removes some of the material that Porter (1992: Chapter 1, section 
3.1) might argue reduced the potential for reading the phrase as  periphrastic. 
The two points together bring the  participle four words closer to the auxiliary 
verb, as well as reframing it. This makes it much easier to read the clause as a 
multi-word expression, as opposed to an existential use of the copula with an 
adjective. It is not a definitive point, but it potentially demonstrates ways in 
which Luke, in identical  circumstances, uses multi-word expressions differently.
This difference also applies to his tense usage within the constructions more 
generally; Luke uses a broader  range of tenses in his multi-word constructions 
than does Mark.  Levinsohn (2016b: 311) determines the tense of a  periphrastic 
construction from the tense of the participle, not the copula.30 In this chapter , I 
have taken the opposite approach. My focus is the imperfect in  general, but also the 
ways in which it can be targeted and nuanced through combination with different 
tenses of  participles. In the imperfect,  both Mark  and Luke predominantly  use the 
present  participle (Mark  74%, Luke 71%), with a  significant remaining number of 
aorist  participles (Mark  26%, Luke 25%), but in  addition, 4% of Luke’s uses (as in 
 Luke 5:17), are perfect participles.31 In the multi-word constructions using other 
tenses of εἰμί (eimi), all four examples in Mark  use present  participles, whereas 
six of the twelve in Luke use perfect  participles (Luke 12:2, 12:52, 14 :8, 20:6, 23:15, 
24:38). These constructions give Luke a way to place  things both temporally and 
aspectually with more care than we see in Mark,  and with a kind of perfectivity 
not seen elsewhere in the New  Testament.

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages206 
Mark’s  more stative use of the multi-word imperfect is  in keeping with his less 
literary style;  periphrastic constructions may move from stative to progressive, 
to habitual. 32 Bentein has argued for Luke’s progressive use. With this sense 
of an ongoing narrative into which phrases like ἦν διδάσκων ( ēn didsakōn ) 
enable us to dip, we see a move further along this spectrum to something that is 
potentially more habitual. This makes sense within the context of Luke’s general 
use  of both multi-word expressions, and the imperfect.  There are eighteen uses 
of the imperfect of  μέλλω (mellō) “to be about to” in the New  Testament, for 
example, seven of which are in Luke-Acts (and none  in Mark),  a disproportionate 
number .33 It shows us how carefully Luke uses imperfect verbs within multi-
word expressions to demarcate and locate his actions precisely.
What we see in Luke, therefore, is  a careful balance of καὶ ἐγένετο ( kai 
egeneto), particularly with the articular infinitive), a synthetic imperfect,  and 
a multi-word imperfect, to   demarcate different kinds of scene. Luke may not 
 necessarily use the imperfect  tense more often than Mark,  but he does use it in 
different ways, elements of which are seen in Mark,  but which Luke develops 
much  further . We find, in particular , a pattern of enquiry and discussion 
expressed using the imperfect,  and movements in narrative demarcated using 
the imperfect,  often as a way to reorient us within this ongoing discussion with 
the Pharisees. With Luke’s use of the  multi-word imperfect, I  suggest we see a 
further development of this, offering three different ways to orient a reader in 
action: aorist, synthetic imperfect,  multi-word imperfect.
6.  Conclusion
In this chapter , I aimed to blend an understanding of how the imperfect  functions 
for scene-setting purposes in the Greek New  Testament, with an understanding of 
how a multi-word expression of the imperfect  differs from a synthetic one. In so 
doing, across the gospels of Luke and Mark,  I  have demonstrated a  narratological 
and exegetical difference between the formulations, and indeed, between the 
gospels. While Mark  and Luke use the  imperfect  tense a broadly similar amount 
of the time, they do different things with it; in some places, Luke develops an 
 idea already seen in Mark,  while in others, his use is more contrasting. Mark’s   
use of ἔλεγεν (elegen) is distinctive, and has long been recognised as such. What 
has been less appreciated, however , is the extent to which Luke specifically 
 uses the imperfect to  set scenes within a framework involving discussion. Luke,

directly relevant to Greek, and not directly cited in this chapter . See also Nardi and Romagno 
(2025: 51) for data and discussion about the stative use of these phrases.
33 Ten are John/Revelation. Revelation is highly eschatological, and often uses periphrastic ways 
of expressing the future in place of a synthetic future tense.

8. Roundabout ways of setting up scenes in the Greek New Testament 207
moreover , uses  the multi-word expression of the imperfect to  set up a scene 
where action matters, or describe a state of being, whereas Mark  uses it more 
for describing specific conditions rather than background action. 
In addition, Luke makes greater  use of the tenses of  participles available, 
particularly pairing an imperfect  auxiliary verb with a perfect  participle, to 
describe the results of past actions that continue to be relevant. With this further 
observation regarding Luke’s unusual use  of the perfect  participle in multi-word 
clauses, we return to Herodotus, and Luke the  historiographer . Gonda (1959: 
112) suggests that part of the reason the  periphrastic construction developed in 
Greek was the increased downplaying of the pluperfect. She argues that in order 
to maintain a vivid narrative,  periphrasis began to be needed. Additionally, 
the  periphrastic construction allows an author to modify any idea expressed 
by the copula more clearly. Nardi (2025) extends this  diachronic assessment 
by considering the relative frequencies of  participle tenses through time, and 
the impact of the  Old Testament on that distribution. Luke’s use of the  perfect 
 participle reflects an older style, further underpinning our understanding of 
his language as more Hellenic, and indeed Atticising or archaising than other 
gospel writers.
Given what I have demonstrated about both the imperfect and   the multi-
word construction in Luke, what we may be  seeing, therefore, is an author who 
archaises (Atticising, particularly with a view to historiography), integrates and 
synthesises (absorbing Latin and Semitic strategies into Greek), and innovates. 
This innovation takes several forms. Luke’s use of the  multi-word imperfect 
 moves us into an ongoing dialogue with the didache, curating our journey 
through the lessons of the New  Testament. In using multiple  participle tenses, 
he situates the actions more carefully, and balances both stative and progressive 
concepts with more precision. Like a good cinematographer , Luke draws our 
 attention to different elements of the story, through different people’s eyes and 
perspectives.  By framing Jesus’s teaching through the multi-word imperfect, 
 Luke suggests that  the didache is not merely a series of historical incidents, but 
a continuous, backgrounded reality. Through this aspectual foregrounding, the 
multi-word construction functions as a tool of extradiegetic framing, stretching 
the narrative duration to encompass the reader in the ongoing dialogue. The 
specific events—the healings and the parables—are thus presented not as 
isolated snapshots but as “breakthroughs” into a persistent divine discourse.

1. Introduction
Support-verb constructions consist of a fixed combination of a semantically 
faded verb, like dare (“to give”) and facere (“to make”) or venire (“to come”) 
in Latin, which can be called a support verb and an  abstract noun that refers 
to an entire state of affairs, such as spes (“hope”) to sperare (“to hope”) and 
cogitatio (“thought”) to cogitare (“to think”) in (1) and (2). In Latin linguistics 
the term “Support-verb constructions” (cf. Pinkster 2015: 74, n.4) is normally 
used, whereas in German linguistics the term “Funktionsverbgefüge” has been 
coined and the typological term is “  light-verb constructions” (cf. Hoffmann 
2023). In the following, the first term, namely “  support-verb constructions” 
( SVCs henceforth), will be used.  SVCs consist of a verbal component, the support 
verb (SV henceforth), and a nominal component derived from a noun referring 
to a state of affairs, the  abstract noun ( AN henceforth). The underlying verbs 
as sperare (“to hope”) in (1) and cogitare (“to think”) in (2) are called the  base 
verbs. Such  SVCs occur in many languages, including Latin and Ancient Greek 
in all their phases, as well as in German, English, and French. They can mark

9. Support-verb constructions with causative force  213
2. Defining the  causative
 A  causative is the formulation of a state of affairs with an agent as a subject, 
which does not itself determine the state of affairs, but functions as a caused 
constituent, a  causee. This function which is syntactically and semantically 
defined is brought to carry out the action of the situation by an added  causer 
(Comrie 1989; Dixon 2000). Often, the  causer takes the nominative case, while 
the  causee takes an oblique case, for instance a dative case. 
This syntagm is therefore a grammaticalised phenomenon, and not only, as 
van Pottelberge (2007: 436) assumes, one of the stylistic forms that are located 
“(i)n einem umstrittenen Grenzbereich zwischen Syntax und Phraseologie 
[in a controversial border area between syntax and phraseology] […] Verb-
Substantiv-Verbindungen [verb-noun combinations] […]”. Nevertheless, this 
author names as the four main characteristics (van Pottelberge 2007: 437):
1. A “meaningless” or a “stereotypical everyday verb”;
2. a noun that is a  verbal abstract and describes a fact;
3. noun and verb form a close and semantic unity, whereby the noun can 
almost never be omitted;
4. this verb-noun connection can be paraphrased using a synonymous verb.
There are other criteria that vary from author to author (Helbig 1984; Hoffmann 
2018). An  SVC is the result of a grammaticalisation process. Regardless of van 
Pottelberge’s scepticism, in this chapter such verb-noun syntagms are viewed as 
grammatical phenomena.
A test for defining a  causative is that of machen “to make” in languages like 
German, which form an analytic  causative with the meaningless verb machen “to 
make”. The German example cited in (4) in Section 1 would allow the following 
two synonymous clauses according to this machen “to make” test.
(5a) Ich bringe sie zum Lachen. (“I make her laugh”) [repeated from above, (4)]
(5b) Ich mache, dass sie lacht. (literally “I make that she laughs.”)

As is well known, the Bible was written partly in  Hebrew (in the  Old Testament 
( OT) with the exception of the Apocrypha written in Greek and a few passages 
written in Aramaic), 3 partly in Greek (in the New Testament (  NT) together 
with the Apocrypha of the  Old Testament). Both parts were translated early. 
3 The following passages in the Old Testament are written in Aramaic. Daniel 2:4b-7:28; Esra

4.2 Two other tests: Verba timendi and the two most frequent 
support verbs 
The lassen “to let” method has yielded few instances, which is more a limitation 
of the test than an indication of the robustness of the  causative  SVC category. 
It had the only function to show  causative constructions in the (Pentateuch 
of the)  Old Testament. Thus, another method must be found. Since  SVCs are 
a grammatical means, they are everywhere possible and never translation-
induced. We take two methods and combine them. On the one hand, we

4.2.1 Abstract nouns with the meaning of FEAR and TERROR
A brief explanation of this specific semantic verb group is required, as they are 
used here as  causative verbs. A look at German grammar is helpful here. The 
verb (er)schrecken “to frighten”, which belongs to the  AN Schrecken “horror”, 
has two meanings. According to Grimmʼs Dictionary (2004: 970), it is, on the 
one hand, an intransitive erschrecken “to frighten”, meaning “to get a fright, to 
scare”; on the other hand, this verb has the meaning “to put someone in fear and 
terror .” Thus, in the second variant, it is undoubtedly a  causative verb with the 
meaning “to cause someone else to get a fright.” 17 Both meanings are reflected 
in German with different tense formation. While the intransitive verb forms 
a strong preterite, for example, when the cat suddenly entered the room, I was 
frightened translates as “ich war erschrocken“, the causative   verb has a weak 
preterite, for example, the cat frightened me  ( when it suddenly stood in front 
of me) translates as “sie erschreckte mich“ or “ich war erschreckt”. In Latin, a 
noun like terror “panic”, formido “fearfulness”, or metus “dread” derives from 
a causative  verb.18 A first striking aspect is that the same verb dare “to give” is 
used as the SV in all eight Latin examples. It will be further investigated whether 
this is a typical feature of the  SVC in the  Vulgate, and at the same time, this 
verb will need to be examined more closely in terms of semantics and valency 
grammar .

9. Support-verb constructions with causative force  235
In instances (44) to (46), the question of why the example in (44) is not causative,  
whereas examples (45) and (46) are causative,   is raised. While the SVC in (44) 
fecistis  [...] misericordiam “you have shown kindness” has a normal  transitive 
function and does not have a  causee in the form of a dative complement, the 
example admirationem faciam “I will cause … to marvel” in Isaiah 29:14 (45) has 
a dative that functions as a  causee, populo “people”. Furthermore, the subject 
in the nominative case, namely malitia horae “misfortune of an hour” in (46), 
functions as a  causer . A similar example of a causative  SVC with adferre “to   
bring” as an SV is, for example, spem adferre “to make hope” (39), which occurs 
20 times in Cicero’s philosophical writings.23 It usually has an accusative plus 
infinitive construction as a second complement and a dative as the  causee. So, 
the answer is that  transitive verbs that do not have constituents acting as  causee 
or  causer cannot, however , function causatively, but remain  transitive even as 
an SVC (Hoffmann 2005:  555). 
Here, the difference between  transitive and causative  must be discussed. 
The first term,  transitivity, is also used as a generic term, of which the term 
 causativity forms a subclass. However , the term  transitive is also used in a 
narrower sense when it means non-causative.   Morphologically, a causative 
 can be marked in various ways, including the form of an SVC. Overlaps 
 between the two phenomena only occur in the case of verbs with an accusative 
object. Here, the subject of a  transitive verb differs in role from the subject of 
a causative  verb form. In the  transitive case, the subject is directly involved 
in the execution of the action, i.e., it is the constituent that acts as the agent 
and triggers or initiates the action and also executes it. In the causative  case, 
on the other hand, the subject is the  causer , i.e., it merely initiates the action, 
while another constituent executes it. The forms are the same in both cases, 
except that in the causative  form, a  causee usually appears in a different case. 
However , similar to the agent in the passive voice, a  causee may also be missing. 
In this case, it can be recognised pragmatically whether the action is initiated 
by the subject or also performed at the same time. In the first case, the subject 
is often also an  AN (emissio “release” in (47) and exspectatio “expectation” in 
(48)) (cf. Hoffmann 1996: 209f.), because  causativity is strictly speaking the

5. Morphological Analysis
The first question that arises here is whether and to what extent Biblical 
 Hebrew already possessed  SVCs, apart from the verse about Sarahʼs laughter 
in (6a). Secondly, it has to be asked whether Latin simply adopts the SVC of the 
 Septuagint or even forms some of its own.
The first question can be answered in the affirmative in view of the evidence 
found so far in both groups, and especially in view of the evidence in Genesis 
21:6. Both translations also retain this SVC, which consists  of ‘ ɔsɔh “to do, to 
make” and the accusative of a  verbal  AN. If we take the Latin  SVCs from the 
 Vulgate text as our starting point, there is a total of 106 unambiguous  SVCs for 
facere “to do” and dare “to give” in the  Old Testament where an SVC is used in 
 Hebrew.25 Conversely, there are 22 instances where  Hebrew uses an SVC.26
The difference   between the  Vulgate and the  Septuagint is evident in the 
different rendering of two frequently used verb forms: while  Hebrew uses the 
Hifil  verbs in most cases, namely šɔqɔh “to let (someone) drink” and nuaḥ “to let 
(someone) rest,” Greek has two synthetic verbs, namely ποτίζω ( potízō) “to let 
drink”, see (49), for the first verb and παύω ( pauō) “to finish” and compounds 
(καταπαύω (katapaúō), see (50), and ἀναπαύω (anapaúō)) for the second.

7. Semantic Analysis
In this step of the analysis, it is first important to identify the nature of the causal 
relationship. It is also important to see whether there are certain semantic 
verb classes that are particularly prone to forming  SVCs. We have already seen 
that verba sentiendi, and especially verba timendi, are particularly suitable for 
forming  SVCs. 
With regard to the first question, it must be clarified what kind of semantic 
relationship exists between the causative  and the  base verb. According to 
Haspelmath and Müller-Bardey (2004), a rough distinction must first be made 
between direct and indirect causatives. Within the direct type, one must 
determine whether it is an immediate causative;  within the indirect type, 
whether it may be assistive or permissive—or whether these distinctions are 
irrelevant, as assumed by Kedar-Kopfstein (1973) in the case of the  Vulgate. To 
this end, we start from the five most common ANs listed in Table 9.6. Requiem 
dare “to give rest”, in the literal sense of falling asleep, is a process that becomes 
a state in which the  causer is mainly involved, but the  causee less so. The same 
applies to hereditatem dare “to bequeath to”. Thus, bibere “to drink” and frui “to

rejoice” belong to the semantic class of TAKING FOOD, requiescere “to rest” is a 
verb of RESTING, timere “to be afraid” is a verbum sentiendi, while heredem esse 
“to be an heir” denotes TAKING POSSESSION. Nor are all cases controllable. This 
does not seem to be the case with requiescere “to rest” and timere “to be afraid”. In 
the case of fructum dare “to bear fruit” and potum dare “to let drink”, the  causer 
is only the trigger of an action that the  causee performs themselves. Timorem 
dare “to scare” is a subjective feeling that is triggered solely by the  causer . In 
contrast, potestatem dare “to empower” is a process that is only initiated by the 
 causer but continued solely by the  causee. These six  causative  SVCs clearly show 
that the causative  relationship can vary considerably.
As for the second question, here too we can assume the most common SVC 
from Table 9.6,  namely hereditas “inheritance”, potestas “power , permission”, 
fructus “fruit”, potus “drink”, timor “fear”, requies “rest”, to which the following 
verbs belong: heredem esse “to be an heir”, posse/potentem esse “to be able to”, 
frui “to rejoice”, bibere “to drink”, timere “to fear”, and requiescere “to rest”. They 
seem to have little or nothing to do with each other . 
8. Conclusions and outlook
A summary of the causatively used  SVCs attested in the Bible, especially the 
 Old Testament, shows that, even though this chapter could only examine them 
selectively, there are quite a few  SVCs already in the  Hebrew original. A prime 
example of this is Genesis 21:6, (28c). Compared to the 239 occurrences of 
facere “to make” with infinitive (see n. 10 above), this linguistic device is even 
more predominant, with about 400 occurrences in the Latin Bible. 29 Hebrew 
SVs are usually formed with ‘ɔsɔh (“to do”) or nɔtan (“to give”) and the  abstract 
noun appearing in the accusative. In Greek, the two SVs of active ποιῶ ( poiô) 
“to make” and medial ποιοῦμαι ( poioûmai) “to do” and more often δίδωμι 
didōmi (“to give”) are used. In Latin, dare “to give” and facere “to make” are 
the preferred SVs; in the upmost cases the AN  appears in the accusative, but 
only seldom with a preposition (in our corpus only (24), Numbers 34:5, and (36), 
Jeremiah 20:4).30 Since in Hebrew there are two verb stems—mainly the Hifil 
 verb  stem (for example, ya’akilenuw “he will let us eat”) and also, in the factitive 
subtype, the  Piel  verb stem—and Greek likewise has morphological means for 
forming special synthetic causative  verbs, especially those ending in -ίζω (- ízō) 
as for instance ποτίζω ( potízō “I let drink”), the largest number of  causative

 SVCs appears in the Latin of the  Vulgate. In this language the two most frequent 
SVs are dare “to give” and facere “to make”. The number of  SVCs formed with 
dare “to give” is disproportionately larger (about 400 : 250), although it must 
be taken into account that facere “to make” often can express  causativity with 
the infinitive (cf. n. 10). Compared to the  Hebrew original, already the Greek 
language shows a significant increase. Because of the morphological resources 
that Latin does not have—apart from the words combined with -efacere as for 
example mansuefacere (“to tame”)—the  Vulgate as a whole has the greatest 
amount of  causative  SVCs among the three languages. So  late Latin reflects more 
grammaticalisation than the other two languages. In using these syntagms, the 
language of the  Vulgate did not create any new linguistic possibilities, but used 
a linguistic tool to express  causativity, which already the Early Latin of Plautus 
(Rosén 1981) and the  classical Latin of Cicero, Livy, and other authors (Hoffmann 
1996; Pinkster 2015: 74–77) possessed to a sufficient degree. 
It would be interesting to investigate the total extent of  SVCs in the  Vulgate 
in order to determine the quantitative extent of  SVCs in the  Vulgate compared 
to the number in, for example, Cicero’s  philosophical writings. On the one hand, 
one would expect a greater quantity in a translation text from a language with 
a morphological causative,  but on the other , there is the other candidate of 
facere “to make” and infinitive, which was in  classical Latin only rarely used, 
but arose in Late antiquity (Chamberlain 1986). As for this construction, it 
would be interesting to see whether there is a clear distinction between both 
Latin causative  constructions. A parameter could be the obligatory degree of 
the expression of a  causee which in a three-place verb like dare “to give” can

also be interesting to examine the extent to which  SVCs form a system in the

durative) and the question, how far the  Vulgate uses such distinctions which

10. Understanding the expression 
of  pain across time: Metaphor and 
 intensity in Latin (and Spanish) 
 support-verb constructions with 
 dolor (2nd c. BCE to 15th c. CE)
 María Isabel Jiménez Martínez
1. Introduction
In this study, we analyse  support-verb constructions (SVCs   henceforth) with 
the noun  dolor from a  diachronic perspective, using a corpus that spans from 
 archaic and  classical Latin (second century BCE to the second century CE), 
through  late Latin in southern Europe (seventh to the ninth century CE)—to 
 medieval Spanish (thirteenth to the fifteenth century CE).1 Our aim is to identify 
the constructions and  metaphorical patterns that encode the experience of  pain, 
particularly its  intensity, and to examine how these patterns are preserved, 
reshaped, or innovated over time. To this end, the research addresses the 
following questions: 
1. How is the experience of  pain linguistically structured in  classical 
Latin, and how do these patterns evolve into  late Latin and  medieval 
Spanish? 
2. How is  pain conceptualised at the semantic and syntactic levels through 
SVCs ? 
3. Which  metaphorical networks are activated in these constructions, 
and how do they contribute to the encoding of  intensity?

The chapter is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the state of the art, 
discussing the concept of SVCs  , particularly their intensive extensions, and 
their relationship to  metaphor theory. Section 3 presents the methodology and 
describes the corpora, including how examples were selected and coded. In 
Section 4, we examine the SVCs  identified in the  classical Latin corpus, analysing 
their semantic types and underlying  metaphors. Section 5 provides a parallel 
analysis of SVCs   in  late Latin and  medieval Spanish, comparing them with 
those in Latin in terms of diversity, complexity, and  metaphorical strategies. 
Finally, we summarise the main findings, highlighting the cognitive and cultural 
implications of how  pain is conceptualised in these languages over time in 
Section 6. 
2. State of the art
2.1 Support-verb constructions: A definition
In this study, we understand SVCs  as multi-word expressions formed by a noun 
and a verb that jointly occupy the predicate slot of a sentence; accordingly, 
they are understood at the lexicon-syntax interface. In SVCs  , the noun—always 
predicative—serves as the semantic and syntactic nucleus of the construction, 
providing its argument structure, 2 while the support verb acts as a structural 
frame, supplying person, tense, number , voice, and mood (Baños and Jiménez 
López 2024: 94ff.). Given the semantic primacy of the noun, it also constrains the 
range of verbs with which it may combine.
Under this definition, the most prototypical SVCs  are multi-word combinations 
in which the verb has a general or weak lexical meaning, as have, make, or give, 
and a subject that is coreferential with the first argument of the predicative 
noun, for example, she made a decision, where she is both the syntactic subject 
of made and the semantic agent of decision. However , in these combinations 
we also include constructions in which the verb carries fuller lexical content 
(Baños and Jiménez López 2024: 94ff.). In these cases, the verb is metaphoric 
(and constitutes a lexical alternative to a general support verb, as illustrated 
by English shoot an answer  which functions as a lexical substitute for give 
an answer ) or/and contribute aspectual (inchoative or terminative), diathetic 
(causative or  passive), or intensive nuances. The syntactic configuration inside 
SVCs  may vary: the noun may appear as the object, as in English make a decision, 
as the subject, as in Latin, cupiditas nascitur “desire arises”, or even as a locative 
complement, as in Spanish entrar en razón “to come to one’s senses”.3
2 Here we adopt the terminology of Functional Grammar adapted to Latin (Baños 2023).
3 The definition of SVC adopted here is broader than that commonly found in the literature

10. Understanding the expression of pain across time  251
Among SVCs , aspectual and diathetic extensions have been widely studied 
in Latin and the Romance languages (Gross 2022; Vivès 1983; Cicalese 1999; 
Mendózar Cruz 2020; Salas 2024). By contrast, intensive SVCs , those that highlight 
the degree or force with which an event unfolds, have received far less attention 
(Gavriilidou 2004), and these are of particular interest here.
As Gavriilidou (2004: 298) notes, languages have multiple strategies to 
encode  intensity: morphological, for example, intensive prefixation, suffixation, 
or compounding, prosodic, for example, stress, emphasis, and intonation, and 
syntactic, including intensive adjectives, such as Latin magnum, intensive 
adverbs, such as Latin ualde, and intensive SVCs . 
In this study, we distinguish two mechanisms through which SVCs   code 
 intensity: (i) degree constructions, which encode an increase or decrease in the 
 intensity of the event, (1a), and (ii) intensive extensions, which occur in SVCs  of 
any semantic type (general, aspectual, or diathetic) and add an explicit nuance 
of  intensity, as illustrated in (1b).
(1a) Cicero, Ad familiares, 4.5.6
nullus  dolor est quem non longinquitas temporis minuat ac molliat.
“There is no grief that is not diminished and mitigated by the lapse of years.”
(1b) J. Fernández de Heredia, Historia Troyana (1376–1396 CE)
fue turbado grandemente et atormentado de grant  dolor .
“He was greatly disturbed and tormented by intense  pain.”
In sum, the concept of SVC used in this  study includes not only support verbs 
in the strict sense but also their extensions. This broader approach is necessary 
because it captures the full combinational behaviour of the predicative noun 
 dolor and helps explain why they combine with particular verbs.
2.2 Support-verb constructions and  metaphor
The almost automatic association we establish between concrete and abstract 
realities through  metaphor constitutes one of the  cognitive foundations of 
(see, e.g., Bodelot and Spevak 2018), where such constructions are restricted to combinations 
involving prototypical support verbs, i.e. verbs that do not contribute independent semantic 
content but merely function as a syntactic support for the predicative noun. From our 
perspective—also adopted in Baños et al. (2022)—these constructions include not only proper 
support verbs but also other verbs, typically of a  metaphorical nature, which can be analysed 
as extensions of support verbs. In such cases, the verb may serve as a lexical alternative to 
the canonical support verb, e.g. Spanish dar una bofetada “give a slap” vs. soltar una bofetada 
“let loose a slap”, or it may contribute aspectual or diathetic information to a more generic 
 support-verb construction.

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages252 
human thought, enabling us to organise, interpret, and communicate our 
experiences. This perspective, developed in the 1980s by scholars such as Lakoff, 
Johnson, and Langacker (Lakoff and Johnson 1980; Lakoff 1987, 1993; Langacker 
1987, 1991; Kövecses 2000, 2002) understands  metaphor as a mechanism that 
systematically maps a concrete, literal source domain onto a more abstract 
target domain (as in time is money). 
SVCs  provide a particularly insightful site for exploring the interaction 
between grammar and  metaphor . As noted, an SVC combines an  abstract noun 
with a verb to form a single predicate, in which the noun carries the core 
meaning and the verb adapts its sense accordingly, often in a  metaphorical way. 
For instance, in Livy (first century BCE/first century CE), the SVC concoquere 
 consilia does not refer to literal cooking but to careful deliberation, because 
in Latin—as in many other languages—the domains of cooking and digestion 
function as  metaphorical frameworks for thinking, conceptualised as a slow, 
elaborate, and transformative process. Crucially, this noun-verb combination 
reflects a conventionalised  metaphorical pattern, systematically realised within 
the SVC.
Metaphorical SVCs4 are, therefore, multi-word combinations in which the 
meaning arises from the interaction of a  metaphorical verb with the noun. This 
noun-verb pairing, which exhibits semantic interdependence and motivation, 
evokes a well-established  metaphorical pattern within a given linguistic 
community, often recognised across languages. In other words, these are concrete 
lexical combinations that activate and reinforce familiar  metaphorical patterns, 
allowing speakers to convey and understand complex concepts through more 
concrete experiences, as in thinking is cooking. 
Metaphorical SVCs  vary in their degree of conventionalisation and frequency. 
Some, like English keep a secret, are highly  lexicalised and frequent, while others 
appear rarely in speech and corpora, like Latin  dolor tenebrat “ pain darkens”. 
Yet both qualify as SVCs  , as they meet the definitional criteria and function 
as potentially  metaphorical expressions within the same underlying pattern, 
reflecting the broader system of  metaphorical cognition they encode. 
3. Methodology and corpus
The analysis in this study is based on the target-oriented methodology 
(Stefanowitsch 2006; Deignan 2005; Buccheri et al. 2021), which examines 
linguistic  metaphors by starting from the abstract nouns most closely associated 
4 The convergence of these two linguistic phenomena gives rise to the notion of metaphorical 
collocation, that is, the conventional association of  metaphorical meanings with specific 
lexical combinations. Although frequently invoked, the concept has rarely been defined with 
precision in the literature. Patekar (2022) and Malik et al. (2025) represent recent efforts to fill 
this theoretical gap.

10. Understanding the expression of pain across time  253
with a target domain. In our case, the domain is “ pain”, in  archaic and  classical 
Latin (second century BCE to the second century CE),  late Latin (seventh to ninth 
centuries CE) and  medieval Spanish (thirteenth to fifteenth centuries CE), using 
 dolor as the keyword.
This approach has clear advantages. As Fedriani (2025: 219 ff.) notes, it allows 
for the systematic identification and classification of  metaphors in large corpora, 
enabling both quantitative and qualitative comparisons while avoiding reliance 
on researcher intuition. Its main limitation is that it only captures  metaphors 
triggered by the chosen term, excluding other expressions of the concept that use 
different words, alternative  metaphorical patterns, or discursive contexts without 
the lexeme (Fedriani 2025: 219). These forms, though outside the scope of this 
study, remain relevant for a full understanding of how pain is conceptualised.5
With this limitation in mind, we created three separate corpora: 
1. The  archaic and  classical Latin corpus: we analysed all the contexts 
in which the noun  dolor appears in its various forms in seven authors 
representing different periods, selected from the Latin corpus of 
the Packard Humanities Institute .6 This process yielded a total of 640 
attestations.
2. The  late Latin corpus: we studied all occurrences of the term  dolor 
between 650 and 850 CE across authors from the Iberian Peninsula, the 
Italian Peninsula, and the territory of present-day France, as provided 
by the Corpus Corporum. In total, we collected 542 examples.
3. The  medieval Spanish corpus: we extracted the data from the Corpus 
Diacrónico del Español (RAE), compiling a body of 600 examples in which 
the term  dolor appears, evenly distributed across the 13th, 14th, and 15th 
centuries, with 200 randomly selected examples from each century.
This selection provides a representative sample of the various historical and 
linguistic contexts in which the concept of “pain”  emerges, allowing us to analyse 
both the  metaphors and the figurative patterns associated with this emotion in 
both languages.7 
5 Therefore, due to methodological limitations, this study does not aim to capture the general

approach captures only part of the picture, it provides meaningful insight into how  pain was 
historically conceptualised, revealing patterns in Latin and  medieval Spanish and offering a

10. Understanding the expression of pain across time  255
It is important to consider the argument structure of the noun under study. Like 
all psychological predicates,  dolor involves two semantic actants: an entity that 
undergoes the feeling (the experiencer) and a stimulus or source of that feeling 
(the cause). As we will see, in the various SVCs  these actants take on different 
syntactic realisations.
4. Pain in  archaic and  classical Latin
Based on the analysis of the data for the  archaic and  classical Latin noun  dolor, 
we have been able to outline the network of SVCs in  which it appears, most of 
them  metaphorical in nature and many carrying an intensifying function, as 
illustrated in the following examples (3):
(3a) Celsus, De Medicina, 1.3.20
isque, quibus, si per plures dies non uomerunt,  dolor praecordia infestat.
“as well as in the case of those who become troubled by pain  over the heart when 
they have not vomited for several days.”
(3b) Cicero, Ad familiares, 5.17.4
…sin autem omnia quae sentio perscripserim, ne refricem meis litteris desiderium 
ac dolorem tuum.
“…whereas if I write down all I feel, my letter may exacerbate the pain of  your 
separation.”
The SVC  dolor infestat  “  pain  infests (sb.)” in example (3a) is inchoative, as it 
focusses on the initial moment in which the sensation begins to be felt. To 
convey this aspectual meaning, Celsus draws on the  metaphor pain is  an 
opponent. Here, pain is  conceptualised as an adversary launching an attack 
on the body ( praecordia “diaphragm”). The  intensity of the sensation is, thus, 
expressed through a familiar and sensorially recognizable schema—war—
which highlights both its force and its aggressiveness.
Since pain is  a gradable psychological state, its collocational range includes 
verbs that express both increases and decreases in  intensity. This is precisely 
the case of the SVC dolorem refricere  “to re-rub pain” in   example (3b), which 
instantiates the  metaphor pain is  an object. In this construction, the intensification 
of pain is  represented through the manipulation of the  metaphorical object: 
to “re-rub” the pain  implies heightening it, so the idea of “rubbing it strongly” 
becomes a linguistic image that conveys an especially forceful and intense 
experience of the emotion.
As we can see, these constructions are inherently intensifying, which is

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages256 
why we regard them as extensions of SVC. A construction  can be considered 
an intensifying extension of an SVC when, in addition  to a neutral form, there 
exists an alternative that expresses the same basic meaning but does so with a 
stronger or more forceful degree of  intensity (Tur 2019: 178 ff.).
In what follows, we analyse the interconnections among the SVCs in  which 
the noun  dolor appears, the  metaphors that operate within them, and the 
different degrees of  intensity with which this sensation is expressed.
4.1 Support-verb constructions with  dolor “pain”
 Table 10.2 presents the set of SVC in which the noun  dolor appears in our corpus,

From the information presented in Table 10.2, several conclusions can be 
drawn that offer an overall view of the collocational behaviour of this noun. 
From a quantitative perspective, dolor proves  to be a quite collocational noun: 
one quarter of all its occurrences in the authors examined (166 out of the 640 
contexts analysed) appear in SVCs.  These 166 examples are distributed across 
104 SVCs,  which highlights the remarkable versatility and creativity surrounding 
this concept.
The highest productivity, in both diversity and frequency, is found in the 
inchoative aspectual constructions, which account for 55 examples across 38 
SVCs.  These are followed by the general constructions expressing the basic idea 
of “experiencing/suffering pain” (36 examples in 23 SVCs ),  and by the inchoative 
causatives (28 examples in 14 SVCs).  This distribution shows that the culturally 
and cognitively most salient elements in the conceptualisation of pain are its

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages258 
onset—attested in  83 examples—and, secondly, the experience of suffering itself. 
Latin, therefore, structures the narrative of pain by emphasising its  emergence. 
By contrast, combinations referring to the end of pain are scarce: only 30 in  total 
(15 terminative aspectual constructions and 15 terminative causatives).
Five of these SVCs  appear more than five times in our corpus and belong to 
different semantic types: the general SVC dolorem ferre “to  suffer pain” (4a); the 
inchoative  construction dolor [ex-/ ob-/co-]oritur “pain arises” (4b); the  causative

[in] crescit “ pain grows” (4e).

4.1.1 General  support-verb constructions
Indeed, within the group of general constructions—or SVCs in  the strict sense—
characterised by the use of a verb with a broad meaning and by their semantic 
equivalence to the simple verb doleo “to feel pain, to suffer”, the  construction 
dolorem ferre “to suffer pain”, which conveys the idea  that the experiencer 
endures or bears the pain, is the option most  favoured by the authors in the 
corpus, (4a). Alongside this construction, the next most frequent general SVCs 
are  also formed with verbs of a broad and  polysemous meaning, such as habere 
“to have”, (5a), and esse “to be”, (5b):
(5a) Celsus, De medicina, 2.7.8.1
Si mulier a partu vehementes dolores habet.
“If after childbirth a woman has severe pains.”
(5b) Cicero, Ad familiares, 6.4.4
Quanto fuerim dolore meministi.
“You remember how sorely distressed I was.”
In addition to these, the analysed contexts contain other SVCs that  likewise 
predicate the experience of pain but introduce an element  of  intensity. For this 
reason, we classify them as intensifying extensions of the general SVCs.  Among 
the most notable are dolor  deuorat “pain consumes”, (6a), dolor  feruet  “pain 
blazes”, (6b), and dolor  incubat “pain reclines”, (6c):
(6a)  Ovid, Metamorphoses, 13.538–540
Troades exclamant, obmutuit illa dolore, / et pariter vocem lacrimasque introrsus 
obortas / deuorat ipse dolor.
“The  Trojan women shrieked at the sight; but she was dumb with grief; her very 
grief engulfed her powers of speech, her rising tears.”
(6b) Seneca, Phoenissae, 352
timet animus ira, feruet immensum dolor.
“My  spirit is swelling with anger , my pain is burning beyond measure .”
(6c) Seneca, Phaedra, 99
Sed maior alius incubat maestae dolor.
“But  another , greater pain weighs on my distress.”

 As can be observed, the syntactic expression of these constructions is also 
variable. The most common pattern is for the experiencer to appear as the 
grammatical subject, as in (4a) and (5); however , the way “pain” is encoded 
differs  across constructions. In dolorem ferre “to suffer pain”, (4a), and dolorem 
 habere “to have pain”, (5a), the noun  functions as the object of the verb, whereas 
in dolore esse “to be in pain”, (5b), it appears in the  ablative case as a complement 
of manner (Mendózar Cruz 2019: 190). In all the constructions in (6), finally, 
“pain” is expressed as the  subject of the construction in the nominative case.
4.1.2 Aspectual  support-verb constructions
Among the  aspectual SVCs  involving dolor, those  that focus on the onset of the 
sensation are the most frequent. In addition to dolor [ex-/ co-/ob-]oritur “pain 
arises”, (4b), highly  productive constructions are formed with haptic verbs, such 
as dolorem capere “to take pain”, (7a), or dolorem  accipere “to receive pain”, (7b) in 
which the  experiencer is conceptualised as the grammatical subject and “pain” as 
the object that is  taken. These combinations can be understood as the inchoative 
counterpart of the general SVCs  constructed with possession verbs: the relation 
dolorem capere—dolorem habere “to take pain—to have pain” reflects  the conceptual 
 transition from the acquisition of pain to its possession by the  experiencer .
(7a) Plautus, Truculentus, 455–456
quanta est cura in animo, quantum corde capio / dolorem.
“What anxiety of mind, what agony of heart I feel.”
(7b) Cicero, In Verrem, 2.4.135
verum illud est quam ob rem haec commemorem, quod existimare uos hoc uolo, 
mirum quondam dolorem accipere eos ex quorum urbibus haec auferantur .
“my purpose in mentioning these few is to convince you that an extraordinary 
degree of pain has been caused to those whose towns have been robbed of such 
treasures.”
Another group of verbs that frequently occurs in inchoative constructions is 
that of motion. On the one hand,  transitive verbs such as commouere “to move” 
participate, giving rise to constructions in which the subject is the noun dolor 
and  the displaced object is the person or being who experiences it, (8):
(8) Cicero, Ad familiares, 4.5.2
Quid est quod tanto opere te commoueat tuus dolor  intestinus? 
“What reason is there why your domestic sorrow should affect you so sorely?”

On the other hand, in these SVCs we  also find intransitive  telic motion verbs. 
In these cases, as we will discuss later (Section 4.2.2), the idea of reaching the 
endpoint of a movement is used to express the onset of a state. This occurs in 
dolor tendit  “pain extends”, (9a), and dolor   transit “pain passes” (9b). In these

( 9a) Celsus, De  medicina, 2.8.39

(9b) Celsus, De medicina, 2.7.22

although their frequency is very low: all of them are attested only once, except 
for dolorem finire “to finish pain”, (10a), which appears  twice. Within this group, 
some constructions—such as the one just mentioned—have the experiencer as the 
subject and “pain” as the object; in others , by contrast, dolor  occupies the position 
of the grammatical subject, as in dolor fugit  “pain flees”, (10b), referring  to an entity 
with its own agency, capable of deciding to withdraw from the pain sufferer:
(10a) Vergil,  Aeneid, 12.880-881

“Then I could end this anguish, and pass through the shadows at my poor brother’s 
side!”
(10b) Vergil, Aeneid, 12.422
subitoque omnis de corpore fugit quippe dolor.
“and  suddenly, in truth, all pain fled from the body.”
4.1. 3 Causative  support-verb constructions
The most productive SVC of our corpus is  dolore adficere “to affect sb. with pain” 
with a total of ten  examples. This is a  causative  construction with inchoative

value, as it can be paraphrased as “to make someone begin to feel pain.” In this, 
the cause of  the pain is expressed in the  nominative case, the experiencer in 
the accusative, and “pain” in the ablative, as it  is understood as the instrument 
that inflicts the pain. Example (4c) above and (  11) below clearly illustrate this 
syntactic configuration:
(11) Cicero, In Verrem, 2.5.123
an uos quoque hic acerbissimus innocentium cruciatus et maeror pari sensu 
doloris adficit? 
“Or are the agonies of pain and grief inflicted on  these innocent persons causing 
yourselves equal distress?”
Other  causative SVCs  with  this value among the authors studied are dolorem 
afferre “to bring pain” (12a) and dolorem mouere  “to stir up pain” (12b). In these 
constructions, the subject is an entity that causes the pain, the “pain” appears as 
 the object of  the verb, and the experiencer is expressed in the dative case:
(12a) Cicero, Ad familiares, 16.21.2
tantum enim mihi dolorem cruciatumque attulerunt errata aetatis meae.
“Young men make mistakes, and mine have brought me so much unhappiness and 
torment.”
(12b) Ovid, Metamorphoses, 5.401
haec quoque uirgineum mouit iactura dolorem.
“the loss of her flowers even at such a time aroused new grief.”
We have also identified  causative SVCs   with   terminative value, that is, 
constructions in which an entity acts as the cause and brings about the cessation 
of the pain experienced by the  experiencer . This group includes dolorem leuare 
“to alleviate pain”, (4d), as well as other  constructions that follow the same 
semantic-syntactic pattern, such as dolorem sanare  “to cure pain”, (4d), and 
dolorem  comprimere “to compress pain”.
4.1.4  Degree  support- verb constructions
Finally, the noun dolor  participates in SVCs that  predicate the increase or decrease 
of the sensation, which are organised into three distinct syntactic patterns. First, 
there are constructions in which dolor  functions as the grammatical subject and 
the verb expresses the intensification of the sensation, as in dolor [in] crescit “pain 
grows”, (4e); in these  cases, the emotion is identified with a living being, that is 
developing its body. Second, there are SVCs in  which the experiencer occupies

the subject position and “pain” is encoded as the object  ; this is the case with 
dolorem lenire “to soothe pain”, (14a), where the verb  describes the alleviation 
of suffering. Finally, constructions are attested in which a cause appears as the 
subject and “pain” as the object, a pattern  that allows the explicit representation 
of the agent responsible for increasing or reducing the sensation, as in dolorem 
augere “to increase pain” or dolorem minuere “to  decrease pain”, (14b):
(14a) Ovid,  Metamorphoses, 13.317
…temptaretque feros requie lenire dolores.
“and seek to soothe his terrible anguish by a time of rest.”
(14b) Cicero, Ad familiares, 6.1.1
…tamen oculi augent dolorem, qui ea quae ceteri audiunt intueri cogunt.
“But the eyes add to the pain, forcing us to look at  what others only hear .”
4.2 Metaphors of pain 
Many of the verbs in the  constructions analysed carry a figurative meaning. As 
noted, pain intertwines physical,  psychological, and cultural dimensions that 
are difficult to conceptualise and express. When describing this unpleasant 
experience, speakers often invoke causes of physical harm, even in cases of 
psychological pain (Semino 2010). Thus,  images such as fire, sharp objects, 
or wild animals are frequently used, as they threaten bodily integrity and 
effectively convey  intensity. These  metaphors also aim to elicit an embodied, 
empathetic response in the listener or reader , highlighting the deeply corporeal 
grounding of pain expressions.
The close  link between physical and mental pain (Fedriani 2025: 215)  further 
explains this preference: psychological pain often somatises, while  physical pain 
generates emotional  distress. Embodied  metaphors are therefore especially 
powerful, projecting familiar sensory experiences onto the mental domain and 
enabling us to understand and communicate suffering more effectively.
In this regard, one of the most salient features of  metaphorical descriptions 
of pain is their high level of  detail, creativity, and textual complexity (Semino 
2010), traits that reflect the inherent difficulty of verbally representing such 
an intense and complex experience. Table 10.3 presents the  metaphors in our 
corpus organised according to the type of SVC. 10

Another important figurative schema to talk about pain is pain is  fire . As 
 Kövecses ( 2000: 81–97) has amply demonstrated, the  metaphor emotion is heat 
or fire constitutes a fundamental conceptual resource for representing a wide 
range of human feelings whose most salient feature is  intensity: anger , passion, 
love, desire, ambition, lust, hatred, or pain, among others.
In the  case of pain, its association with  fire and extreme heat can be explained 
in two ways. First, it reflects intense, almost unbearable emotional experiences, 
often merging with anger or related emotions. As Fedriani (2025: 230) observes, 
these  metaphors commonly convey emotional suffering connected to anger , 
and the fire domain is central to Latin conceptualisations of anger , making this 
overlap significant. Second, the  metaphors involve a metonymic component

grounded in bodily experience: fire causes actual physical pain. This causal link 
allows  the fire domain to function both as a  metaphor for emotional  intensity 
and as a metonymic extension of physical sensation into the affective realm, 
integrating physical and emotional experience.
Our corpus records eleven SVCs based   on this fire  metaphor . To understand 
how Latin conceptualises pain through this  metaphor , we  will analyse 
the most productive constructions, distinguishing between: (a) those that 
express the internal experience of the emotion through intransitive verbs, 
formalising intensive extensions of general SVCs (six  examples), and (b) those 
that metaphorically evoke the act of igniting the sensation in the experiencer 
through  transitive verbs, that is, intensive variants of inchoative  aspectual SVCs 
( three examples) and inchoative  causative SVCs  (two  examples).

 and progressive reality that grows in size and  intensity (cf. Roesch 2016; 2017).

4.2.2 Inchoative  support-verb constructions: pain is an opponent, 
pain is a  living being and the  beginning of an event is the endpoint 
of  telic motion
As noted in Section 4.1.2, inchoative  aspectual SVCs are  the most frequent in 
the corpus. These constructions, referring to the spontaneous onset of pain, 
typically instantiate  the  metaphor pain is an opponent (17  examples). Pain is 
thus conceptualised as an enemy that attacks the experiencer with  intensity and 
violence: it can seize (dolor rapit  “pain seizes”), overcome (dolor  [e] vincit “pain 
overcomes”), suffocate (  dolor  angitur “pain is suffocated”), or  disturb ( dolor 
turbat  “pain disturbs”). Through such  verbs, the beginning of pain is framed as 
a forceful  and often overwhelming assault.
(22a) Vergil, Aeneid, 4.474–475
Ergo ubi concepit furias evicta dolore / decreuitque mori.
“So when, conquered by anguish, she caught the madness and resolved to die.”
(22b) Celsus, De Medicina, 2.7.25
Auris quoque dolor acutus  cum febre continua uehementique saepe mentem turbat.
“Acute pain in ear with continuous  severe fever also often disturbs the mind.”
The opponent  metaphor is typically associated with the beginning of negative 
emotions, such as anger , hatred, or rage, which involve experiences of violence, 
aggression, or helplessness. Indeed, this image is one of the most productive for 
describing emotional states that affect human beings (Jiménez Martínez 2025; 
Buccheri et al., 2021: 170). Closely related is the  metaphor pain is a wild animal, 
which  portrays pain as attacking with  uncontrolled strength, (6a). This vivid, 
concrete imagery renders an otherwise intangible sensation more expressible.
The second most productive  metaphorical domain among inchoative

pain is the birth of a living  being. In this framework, coming into the world 
becomes a figurative way of referring to the beginning of an abstract event. 
Within this pattern, we find constructions such as dolor oritur  “pain arises” and 
dolor  nascitur “pain is born”:
(23a) Plautus,  Stichus, 165
uteri dolores mihi oboriuntur cotidie.
“I get my pains there every day.”
(23b) Celsus, De Medicina, 1pr .23.1
Praeter haec, cum in interioribus partibus et dolores et morborum uaria genera 
nascantur… 
“Moreover , as pains, and also various kinds of diseases, arise in the more internal 
parts…”
This figurative domain extends beyond inchoative SVCs.  Particularly productive 
are degree constructions in which the increase in the  intensity of pain is 
expressed through the  image of a living organism that grows, as dolor [in] crescit 
“pain grows” in (4e). 
Another  highly productive  metaphorical schema for expressing the onset of 
pain is the one articulated  through verbs of movement and spatial orientation, 
such as dolor  peruenit “pain arrives” or dolor  transit “pain passes”, already 
examined  in (Section 4.1) and in example (9). In this group of constructions, 
known as orientational  metaphors (Fedriani 2025; Jiménez Martínez 2020), pain 
is conceptualised as an  entity that moves, advances, settles, or passes through 
the experiencer’s body.
Unlike the  metaphors discussed above, which render the internal experience 
of pain as objects, animals, fire  , or even persons, these  metaphors activate a 
spatial projection: pain behaves as a mobile  element within a territory, the 
body. In this way, the different stages of the painful episode are metaphorically 
expressed through patterns of movement and position in physical space, drawing 
on the very general and schematic macro-  metaphor events are movements 
(Lakoff and Johnson 1980: 25).

Ad ceteras meas miserias accessit dolor et de  Dollabellae ualetudine et de Tullia.
“To all my other woes must now be added the sorrow caused me by the ill-health 
of Dolabella and Tullia.”

(24b) Celsus, De medicina, 1pr .25.1
neque enim, cum dolor intus  incidit, scire quid doleat eum.
“For when pain occurs internally,  neither is it possible for one to learn what hurts 
the patient.”
In example (24a), pain is construed as a  material entity entering the speaker’s 
emotional sphere. The verb accedere “to approach” denotes  telic motion, 
oriented toward an endpoint that, when abstract, marks the beginning of the 
situation, process, or event represented by the noun, following the  metaphor 
the beginning of an event is the endpoint of a  telic motion. Similarly, incidit 
“to fall” in (24b) conveys the sudden onset of pain rather than physical  falling. 
As a  telic verb, it implies lack of control and agency, often associated with 
negative events (in vitium incidere “fault strikes”, in morbum incidere “to fall ill”), 
activating the  metaphor the beginning of a negative situation  is a fall. This 
reflects the general schema down is bad and introduces an  intensity nuance 
absent in dolor  accedit “pain approaches”.
4.2.3  Causative  support-verb constructions: pain is an object
We continue  our analysis of SVCs with  the noun dolor by  examining the 
inchoative causative  constructions. In these cases, one  metaphorical schema 
clearly predominates: pain is an object (15  instances). More specifically, the 
most frequent construction in our corpus— dolore adficere “to inflict pain” (10 
examples)— conceptualises this object as a tool or weapon capable of inflicting 
harm, that is, of producing the painful experience, (25).
(25) Cicero, In Verrem, 2.4.83

uideatur .
“Here, indeed, I am so overwhelmed by pain that nothing seems to me  more 
unworthy or less bearable.”
When this sensation is conceptualised as a thing, it is understood as an entity 
that can be produced, (26), possessed, (27a), taken up, or thrown, (27b):
(26) Celsus, De medicina, 2.3.6
Si inflatio in superioribus partibus dolorem tumoremque fecit, bonum signum est 
sonus uentris.
“When flatulence causes pain and swelling in the upper   part of the abdomen, it 
is a good sign when intestinal rumbling passes thence downwards towards the 
lower belly.”

(27a) Celsus, De medicina, 1.5.2

quoslibet alios oris adfectus.
“it is especially so to those who are disposed to pains in the head or windpipe, or 
to other forms of oral affections.”
 (27b) Cicero, Ad familiares, 5.13.3
…quamquam tuis monitis praeceptisque omnis est abiciendus dolor.
“and  yet, according to your admonitions and instructions, all sorrow must be 
thrown to the winds.”
In (26), dolorem facere  “to cause pain” conveys the idea of  generating pain 
in someone. 11 In this case , the inflammation of the upper part of the body 
produces pain in the patient. It is  therefore a causative  incoative SVC. 
However , this  metaphor appears across almost all semantic types of SVCs 
with  dolor, since  the idea that events are objects constitutes a widespread 
 metaphorical domain through which we communicate in everyday language 
across all languages. Thanks to this schema, we are able to speak about 
the beginning, duration, or end of any kind of abstract situation. Thus, for 
example, the construction dolorem abicere  “to cast away pain”, (27b), by 
incorporating  a verb that denotes an action in which the possessed object 
is forcefully released, can be interpreted as conveying a terminative and 
intensive meaning.
A particularly interesting specification of this  metaphor is pain is a chain, as 
shown in ( 28). Through this image, Cicero exploits the physical connotations of 
the object—its capacity to bind, restrain, and immobilise—in order to express 
how pain can hold us captive and  render us motionless:
