In  SVCs with  dolor, a state noun, dolorem habere “to have  pain” represents a prototypical 
construction in which the verb functions as a structural support expressing the experience 
of the sensation. Likewise, facere “to make” operates as a general  causative verb, encoding 
the broad notion of “causing”. Their inclusion in the  metaphorical analysis is justified by the 
figurative interpretation of constructions with  dolor: although both are prototypical support 
verbs, they convey abstract possession and causation, that is,  metaphorical meanings.

4.2.4 Terminative  support-verb constructions: pain is a fluid and 
pain is a  container
The final  group of  metaphors we will analyse is primarily associated with 
terminative SVCs, that  is, constructions that predicate the final moment of the 
pain suffered by the  experiencer . To convey this, the authors in our corpus, in 
addition to the analogy of a burden from which one must be freed, draw on 
two further  metaphorical strategies. On the one hand, they create an analogy 
between pain and a fluid ( pain is a  fluid), which can  dissipate just as a drink 
disappears when someone quenches their thirst, as illustrated in the following 
example from Cicero (first century BCE):
(29) Cicero, Ad familiares, 5.16.4
non facile exhauriri tibi istum dolorem posse uniuersum puto.
“I doubt if your mind can easily be purged of so personal a sorrow altogether .”
On the other hand, the authors link pain to a container that can be  filled or emptied 
(pain is a container). In  dolorem saturare “to satiate pain” (30), pain is understood 
 as a vessel  that is not yet full, which evokes a further image often associated with 
this verb: that of a wild animal whose hunger is not easily sated. The combination 
of these two schemas produces a particularly vivid image of the cessation of pain:
(30) Vergil, Aeneid, 5. 608
multa mouens necdum antiquum saturata dolorem.
“Moving many things, not yet satisfied with ancient pain.”
5. Intensity in the  expression of pain in Latin
As Pérez Rull ( 2002: 324) observes, emotional  intensity is an abstract notion that 
can only be grasped through more concrete concepts such as depth, quantity, 
force, or impact (also in Kövecses 1986: 82; 2000: 41). In our  archaic and 
 classical Latin corpus with dolor, this  intensity is expressed through two main 
mechanisms.

Verbal Multi-Word Expressions in Corpus Languages272 
First, degree-type SVCs depict  pain as increasing or  decreasing along a scale 
that quantifies its magnitude. When pain “grows” ( dolor crescit  “ pain grows”, 
dolorem augere “to  increase pain”), it is felt as more  intense; when it “lessens” 
(dolorem minuere “to reduce pain”), it is weaker . This  mechanism relies on 
 metaphors that conceptualise  intensity as size or extension ( emotional 
 intensity is size).
The second, and more relevant type for our purposes, involves intensive 
extensions of support verbs in SVCs. These  constructions conceptualise pain 
through  metaphors drawn  from domains of strength, impact, or violence, 
presenting it as forceful, sudden, or overwhelming. In this respect, the linguistic 
expression of pain is particularly revealing.  As a universally graded experience, 
both physical and emotional pain is frequently  conceptualised in terms of 
degree. Although some  metaphors with dolor function  as cognitive frameworks 
that help us navigate its concept, most of the  metaphorical SVCs  identified with 
this noun directly or indirectly encode the  intensity of the experience.
Overall, we can say that pain  intensity in  archaic and    classical Latin is 
expressed through the association of this sensation with violent everyday 
experiences ( pain is an opponent, pain is a  damaging object , pain  is a wild 
animal, pain is  fire, or pain is a  destructive natural  force) or with very heavy 
material entities that exhaust, suffocate, paralyze, or immobilise us, such as pain 
is a burden or pain is a  chain. 
6. Some  remarks on  diachrony: dolor in  late  Latin and 
 medieval Spanish
We now take a temporal leap to examine the evolution of SVCs with  the noun 
dolor in  late  Latin and  medieval Spanish. This shift allows us to address a key 
linguistic question: how did Latin function in the  Christian era with respect to 
expressing pain, and to what extent did  early Spanish, as Latin’s direct heir , 
inherit these figurative patterns? Specifically, we ask whether  late Latin and 
 medieval Spanish preserved the rich  metaphorical repertoire of  classical Latin 
or whether they developed new  metaphorical projections shaped by their own 
linguistic and cultural contexts.
It is important to note the limitations of the corpus, especially for the Romance 
language: surviving texts rarely reflect everyday speech, as they mostly belong 
to legal, administrative, or formulaic genres that often retain archaism or 
clerical conventions. Nonetheless, our aim is to outline the main features of 
pain expressions in this period  and provide a preliminary  diachronic reflection 
based on the available evidence. We begin by presenting our  late Latin and 
 medieval Spanish data in Table 10.4.

The most  immediate conclusion drawn from the table is that  expressions of pain 
in  late Latin and  medieval Spanish display considerably less diversity than in 
 archaic and  classical Latin. In the earlier period, 166 examples are distributed 
across 104 constructions; in  late Latin, 201 examples occur in 76 SVCs; and in   
 medieval Spanish, 293 examples are concentrated in only 60 constructions. This 
distribution suggests a gradual reduction in creative variation after the classical 
period.12
Beyond this quantitative trend, the overall picture reveals a clear  diachronic 
development. Late Latin occupies an intermediate position between  archaic and 
 classical Latin and  medieval Spanish. Like the earlier stage, seventh- to ninth-
century Latin still assigns an important role to inchoative SVCs—both  aspectual 
and causative—in  conceptualising pain, highlighting the cultural salience of its 
emergence. At the same time, however ,  late Latin grants  greater prominence to 
general constructions referring to the experience of pain itself (85 examples), 
a tendency that becomes dominant in  medieval Spanish. There, haver dolor  
“to  have pain” clearly predominates with 113 occurrences (39%  of the total), 
whereas in  late Latin no construction  exceeds 15 tokens, reflecting a more even 
distribution.
The remaining SVCs occur  with much lower frequencies in both periods: 
even relatively general constructions such as dolorem pati  “to suffer pain” 
and dolore ardere  “to burn with pain” in  late Latin, or tener dolor  “to have 
pain” and sentir dolor  “  to experience pain” in  medieval  Spanish, reach no 
more than  12 examples each.  This quantitative imbalance suggests not  only 
reduced lexical productivity but also a gradual narrowing of  metaphorical 
variation. While only moderately perceptible in  late Latin, this tendency 
becomes markedly pronounced in  medieval Spanish, where the dominance 
of a single construction points to an ongoing process of conventionalisation in 
the expression of pain.
Regarding the  metaphorical expression of pain,  late Latin displays a 
distribution largely comparable   to that observed in  archaic and  classical 
 Latin. Medieval Spanish, by contrast, exhibits a noticeably narrower range 
of figurative patterns than Latin in either period. The data thus suggest 
continuity between the two Latin stages, alongside a subsequent restriction 
in  metaphorical diversity in  medieval Spanish. Below, we present the 
 metaphorical schemas identified in the corpus, organised according to the 
semantic types of SVCs (see  Table 10.5).

A  review of Table 10.5 reveals several key  findings. Regarding  late Latin, its 
 metaphorical landscape resembles that of  archaic and  classical Latin, displaying 
comparable richness and diversity, but with some novel tendencies—such as 
the predominance of the  metaphor pain is an opponent (61 examples)—and a 
decline in the prominence of others, like pain is a burden. In  contrast,  medieval 
Spanish appears less creative than  archaic and  classical Latin in   expressing 
pain and tends to conceptualise it more generally, often through the image of an 
object, a pattern  consistent across all semantic types of SVC.
Concerning the situation of   medieval Spanish, it is striking that no examples of

SVC based on the  metaphor of  fire—so prominent in Latin—appear in our corpus, 
and that there are only six instances of the pain is a burden schema. Additionally, 
the  metaphors pain is a fluid and pain is a human being are  completely absent, 
suggesting a simplification or selective  adoption of  metaphorical projections.
As for the second observation, the systematic use of the  metaphorical pattern 
pain is an object, a simple and generalised projection, reinforces the impression 
that  medieval Spanish, at  least in the texts studied, lacks the  metaphorical richness 
found in Latin of both moments. Pain is thus conceptualised primarily in terms 
of the experience itself and through accessible  cognitive schemas, whereas Latin 
displays greater variety and creativity in representing its different dimensions, 
at least in the contexts we have examined. To illustrate this, we present Figure

Although the lower diversity of  metaphorical schemas in  medieval Spanish 
reflects accurately the corpus data, these findings must be interpreted 
cautiously, as emphasised throughout this study. The limited variety of Spanish 
textual genres likely prevents us from detecting many  metaphorical patterns 
that consistently appeared in Latin. It is therefore plausible that  metaphors 
present in  late Latin—a language spoken in the same regions only two centuries 
earlier—persisted into thirteenth-century Spanish. Deeply ingrained  cognitive 
schemas are unlikely to disappear within a few generations. The most plausible 
explanation is thus either (i) that surviving texts fail to capture these structures,

10. Understanding the expression of pain across time  279
perhaps preserved in oral genres or lost over time, or (ii) that these  metaphors 
lived on in constructions excluded from this study, such as SVCs without   the 
noun pain or in idiomatic expressions.
Finally, the expression of the  intensity inherent to this sensation—  although 
our data of  medieval Spanish relies less on SVCs than  Latin—is mainly conveyed 
through the same strategies as in  archaic and  classical Latin: degree constructions, 
such as dolor ingrauescit “pain grows burdensome” or amansar el dolor “to  ease 
the pain”, and intensified extensions of support  verbs . Two strategies stand out: 
the notion of violence,  reflected in the  metaphor pain is an  opponent, and the 
concept of a material force that immobilises, as in pain is a chain. In  late  Latin, the 
association of pain with fire (pain is fire) is also particularly  prominent.
7. Conclusions
Throughout this corpus-based  study, in which we   analysed the expression of 
pain through SVCs in  archaic and  classical Latin (second century BCE to the 
second century CE),  late  Latin (seventh to ninth centuries CE), and  medieval 
Spanish (thirteenth to fifteenth centuries CE), we observed that constructions 
expressing the experience of pain—characterised by an inherent  intensity—
span a wide range of  metaphorical patterns, covering all stages  and dimensions 
of this experience.13
In Latin, we identified an extensive collocational network rich in  metaphorical 
projections that describe, with considerable creativity and detail, an experience 
notoriously difficult to express in words. Two main strategies stand out for 
conveying the  intensity of pain: first, the notion of violence that assaults and 
terrifies the experiencer , expressed through  metaphors  such as pain is an 
opponent, a wild animal, a weapon , or fire; and second, the conception of pain 
as an extremely  heavy material reality that immobilises the sufferer , reflecting 
both physical and  mental aspects of the experience.
Examining  late Latin reveals a similarly rich, diverse, and creative set of 
images used to express pain in the seventh to ninth centuries. The data from 
 medieval Spanish, however , show a notable reduction  in complexity and 
diversity in generating pain  metaphors. Most SVCs are  based on the simple 
figurative schema pain is an object , likely reflecting the   more limited range of 
textual genres studied rather than the actual   linguistic reality, in which the 
same  cognitive schemas probably persisted as in Latin three centuries earlier . 
Nevertheless, even with less elaborate examples,  medieval Spanish employs 
the same mechanisms as Latin—violence and immobilisation—to convey the 
 intensity of pain, suggesting the persistence of a generalised cognitive pattern in 
the conceptualisation of this  experience, as noted by Kövecses (2006).

11. Epilogue: A brave new world 
beyond the canon
 Victoria Beatrix Fendel
According to the Oxford English Dictionary (Mcarthur et al. 2018), a canon is a 
general rule, a standard for judgement or authority, or a baseline epoch or era. 
Oxford English Dictionary, s. v. canon (noun)
…
2. Gen[eral]
2a. A law, rule, edict (other than ecclesiastical) [already in Old English]
2b. A general rule, fundamental principle, aphorism, or axiom governing the 
systematic or scientific treatment of a subject; e.g. canons of descent or inheritance; 
a logical, grammatical, or metrical canon; canons of criticism, taste, art, etc. [since 
1588]
2c. A standard of judgement or authority; a test, criterion, means of discrimination 
[since 1601]
…
4. The collection or list of books of the Bible accepted by the  Christian Church 
as genuine and inspired. Also transferred, any set of sacred books; also, those 
writings of a secular author accepted as authentic [since 1382]
…
9a. A chief epoch or era, serving to date from (Greek κανὼν χρονικός); a basis for 
chronology [since 1833]
The existence of such a canon—here, a canon of texts—presupposes a wider body 
of witnesses, in our case textual ones, that fall outside of the canon because they 
do not conform to its governing rule(s) (see 2b), its standard(s) of judgement and 
authority (see 2c), or its temporal limits in the sense of a chief epoch or era (see 9a) 
(see especially Chapter 4, which questions the concept of a classical period, and 
Chapter 8 which calls the canon of the  New Testament “artificial”). Throughout 
this volume, we have focussed on enhancing the  visibility of non-canonical

datasets, both physical and virtual ones, by showcasing methodologies to do 
so (see especially Part I), on promoting the interoperability of methodological 
approaches, through transparent definitions and guidelines (see especially Part 
II), and on furthering the replicability of analyses, through empirically founded 
approaches with interoperable datasets(see especially Part III). 
 Verbal multi-word expressions are not a type of structure that is limited 
to any one register , genre, dialect, sociolect, or idiolect in any of the language 
varieties assessed here (unlike Marušić 2018 for German). Nor do all verbal 
multi-verb expressions qualify as “idioms” or “phrases” as often assumed for 
corpus languages (see further Fendel 2024). They are, in fact, everywhere, 
a natural part of the lexicon and the grammar . We have observed them 
throughout this volume in funerary inscriptions from Old Kingdom pyramids 
(Chapter 2 ),  philosophical  papyri from the Herculanean school ( Chapter 3 ), 
medical treatises associated with the doctors Hippocrates and Galen (Chapter 4), 
Byzantine saints’ lives (Chapter 6), biblical texts of the Old and New Testaments 
and their translation into various languages (Chapters 8 and 9), the writings 
of  Coptic abbots (especially Shenoute of Atripe, in the  Coptic Scriptorium and 
Leipoldt (1913) (Chapter 7), and Latin/Romance verse literature across centuries 
(Chapter 10). 
Corpora that are less visible for reasons of materiality (for example, 
carbonised  papyrus scrolls (Figure 11.1), inscriptions battered by wind and rain, 
e.g. ISic000136 = CIL X.7379, 1 or papyri exposed to oxygen and a range of little 
animals),2 subject matter (for example, medical procedures and anatomical 
observations), research tradition (for example, the disciplinary affiliation of 
biblical texts and Byzantine saints’ lives), etc. have much to offer .

11. Epilogue  285
They compare and contrast with our canonical texts, thus shining a new light 
on both. They can be assessed and made more visible by means of the tools 
shown in this volume, including  Maque-IT (see D’Angelo and Nicolardi 2024), 
the building of  Sketch Engine corpora, and treebanking. We hope that by making 
all datasets and codebases openly accessible, we can inspire further research 
into the corpora presented here. By making our definitions, frameworks, and 
methodological processes transparent, we hope to contribute to this further . A 
further step to take in order to ensure replicability and transparent reporting of 
all results would be pre-registration of datasets (for example, Hervais-Adelman 
et al. 2025: 311; Santiago et al. 2025: 342–343). A further step in order to ensure 
the lasting impact and interconnectedness of datasets would be to support 
further linked open data (for example, Prag and Chartrand 2019; Depauw 2019).
Several types of  verbal multi-word expressions are comparative concepts 
(Haspelmath 2010) that are realised in language-specific ways. Consider for 
instance  Coptic  light-verb constructions that create statives (for example, ⲕⲁ-
ⲣⲱ= ka-rô= “to keep silence” and ⲕⲁⲣⲁⲉⲓⲧ karaeit ) ( Chapter 7 ), post-classical 
Greek ones that pragmaticalise into discourse markers (for example, ποίησον 
ἀγάπην poiēson agapēn “please”) (Chapter 6), or verb- particle constructions and 
their relationship to Greek  preverbation (for example, ἀπό-βαίνω apo-bainō 
“to go away”) ( Chapter 5). While the chapters of this volume are focussed on 
Indo-European and Afro-Asiatic languages, there are many corpus languages 
other than those treated in this volume which would proffer fertile ground for 
future work (cf. Fleischman 2000). We hope to have inspired those working on 
less well-resourced languages in general to consider multi-word expressions, 
such that comparative concepts can be refined and descriptive categories can 
be polished.
For Greek, Latin/Romance, and Egyptian, we have observed considerable 
variability, diversity, and development across time periods. In fact,  verbal multi-
word expressions, and the micro-variations in their lexicon and morphosyntax 
in particular , can often provide us with “sociocultural, economic, and 
geographical coordinates in time and space” (Tagliamonte 2025: 3), almost like 
a compass. This volume has focussed on the stages of data, methodology, and 
analysis specifically, yet we hope the compass we have created will now guide 
us towards the interpretation stage, that is, the domain of logical reasoning, the 
famous “why” question, and the critical assessment of multiple perspectives 
and avenues.
